• WHAT THE ADULTS DO NOT DO is come in here. Forge knocks. Bose has never been past the door. This is the students' building and the campaign should protect that, so that the moment in Chapter 4 when a teacher does come in lands like a break in the weather.
sections.developments:
• IF YOUR TABLE LOVES DOWNTIME — let it run and give it a whole session. It will pay for itself twice over in Chapter 4 and there is nothing in Chapter 2 that is in a hurry.
• IF YOUR TABLE FINDS DORM SCENES SLOW — do not run them as scenes at all. Open each session with sixty seconds of dorm and then go to the bracket. The effect is cumulative and works fine in one-minute doses.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO START SOMETHING WITH A CLASSMATE — a rivalry, a friendship, a grudge about the chart — say yes immediately and write the classmate's name on your sheet. That NPC is now load-bearing and you have been handed free material for four chapters.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS ABOUT THE GROUND-FLOOR DOOR — the honest answer is that it is Hiro's room, and there is nothing strange about a student having a room. Give it flatly and do not add anything. It is not a clue yet and pressing on it now will only teach the table that the door is interesting, which is exactly the wrong lesson.
• IF THE CLASS FRAGMENTS INTO CLIQUES — good, and let it. Forge's pairs cut straight across every friendship group in the building, which is the entire reason she did it, and the friction is worth playing.
sections.treasure:
Nothing material, and the most valuable section in Chapter 2.

What the players leave with is nineteen classmates they can name without checking. Track which NPCs each PC has actually spoken to; you will want that list in Chapter 4, and the campaign gets significantly crueller if you use it.
sections.dmNote:
A frame, not a session. Chapter 2's job is to make the class legible and likeable, and the bracket alone will not do it — a bracket makes them competitors. The sofa makes them housemates.

The register here is completely straight. No irony, no winking, no foreshadowing. Teenagers arguing about milk in a kitchen is not a break from the campaign; in Chapter 4 it becomes the campaign, and the DM note for that chapter asks you to play the identical argument in the session after somebody dies. You cannot make that land if you have not made it ordinary first.

Hiro's ground-floor door is planted here and never mentioned again in Chapter 2. Do not weight it. Do not describe it twice. It is a door in a corridor, and its whole job is that a player might, four sessions from now, remember it on their own.

aside.label: The fridge chart, week by week
aside.body:
Masahata prints it before the draw and it stays on that fridge for the whole campaign. Update it out loud between sessions; it is thirty seconds and it is the best barometer the class has.

Week one — pristine, laminated, Masahata winning.
Week two — annotated in biro by Ichitaka, accurately and without mercy.
Week three — somebody has drawn on it.
After the festival — amended in red, and Masahata has written BROADLY CORRECT across the top.
Chapter 4 — it comes down. Nobody admits to taking it down and nobody asks for it back.
Chapter 5 — it goes back up over the weekend. Nobody says who.

sections.treasure:
Winning pairs get nothing material — this is a school exercise and the prize is the bracket itself. What they get is standing.

Track it: any pair that reaches the semi-finals is publicly one of the best in the class, which matters at the Sports Festival, and which the class will feel very differently about in Chapter 4.
sections.tag: The bracket, first rounds · 1–2 sessions · full contact
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Battle Centre III is a city block that has never had anyone living in it. Four storeys, rebar showing where Forge has rebuilt it too many times, and a scoreboard bolted to the shell of what would be a bank.

Forge is in the booth with a microphone and a second lunch. Bose is on the floor in a tracksuit, shouting at people who have not done anything yet.

"PAIRS," Bose informs the entire building, at a volume that makes the scoreboard buzz. "YOU FIGHT AS PAIRS. IF I SEE ONE OF YOU FIGHTING AS ONE I WILL COME DOWN THERE."

▶ AT THE START OF EACH MATCH

The klaxon is louder than it needs to be and there is a full three seconds of nothing after it, which is somehow the worst part.

Then the scoreboard flicks over, and the block is yours, and somewhere in it are two people who have been planning for you all week.

▶ THE FIRST TIME A PAIR COMBINES PROPERLY

For a second it doesn't look like two people fighting. It looks like one thing with four hands.

From the booth, Forge stops chewing.

▶ WHEN A MATCH ENDS

Bose is on the floor before the klaxon finishes. He tells the losers exactly what they did wrong, at length, at volume, and with total accuracy, and then he tells the winners the same thing.

aside.label: Bose's ammunition
aside.body: Someone will ask why the drill sergeant with a rifle in his arm never uses it in training. The answer is that every shot costs him an inch of hair, he has a hundred inches, and it regrows at an inch an hour. He will explain this at length and with visible pride in his ponytail.

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Bose at volume → narrate the two play-ins → play the quarter-finals with a PC in them, in full → Bose comes down there → Forge stops chewing, once → out on the scoreboard.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one play-in narrated in thirty seconds, then the single quarter-final your PCs are in. Everything else is a line on the board.

• Run the play-in matches fast and narrate them, then play out the quarter-finals the players' characters are in. Full contact, non-lethal, medical on standby, real stakes for pride only.
• REN + KAZAMA vs TAZATO + ANDO — the match where they discover the bounce. Kazama's hardened skin is mirror-bright rather than the dull grey most Steel users show, and a Laser Beam that hits him at the right angle goes somewhere else. Neither of them planned this. Let a player find it mid-fight and give them the win for it. Tazato's dragon form makes the arena feel small; Ando talks the entire time and is more frightened than he sounds.
• KINJI + KIBI vs YOSHIBARA + NOMI — four bodies and every loose object in the block against a vine user and a girl with no quirk. Kibi's vines only reach what she can anchor to, so she spends the match building cover across the floor while Kinji closes distance on foot. Kinji should win this fight with a technique, not a trick, and the arena should go slightly quiet when she does.
• CHOZEN + TORAGI vs the play-in winner — both of them get better the longer they last and both are nearly useless in round one. Their entire strategy is survive the first ninety seconds, which Chozen has written down, laminated, and given to Toragi, who has read it and said nothing.
• IZUTO + ISOKONO vs the play-in winner — Izuto tries to carry it and burns his juice down doing it. Isokono's tail is the only reason they are still standing at the end. He knows this. He does not say it. Let the table notice that he does not say it.
• Bose comes down there at least twice.
• Rawagi Chiso is meant to be officiating and is not present. Forge covers for him without comment.
• RAKUKA + HIRO vs MASAHATA + ICHITAKA is the play-in worth narrating rather than skipping, because it is the one Masahata loses. He has himself winning the tournament on a laminated chart and he goes out to a theatrical flyer and a boy nobody can describe, and Ichitaka says nothing at all on the walk off, which is worse.
• CLUE TWO — Hiro takes a bad hit in that match. A real one, the kind that gets a wince out of the stands. He does not react at all, does not check it, and gets up. Nobody calls medical over. Everybody in the stands puts it down to the Doll quirk, which is exactly what it looks like and is not what it is.
• THE FLOOR IS A CHARACTER. Battle Centre III is a city block Forge has rebuilt so many times the rebar shows through in places, and she will tell anybody who asks which repairs are hers and roughly what they cost her in rice. Second-storey windows are glassless. The bank shell has a vault door that does not open and that four separate pairs will try to hide behind.
sections.dmNote:
Competence and comedy, played straight. This is the last chapter where a fight is purely a game, so let the table enjoy winning without cost.

Mechanically, 2v2 is a different animal to a party fight and you should lean into it — smaller initiative order, faster rounds, and every action a player takes visibly affecting exactly one ally. Reward genuine combination play with advantage rather than inventing new rules.

Rawagi's absence is the only plot in the session and should get one line of screen time, maximum. He is a strict teacher who believes he has to be, and a strict teacher who has stopped showing up is information the players will file and forget, which is the intention.
sections.developments:
• IF A PAIR SPLITS UP AND FIGHTS SOLO — this is the mistake the whole chapter exists to correct, so let it fail. They lose, Bose comes down there, and nobody is hurt. Do not lecture the player; let Bose do it and let it be funny.
• IF A PLAYER INVENTS A COMBO YOU DIDN'T PLAN FOR — say yes. Give it advantage on the roll and describe it working. Rewarding invention in the first fight sets the tone for sixteen sessions, and this is a training exercise where nothing can go permanently wrong.
• IF THE PCs LOSE EARLY — good, and genuinely fine. Losing pairs spend the rest of the bracket in the stands watching everyone else's mechanics, which is exactly what the antagonist is doing, and the parallel is free. Do not fudge dice to keep them in.
• IF A FIGHT DRAGS PAST FORTY MINUTES — end it. Have Forge call the match on points and move on. Nothing in this bracket is worth a slow hour, and a beginner DM should feel actively permitted to cut a fight short.
• IF SOMEONE ASKS ABOUT RAWAGI'S ABSENCE — Forge shrugs and says he is busy. She does not know more than that. There is nothing to find here yet, and that is not a trick.
sections.heading: Battle Centre III
Nobara Forge

aside.label: What Creation actually costs her
aside.body:
One pound of object per pound of food, minimum half a pound per item, and she has to understand the atomic structure of the thing before she can make it. That is the whole economy and it is worth making concrete at the table, once.

Ten pounds a day is not a joke about appetite. It is a professional requirement, it is expensive, and U.A. pays for it as a line item. She eats during lessons because she has to, is completely unembarrassed about it, and gets genuinely irritated with anyone who treats it as a bit.

Her Sweat Conversion Points build as she works — five per level, and then a rank of Queasy. Students who spend real downtime in the lab will watch her hit that ceiling and keep going, and one of them should eventually tell her to stop. She won't.

sections.treasure:
Each pair gets ONE piece of equipment built for two people. Keep it simple and mechanical — a shared anchor line, an angled bracer that redirects a beam, a reservoir one of them carries for the other, a paired comms set.

Write it on both character sheets, not one. The whole point is that neither of them owns it.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The support lab smells like a canteen. There are eleven half-finished sets of paired equipment on the benches, a fridge that is entirely full, and a whiteboard covered in what appear to be calorie sums.

Forge is sitting on a bench with her legs swinging, a bowl in her lap, looking at a diagram of Kazama's forearm.

"So the problem," she says, "is that your partner's a mirror and nobody built you to be aimed."

▶ WHEN SHE MAKES SOMETHING

She puts the bowl down, holds out her hand, and there is a pause of about four seconds where nothing at all happens and she looks slightly constipated.

Then there is an object in her palm, and it is warm, and it is exactly the thing you asked for.

She picks the bowl back up.

▶ IF SHE OVERDOES IT

She goes grey around the mouth, sits down harder than she meant to, and waves you off before you've finished asking.

"Fine. Fine. It's just sugar. Pass me that."

▶ THE FALSEWORK LINE — drop this into the middle of another conversation

"— which is what Falsework used to say, actually. Construction bloke, came and talked to my second-years about load paths. Nice man." She frowns at a bracket. "He's not answered an email since April. Rude."

▶ THE THING ON THE BENCH — say it once, in passing, and do not look at it again

There is a forearm on the bench next to your elbow. Not a gauntlet. A forearm, palm up, unattached, with the wrist finished and the fingers not.

You have been in this room four times and there is always something like this on the bench, because this is the support lab and about a third of what she builds in here is a piece of somebody.

Forge picks it up, looks along it the way you'd sight down a plank, puts it back, and carries on telling you about load paths.
sections.developments:
• IF PLAYERS ASK FOR SOMETHING COMPLICATED — Forge rolls a Technology or Intelligence check against a DC you set by how exotic it is. On a failure she still spends the calories and produces something unstable: halved range, damage dice one step down, advantage on saves against its effects. She shrugs it off and offers to try again tomorrow.
• IF PLAYERS ASK FOR SOMETHING ABSURD — she says the honest thing, which is that she has to understand its atomic structure to build it. She cannot make you a working phone. She can make you a very good crowbar in four seconds.
• IF A PLAYER CHASES THE FALSEWORK LINE — Forge shrugs and says he's probably busy. That is the entire truth as far as she knows it. Do not reward the follow-up with a clue; the line is there so the players remember it in Chapter 4, not so they solve anything now.
• IF NOBODY REACTS TO THE FALSEWORK LINE — perfect. That is the expected outcome and it costs you nothing.
• IF A PLAYER PUSHES BACK ON HER QUESTION TO IZUTO — she drops it immediately and changes the subject. She asks once. That is how every adult in this campaign handles these kids, and it is worth establishing early.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the lab smells like a canteen → each pair brings her an idea → she builds one thing per pair, warm, in four seconds → the Falsework line, thrown away mid-sentence → she overdoes it once and waves it off → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — go round the pairs, one item each, and drop the Falsework line on whoever is standing closest. Skip the Technology checks and just give them the gear.

• Forge is the class's gear pipeline and the chapter's warmest presence. Creation runs on food — one pound of object per pound eaten, a minimum of half a pound per item, and she must understand the atomic structure of anything she makes. Complex items need a Technology or Intelligence check against a complexity DC, and a failure produces something unstable that still costs the calories.
• She will build for any pair that brings her an idea. Ren and Kazama get an angled bracer. Chozen gets a genuinely excellent binder cover and is delighted out of all proportion. Izuto asks for a fluid reservoir and she asks him, mildly, why he wants to carry more instead of asking someone to hand it to him, and then drops it.
• Her Sweat Conversion Points build as she works — five per level and she gains a rank of Queasy. Students who spend enough downtime in the lab will see her hit that ceiling and keep going.
• Use this section as the recurring downtime frame for the whole campaign. Between chapters, each PC can spend a downtime slot in the lab, the gym, the dorm, or the infirmary. Track it.
• Somewhere in this scene, Forge mentions offhand that a pro called Falsework used to come and talk to her students about construction quirks and hasn't answered his email since spring.
• CLUE THREE — a spare forearm on the bench, unattached, wrist finished and fingers not. Nobody asks what it is for, because a third of what Forge builds in this room is a piece of somebody and the class has been walking past prosthetics and support rigs all term. If a player does ask, she says "spare," and it is the truth and it is the whole answer.
• WHAT CREATION FEELS LIKE FROM THE OUTSIDE. Four seconds of nothing while she looks slightly unwell, and then a warm object. The warmth is the detail players remember — it comes out of her at body heat and cools in your hands over about a minute. Say so once and they will bring it up for four chapters.
• SHE ASKS EVERY PAIR THE SAME QUESTION and it is not about gear: "what does he do that you can't?" Most of them answer about quirks. She is asking about reach, footing and where they stand, and she will keep asking until she gets that answer or gets bored.
sections.dmNote:
Forge exists to make the class feel invested in and to make the equipment part of the story rather than a shopping list. Play her as competent, hungry and slightly too honest.

The Falsework line is the campaign's first real thread and it should be delivered with no weight at all — a teacher complaining about an unanswered email. Nothing more. If a player follows up, she shrugs and says he's probably busy.

The Izuto question is the most important line in the section. She asks it once, gets nothing, and never raises it again. That is how the adults in this campaign handle the students: one honest question, then space.

sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER STOPS AND LISTENS — do not give them more. The report ends, the channel changes, and that is all. Resist the instinct to reward attention with a clue; the horror of this campaign is specifically that the information was public and nobody's business.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS TO RESEARCH CASE 9 — everything in the public record is in the Appendix's victim list, minus the festival connection. It is thin, it is real, and it goes nowhere. Give it to them freely and let it be a dead end.
• IF A PLAYER TRIES TO ROLL TO NOTICE A PATTERN — there is no check here. Tell them so, kindly, out of character if you like. Nothing is hidden and no roll will produce anything.
• IF YOUR TABLE LATCHES ON HARD ANYWAY — that is fine and does not break anything. The campaign does not depend on them being ignorant; it depends on them being unable to act, which is still true. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene earlier if they are impatient.
sections.tag: Slow burn · background plot · woven through sessions
sections.dmNote:
This is a deliberate anti-hook. Class 1-A are fifteen-year-olds in the best week of their lives and a serial killer on the news is not their business — the campaign only works if the table experiences that indifference honestly first and remembers it later.

Do not let a player roll to notice a pattern. There is no check here. The information is plain, public, and repeated, and the reason nobody acts on it is that nobody in this dorm has any reason to.

In Chapter 4, when the class rewatches their own festival footage, cut back to this room.

aside.label: Why there is no roll here
aside.body:
A player will ask to roll something. Investigation, Insight, History, anything. There is no check, and the kindest thing you can do is say so out of character in one sentence: "there's nothing hidden here, it's just the news."

The instinct behind the request is good and you should not punish it. The reason the answer is no is that this campaign's horror is not that information was concealed. It is that the information was public, repeated, free, and nobody's business. A dice roll would turn a fact about the world into a secret the players failed to find, and that is the opposite of what this scene is doing.

Six sessions later, in a silent common room with the archive open, the players will remember that they heard all of this and changed the channel. That memory is the entire point and it only exists if you let them change the channel.

sections.readAloud:
▶ USE ONE OF THESE PER SESSION — read it flatly, mid-conversation, and do not pause afterwards

"— identified as Tsuzuri Hane, the professional hero Falsework, whose body was recovered from an Adachi car park in April. Police have not released—"

"— the fourth such case this year. The Commission has declined to confirm whether the incidents are connected—"

"— a Commission spokesperson described the profile as 'consistent with a single individual targeting high-classification quirk users'—"

"— the file number, Case 9, was leaked to press earlier this month. One tabloid has run the name Appetite across—"

"— confirming that all five victims held Rare classification or above, and that in each case the injuries were confined to the head—"

▶ IMMEDIATELY AFTERWARDS, EVERY TIME

Somebody changes the channel. Or Masahata starts an argument about the fridge chart. Or Rakuka does something theatrical and loud.

The room is louder than the television. It always is.
sections.heading: The Common Room Ticker
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — one line, mid-conversation, flat → do not pause → somebody changes the channel → carry on with whatever the scene actually was.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — this costs you fifteen seconds and is never the reason a session overruns. It is the one thing in Chapter 2 you should never cut, because it costs nothing.

Drop these across the chapter, one per session, always mid-conversation and never as the focus of a scene. Read the line, do not pause, and move on.

• "—identified as Tsuzuri Hane, the professional hero Falsework, whose body was recovered from an Adachi car park in April. Police have not released—"
• "—the fourth such case this year. The Commission has declined to confirm whether the incidents are connected—"
• "—a Commission spokesperson described the profile as 'consistent with a single individual targeting high-classification quirk users'—"
• "—the file number, Case 9, was leaked to press earlier this month. One tabloid has run the name Appetite across—"
• "—confirming that all five victims held Rare classification or above, and that in each case the injuries were confined to the head—"

If a player stops and listens, do not reward them with more. Somebody else changes the channel, or Masahata starts an argument about the fridge chart, or Rakuka does something theatrical. The information is available and the room is louder than it is.

aside.label: If a PC pair loses early
aside.body: Better, honestly. A pair that goes out in the quarter-finals spends the rest of the chapter in the stands learning everyone else's mechanics, which is exactly what the antagonist is doing, and in Chapter 4 that parallel is available for free.

sections.heading: Semis and the Final
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The scoreboard has four names left on it and the whole class is in the stands, which is somehow worse than the whole country would be.

Forge has stopped eating. This is the first time anyone has seen it.

Bose is quiet too, which is significantly more alarming.

▶ IF FORGE COMMENTATES ON KINJI HAMAKIDA

"— and watch what she does with the gap. No quirk. None. She's reading his reset and stepping inside it, and she's been doing that all afternoon."

It is admiring. It is completely accurate. It is the first time anyone has said it out loud, in public, in front of everybody.

▶ FORGE'S CLOSING REMARK — read this whatever the result

"Right. Well done. That was better than last year and most of you know why."

She picks the bento back up.

"None of you were the best fighter in here today. Two of you were the best pair. That's the only thing I was measuring."

▶ THE PHOTOGRAPH — take your time, because you are going to need this twice more

Somebody from the school office has a real camera and makes everybody get on the steps, and it takes four minutes, because it always takes four minutes.

Bose is on the end with his arms folded and is the only person facing straight forward. Masahata has got himself into the middle. Toragi is at the back and has been asked twice to stop crouching. Ando has his sunglasses on. Aikawa has both hands up. Somebody's eyes are shut and it is not clear whose until later.

Forge holds the bento out of shot, which is the only concession she makes to a camera all year.

It goes up in the corridor outside the 1-A room on the Monday, in a frame, at the wrong height.
sections.developments:
• IF NO PC PAIR REACHES THE FINAL — give the emotional climax to whichever PC match went deepest, and hand the final to two NPC pairs the class enjoy. Yoshibara and Nomi winning the whole thing is a great outcome and Nomi will be mortified about it.
• IF A PC PAIR WINS — let them have it completely. Trophy, photograph, the fridge chart amended in red. Do not undercut the victory with a sting; the campaign needs this to be a real, uncomplicated good day.
• IF PLAYERS GO AFTER CARLOS MIGHT — he is already gone. Not mysteriously; they just turn around and he has left. If they persist, someone mentions he does that.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS KINJI ABOUT HIM — she says he offered to train her and she said yes. That is true, complete, and tells them nothing. She will not elaborate and is not being evasive; nobody has ever asked her a second question.
sections.treasure:
A trophy that lives in the 1-A classroom for the rest of the campaign, and a photograph that goes up in the corridor.

Both are props. Refer to the photograph in Chapter 4 and again in Chapter 5. It has everybody in it.
sections.dmNote:
Give this session a genuine ending — a trophy, a photograph, an argument about the fridge chart. The class should finish Chapter 2 closer than they started and pleased with themselves, and the campaign needs that to be real rather than ironic.

Carlos Might's appearance is worth exactly one sentence. He does not speak to anyone and does not stay. If a player goes after him he is already gone, and Kinji, who has been training with him privately for two months, says nothing about it because nobody asks her.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — four names left on the board → semi one → semi two → Forge stops eating → the final → Carlos Might is in the stands, and then is not → the closing remark → trophy, photograph, fridge chart amended in red.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — narrate both semis to their last thirty seconds, play the final, and give Forge her four sentences. The photograph is the part you cannot skip.

• Play the two semi-finals and the final. Whoever the players are, the final should contain at least one PC pair — if the dice have gone otherwise, let a semi-final be the emotional climax instead and give the final to two NPC pairs the class care about.
• The intended shape: Ren and Kazama reach the final having refined the bounce into something genuinely dangerous, and meet either Kinji and Kibi or Chozen and Toragi. All three of those matches are good and none of them need a twist.
• If Chozen and Toragi get here, they get here at almost no hit points, which is the entire point of both quirks, and Chozen is at full Stress and enjoying himself in a way that visibly unsettles his classmates.
• If Kinji and Kibi get here, the commentary problem arrives early: Forge, on the microphone, explains to a room of forty teenagers exactly how Kinji compensates for having no quirk. It is admiring. It is accurate. It is the first time it has been said out loud in public. File it.
• Whoever wins, Forge's closing remark to the class is four sentences and the last one is: "None of you were the best fighter in here today. Two of you were the best pair. That's the only thing I was measuring."
• Carlos Might is in the stands for the final. Nobody saw him arrive. He is eating something. He leaves before the end.
• THE PHOTOGRAPH IS A PROP AND YOU WILL USE IT TWICE MORE — once in Chapter 4, on the table, after roll call, and once in Chapter 5. Describe it properly now, with four or five students named and doing something specific. It has everybody in it. Hiro is at the end of the back row, slightly out of the group, and is the only person in the photograph who is perfectly in focus.
• THE STANDS ARE THE WHOLE CLASS and the class is loud. Eliminated pairs have spent an afternoon developing opinions and will share them. Masahata provides unsolicited live analysis from the second row. Nomi Igisa, who is terrified of attention, is the one who started the chant.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING — slow the pace right down here

The open day is a nothing event — parents, prospective students, a stall selling U.A. merchandise at a markup, and Class 1-A in uniform being polite for four hours.

The man at the west gate is tall and thin and has a scar that runs from his forehead to his chin, straight down, through where a nose ought to be and isn't. He is standing outside the perimeter, on the public side, doing nothing that anyone could ask him to stop doing.

When a student passes close enough, he says, conversationally: "Can I ask you something?"

▶ THE QUESTION — say it to the table, out loud, and then wait

"A man is found dead in a locked room. There are forty-eight puddles of water on the floor and nothing else. No weapon, no marks, no way in or out."

He smiles, and it is not unpleasant, which is the problem.

"How did he die?"

▶ THE MOMENT SOMEONE ANSWERS

They get about two words out.

Then they stop, mid-syllable, and their eyes stay open, and they go down on the paving like a coat sliding off a chair. They are breathing. They are warm. There is nobody in there.

Somewhere behind you a parent starts screaming.

▶ HE BLEEDS

A thin line of blood comes out of the corner of his mouth and runs down his chin, and he does not wipe it away, and he does not stop watching you.

He is not looking at the student on the ground. He is looking at which of you moved first.

▶ WHEN HE LEAVES

He does not run. He turns and walks, at the speed of a man who is not late for anything, and he is on the other side of the road and gone before anybody with the authority to stop him arrives.

▶ THE OPEN DAY, BEFORE ANY OF IT — spend a real minute here, because the contrast is the scene

Trestle tables. A banner that has been zip-tied on slightly crooked and that three separate members of staff have decided is not their problem. A queue for the merchandise stall that has not moved in twenty minutes.

Prospective students in their middle-school uniforms, thirteen years old and trying to look like people who belong here. Their parents asking you questions you do not know the answers to. Somebody's little brother has been sick behind the sports hall.

Bose has been on the west gate since seven in the morning and is directing pedestrian traffic with the intensity of a man landing aircraft.

It is a nothing day. Remember that it was a nothing day.

▶ AFTERWARDS, IN THE HALL — read this and then end the session

Nobody sends the visitors home, because there is no procedure for it and because the thing that happened does not have a name yet. The open day carries on for another forty minutes around a taped-off square of paving.

The student wakes up in Help Woman's office inside the hour and is completely, unremarkably fine, and asks what everyone is staring at.

Out at the west gate a member of the ground staff is already washing the paving, and doing it properly, and getting it all.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — four hours of a nothing open day → the man on the public side of the west gate → the question, asked to the table, and then silence → somebody answers and goes down → the class cannot legally act → Sugitsu in ninety seconds → he lets him go → Rawagi, four minutes late, already knowing.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — do not cut this one. Cut the open day instead — start at the gate, ask the question, and run it from there.

• This is Riddle. He does not enter the campus, does not threaten anybody, and does not touch anyone. He is inside his rights the entire time and he knows exactly where the line is.
• Question One targets one creature within 40 feet who can hear him. Anyone who attempts an answer becomes braindead for five rounds, or until they succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence check. Answering correctly ends it and instantly reveals his location to the answerer. He can only work one target at a time and the question cannot be unanswerable.
• Give him a real question — something mild, almost pleasant, that a polite student would answer without thinking. The horror is entirely in how ordinary the opening is.
• Whoever answers goes down where they stand, eyes open, breathing, gone. Five rounds is a long time in a crowd of parents.
• He bleeds from the mouth afterwards and does not wipe it. He watches the class react. He is not measuring their strength; he is measuring which of them moves first, and toward whom.
• The class cannot legally engage — provisional students, public ground, a man committing no visible offence. Play that constraint honestly and let it be intolerable.
• Sugitsu Jarvichi arrives inside ninety seconds because he scans the campus perimeter as a matter of routine, and Riddle is already walking. Sugitsu does not pursue. He gets between the man and the students and lets him go, and then has to explain that decision to twenty furious teenagers.
• Rawagi Chiso arrives four minutes later, out of breath, and is the only adult present who is not surprised.
• THE OPEN DAY SHOULD BE BORING ON PURPOSE. Give it four minutes of trestle tables, crooked banners, thirteen-year-olds in middle-school uniform, and Class 1-A being polite at strangers for four hours. The scene does not work if the players walk in braced.
• WHAT HE LOOKS LIKE, IN THIS ORDER — tall, thin, white hair. Then the scar: forehead to chin, straight down, through where a nose ought to be and is not. Then that he is standing entirely still on the public pavement, doing nothing anyone could ask him to stop doing. Give them the details one at a time and let the table assemble him.
• HE IS POLITE THROUGHOUT. He says please. He waits to be looked at before he speaks. When the parent starts screaming he glances over, mildly, the way you would at a car alarm, and then goes back to watching which of the students moved first.
• THE PACE IS THE ENCOUNTER. Slow everything down. Ask individual players what their character is doing while the classmate is on the paving. Let a real silence happen before Sugitsu arrives; ninety seconds is a long time and you should let some of it be felt.
sections.dmNote:
The chapter's turn, and it should be sharp. Six sessions of school and competition, and then a man at a gate asks a polite question and a classmate drops.

Do not let this become a fight. If the players force one, Riddle asks a second question of whoever closes first and leaves during the confusion — he is not a combat encounter and losing to him physically would misrepresent what he is.

Sugitsu's non-pursuit is the important beat. He is right: he cannot leave the campus undefended to chase one man, and his quirk means he can follow Riddle across five miles without moving. He is also, visibly, furious about being right. This is the first crack in 'the safest school in Japan' and it is a hairline one.

End the chapter on Rawagi Chiso, who has arrived too late, looking at where the man was standing, and saying — to himself, not to the students — "He's never done one at a school."
sections.developments:
• IF THE PLAYERS ATTACK HIM — they are provisional students, on public ground, attacking a man who has committed no visible offence, in front of prospective parents. Let them do it if they insist. He asks a second question of whoever closes first, takes whatever damage lands without commenting on it, and leaves during the confusion. He is not a combat encounter and cannot be beaten into anything useful.
• IF THE PLAYERS DO NOTHING — entirely correct, and they will hate it. Play the constraint honestly. This is the intended outcome.
• IF A PLAYER ANSWERS THE RIDDLE CORRECTLY — the effect ends instantly and they know exactly where he is standing. Give them that. It is a real reward for a real answer, and it still does not help, because knowing where he is and being allowed to touch him are different problems. (The answer, if you need it: the puddles were ice.)
• IF A PC IS THE ONE WHO ANSWERS — allowed, but it is better on an NPC classmate. If a player insists on answering, let them, and give the five rounds to the player rather than skipping past them: ask them to sit out and watch, and let the table feel the length of it.
• IF THE PLAYERS DEMAND SUGITSU CHASE HIM — he refuses and explains why in one sentence: he cannot leave four hundred students undefended to chase one man, and he does not need to move to follow him. He is right. He is also visibly furious about being right.
sections.treasure:
No reward. This is the first section in the campaign that gives the players nothing at all, and that is deliberate.

What they leave with is a description — tall, thin, white hair, a scar from forehead to chin, no nose, bleeds from the mouth. Write it on an index card for them. It is the only thing they have for two chapters and they will use it in Chapter 4 when Kuma mentions a stain on a carpet.
sections.heading: A Question at the Gate

aside.label: Who gets asked
aside.body: Pick an NPC classmate rather than a PC, and pick one the class likes without thinking about it — Isokono Yoromu, or Nomi Igisa, or Ando Iorai. They recover fully within the hour. The recovery is complete and the campaign never revisits it, which is what makes it frightening rather than tragic.

chapters.intro: The door opens, and Nobara Forge puts twenty names on a board in ten pairs and refuses to explain herself. Chapter 2 is the 2v2 bracket — full contact, Battle Centre III, a scoreboard, and Aditya Bose shouting at people who have not done anything yet. It is a school story and it is meant to be fun: the class learns to fight as twos, twenty students become twenty legible people, and the fridge in Heights Alliance acquires a printed ranking chart that nobody asked for. In the background, on a television nobody is watching, five professional heroes have been found dead with the tops of their skulls removed, and a teacher who is meant to be officiating the bracket keeps not showing up. The chapter ends at a school open day with a polite man on the public side of the gate asking a student a question.
chapters.title: Ten Pairs
chapters.dmNote:
Play this chapter as if it were the whole campaign. No foreshadowing, no ominous music, no rolls to notice a pattern — Class 1-A are fifteen and this is the best week of their lives, and the table needs to feel that unguardedly before anything is taken from it.

The bracket is doing structural work as well as tonal work. Every session your players spend learning how their pair fights is a session invested in the campaign's central mechanic, and the Sports Festival in Chapter 3 runs pairs specifically because this bracket happened. Reward combination play generously here so the habit is set.

The only plot in the chapter is the ticker and Rawagi Chiso's absences, and both should be handled with almost insulting lightness. If a player chases either thread they should find nothing, because there is nothing to find yet — a busy teacher and a news story that has not got anything to do with a school.

The gate scene is the exception and should be played with total control. Slow it down, keep it quiet, and do not roll initiative.

closing.label: Chapter Note — What the class knows
closing.body: A man came to the gate, asked a classmate a question, and put them on the floor for thirty seconds without touching them. He left before anyone could legally stop him. The principal chose not to pursue and will not say why in a way anyone finds satisfying, and the strictest teacher on staff has been missing lessons since April and arrived at the gate already knowing what he was looking at. Nobody in Class 1-A has connected any of that to the news. Why would they? They have a Sports Festival in six weeks.

chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 2 when the bracket reaches the semi-finals — the class has learned to fight as twos and the mechanic the campaign is built on is now habit.
LEVEL 3 at the end of "A Question at the Gate," whatever the players did or failed to do. They earn this one by standing still while a man walked away, which is the only time in this campaign that doing nothing is worth a level.

chapters.title: The Shortlist

closing.body:
Eleven hours of footage. Forty first-years. Every quirk demonstrated repeatedly, under pressure, at range, against varied opposition, with professional commentary explaining the mechanism and the weakness, because good commentary explains the weakness. Free to watch. Searchable by student and by quirk. Archived indefinitely.

Four of the five Case 9 victims are in an archive exactly like it. Rawagi Chiso worked that out on the Tuesday and has told nobody except Inspector Okuma, who has told nobody at all, because the alternative is telling four hundred students that the most important week of their lives was a shop window.
closing.label: Chapter Note — The archive

aside.body: Every class he runs is a quirkless class. He never says why. When somebody eventually asks, in Chapter 5, he says that a quirk is a thing you can be separated from and a body isn't, and then he shouts at them for standing badly.
aside.label: What Bose is actually teaching

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Bose has a whistle → each PC picks two training focuses and you name the benefits out loud → one scene each with three different teachers → Forge fits the final gear → somebody walks in on the training room at the wrong hour → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — go round the table twice: each player names a focus, you name the benefit, write it on the sheet. Twenty minutes, then start Day One in the same sitting.

• Run this as structured downtime with real mechanical payoff. Each PC picks two training focuses over the six weeks; each gives a concrete, named benefit they can use in the festival. Write the benefit on their sheet.
• BOSE (Rifle) — conditioning and marksmanship. Loud, precise, effective. Despite carrying a rifle in his own arm he mostly teaches people to fight without their quirks at all, which he considers obvious and everyone else finds strange. Nobody yet understands why this matters.
• YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — mobility. Her Energy Rings give flight to people who have none, and half the class have never been airborne. She is a genuinely excellent teacher and she will accept credit afterwards for improvements she had nothing to do with, cheerfully, in front of the people who actually did the work.
• FRED ENTOSS (Fridas, Cement) — terrain and cover. Sarcastic throughout, on their side throughout. Teaches the class to read a battlefield as a set of things that can be made to fall over.
• SAKI HIYORI (Creed, Deathly Endurance) — endurance. His lesson is being hit. He gets visibly more muscular and his hair gets spikier as the session goes on, which the class find hilarious for about twenty minutes and then stop finding hilarious.
• SUPER PANDA — maths. He is not involved in festival preparation in any way and continues to teach maths with total commitment while the entire school ignores him. Give him one scene. He is delighted that Nomi Igisa did the reading.
• FORGE — final gear. Every pair leaves the lab with one piece of equipment built for two people, and she runs a Technology check for anything complicated. A failure produces something unstable that still cost her the calories, and she shrugs it off.
• CARLOS MIGHT — in the training room with Kinji Hamakida, at hours when nobody else books it. If a PC walks in on this, he stops immediately, says something warm and evasive, and leaves. Kinji says nothing.
• NAME THE BENEFITS OUT LOUD AND WRITE THEM DOWN. "Bose's Fourth Hour" — once per fight, reroll a failed save against being moved, knocked down or restrained. "Yanami's Rings" — you can spend a bonus action to ignore difficult terrain and fall damage for a round. "Entoss's Reading" — advantage on one check per fight to find cover, footing or a way through a wall. Invent freely and generously; a named benefit is a thing a player will ask for by name in a stadium.
• THE SIX WEEKS SHOULD FEEL LIKE SIX WEEKS. Cut between them — week one everybody is enthusiastic, week three everybody is tired and short with each other, week five Bose stops shouting at one specific student and the class notices and finds it more alarming than the shouting, week six nobody can sleep.
• HIRO'S TRAINING, if a player asks, is with nobody. He books the outdoor track at five in the morning and runs the same route, and Bose has watched him do it twice and has said nothing about it, which for Bose is a form of respect so extreme that nobody else recognises it.
sections.heading: Six Weeks
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Bose has a whistle now. Nobody knows where he got it and everybody wishes he hadn't.

Six weeks to the festival. The gym is open from five in the morning because Bose opens it at five in the morning, and he is already in it, and he is already disappointed in you.

"THE COUNTRY," he explains, at a range of four inches, "IS GOING TO WATCH YOU DO THIS."

▶ WHEN A STUDENT ASKS WHY EVERY DRILL IS QUIRKLESS

"Because that's the training." He does not elaborate. He blows the whistle instead, directly at them, and moves on down the line.

▶ IN SAKI HIYORI'S SESSION

The lesson is being hit. That is the whole lesson.

By the second hour his hair has gone from flat to spiked and there is visibly more of him than there was at nine o'clock, and the class find this hilarious for about twenty minutes and then stop finding it hilarious.

▶ IF A PLAYER WALKS IN ON THE TRAINING ROOM AT AN ODD HOUR

The lights are half off. There are two people in there — a very large man in a sombrero, and Kinji Hamakida, who has no quirk, going through something slowly with her hands.

He stops the moment he sees you. He says something warm and completely evasive. He leaves.

She picks it back up where she left off and does not look over.
sections.treasure:
Two named training benefits per PC, written on the sheet, usable for the rest of the campaign.

Be generous. Most of these benefits are quirk-independent, and in Chapters 4 and 5 they are frequently the only things still working when a fight goes badly.
sections.dmNote:
A pure downtime session, and worth the slot. The festival is three sessions of high-pressure spectacle and the table will play it better having spent an evening choosing what to get good at.

Give every training benefit a name and let players ask for them by name during the festival. Mechanical generosity here costs you nothing and pays off enormously in Chapter 4, when most of these benefits are the only things that still work.

The Carlos Might and Kinji Hamakida thread should be visible and unexplained. Do not have anyone comment on it. If a player asks Kinji directly she says he offered and she said yes, which is true and complete and tells them nothing.
sections.developments:
• PICK TWO TRAINING FOCUSES PER PC and write the benefit on their sheet by name. Keep them small and concrete — advantage on one kind of check, a once-per-fight reroll, +10 movement, the ability to take an action while grappled. Players should be able to ask for them by name during the festival.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO TRAIN WITH A TEACHER NOT LISTED — say yes and invent the benefit on the spot. Every member of staff has something to teach and none of them will refuse a student who asks.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS KINJI DIRECTLY ABOUT CARLOS MIGHT — she says he offered and she said yes. She is not hiding anything. Nobody has ever asked her a follow-up question and she does not volunteer.
• IF A PLAYER FOLLOWS CARLOS MIGHT — he is eating. Wherever they follow him to, he is eating, and he is delighted to see them, and he will not discuss the training room.
• IF YOUR TABLE HATES MONTAGE SESSIONS — compress the whole thing to twenty minutes: everyone names two focuses, you name the benefits, done. Then run Day One of the festival in the same sitting.

aside.label: How to write a commentary line in ten seconds
aside.body:
You are going to need about thirty of these across the chapter and they are the most important prop in the campaign. There is a formula and it is three parts.

ONE — name the thing warmly. "Now, that's Kutsu's Engine—"
TWO — explain the mechanism in plain words, the way a good pundit does. "—those run on fluid, believe it or not."
THREE — name the limit, because that is what real commentary does and it is what makes the line sound authentic. "He'll be drinking between events, and if he runs dry that's the whole quirk gone."

That is it. Warm, accurate, admiring, and it hands a stranger everything they would need.

Deliver them in a different voice from your narration — slightly faster, slightly more pleased. Enjoy them. The players will enjoy them too, which is the trap, because in Chapter 4 you are going to read these exact lines back word for word into a silent room and you will not have to add a thing.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING — this is the biggest moment of these characters' lives so far, so take your time

Forty thousand people. You can hear them through the concrete before you can see them.

The tunnel out to the start line is about eighty metres long and there is a point, roughly two-thirds of the way, where the noise stops being a sound and becomes a physical pressure on your chest.

Above the gate, on a screen the size of a house, is your face. All of your faces. With your quirks written underneath.

▶ THE START

There is no countdown. There is a horn, and forty first-years go through a gate built for about six.

▶ THE COMMENTARY — deliver these in a different, warmer voice, and always explain the limit as well as the trick

"Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his stance, he's rationing. That quirk costs him. Every shot is stamina he doesn't get back."

"Kutsu's engines run on fluid, believe it or not — he'll be drinking between events, and if he runs dry that's the whole quirk gone."

▶ CROSSING THE LINE

Your name goes up on the house-sized screen with a number next to it, and forty thousand people make a noise about it, and for a second you cannot hear yourself think and would not want to.

▶ THE ONE LINE THE BOOTH GIVES HIRO — say it once, all week, and never correct it

"—and that's Hiro, also of 1-A. Reinforced physiology of some sort, I'm told. Not one for the highlights reel, this, but he's still on his feet, which is more than I can say for a dozen of them."

Then the camera cuts away to something more interesting, and so does the commentary, and so does everybody.
sections.heading: Day One — The Obstacle Course
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the tunnel and the noise → the horn, no countdown → the bottleneck → Forge's shifting field → the forty-metre drop → the line, and your name on a screen the size of a house.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — three obstacles and a finish line. Do not roll out four kilometres — and do not cut the commentary, which is the only part of this session that matters later.

• Four kilometres, open campus, all forty first-years, top twenty-four advance. Run it as a skill challenge with three or four set-piece obstacles rather than a full initiative track — the point is spectacle and character, not attrition.
• THE BOTTLENECK — the whole field through one gate. Izuto Kutsu is faster than everyone here and should get to be, once, unambiguously. Domoto Fumiju of 1-B is right behind him and delighted about it.
• FORGE'S FIELD — a kilometre of created terrain that shifts. She built it and she is narrating it and she is enjoying herself enormously.
• THE DROP — a forty-metre gap. Fliers cross it. Everyone else negotiates, and forty thousand people find out which of them is willing to jump.
• THE COMMENTARY — this is the mechanically important part of the session and it is not a mechanic. Every time a student does something notable, the booth explains how it works. Write two lines. Be helpful. Be accurate. Explain the limits, because good commentary explains the limits.
• Suggested booth lines to model the register: "Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his stance, he's rationing. That quirk costs him. Every shot is stamina he doesn't get back." And: "Kutsu's engines run on fluid, believe it or not — he'll be drinking between events, and if he runs dry that's the whole quirk gone."
• Sugitsu Jarvichi is running surveillance over the entire venue. He tells staff, twice, that the perimeter is clean. Both times he is telling the truth.
• CLUE FOUR — that booth line is the only sentence anyone says about Hiro on national television all week, and it is a guess by a professional who had four seconds and a name. Nobody corrects it. Nobody has any reason to.
• THE TUNNEL IS THE BEST DESCRIPTION IN THE CHAPTER. Eighty metres of concrete, and a point two-thirds along where the crowd stops being a sound and becomes pressure on the chest. Take your time on it. These are fifteen-year-olds and this is the largest thing that has ever happened to any of them.
• BETWEEN OBSTACLES, CUT TO THE STANDS ONCE. Somebody's family with a homemade banner. A row of agency scouts with tablets. The 1-B contingent, who have been told to cheer for their own and are cheering for good moves regardless of whose they are.
• PLACEMENTS TO WRITE DOWN — every PC's finishing position, and the fact that Hiro comes in twenty-second. Not last. Not close to it either. Exactly the position that gets no camera time at all.
sections.developments:
• WRITE TWO LINES OF COMMENTARY FOR EVERY NOTABLE THING A PC DOES. This is the single most important instruction in the chapter. Be warm, be admiring, be accurate, and always name the weakness — that is what real sports commentary does. You are building the prop that detonates in Chapter 4.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHETHER THE BROADCAST IS ARCHIVED — yes. Publicly, free, searchable, indefinitely. Everyone is pleased about this. Say it cheerfully.
• IF A PLAYER DELIBERATELY HIDES THEIR ABILITIES — excellent, and honour it. Note which PC did it. In Chapter 5, Sylar's read on that character is wrong in one specific way, and you should let it save them once.
• IF A PC PLACES BADLY — it does not matter mechanically and the campaign does not punish it. Everyone advances to Day Two in some capacity; the cavalry battle is the real filter.
• IF THE SKILL CHALLENGE STALLS — cut to the next obstacle. Do not roll out four kilometres. Three set pieces and a finish line is the whole event.
sections.dmNote:
Play the festival for joy. This is the best day of these kids' lives and the campaign has to earn Chapter 4 by making it genuinely good first.

The commentary is a prop with a second function and you should commit to it fully — write the lines, deliver them in a different voice, enjoy them. When the class rewatches this footage in Chapter 4 and hears their own weaknesses explained to a national audience by a friendly professional, the horror is entirely retroactive and entirely free. Do not tip it now.

If a player asks whether the broadcast is archived, the answer is yes, publicly, indefinitely, and everybody is pleased about that.
sections.treasure:
Placement, publicity, and a place on Day Two. Nothing physical.

Note every PC's finishing position. It feeds the Chapter 3 closing note and the Chapter 4 archive scene, where the top finishers are also the top of two other lists.

sections.dmNote:
The big, loud, joyful set piece. Keep the pace high and let players narrate their own moments.

The single most important instruction in this section is the Moshita Maro commentary. He is a friendly, earnest 1-B student whose quirk is borrowing other people's, and the booth is going to explain exactly how that works to eleven million people. In Chapter 4 he is the student who does not come back. If the table remembers him warmly it is because you spent four segments of commentary here making them.

The man in the stands is one sentence and then never again this session. If a player specifically watches the crowd, they see a tall man in the upper tier reading the screen with a notebook, which is what about four hundred agency scouts are also doing.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER SPECIFICALLY WATCHES THE CROWD — they see a tall man in the upper tier reading the screen and taking notes, which is exactly what about four hundred agency scouts are also doing. Give them that answer flatly and completely. It is true and it is not a clue.
• IF THE PCs END UP ON THE SAME TEAM AS 1-B STUDENTS — encourage it. Achi Homei calling positions through smoke, or Isosato Sari building a platform under a PC, buys you enormous goodwill for Chapter 4.
• IF A PC IS TARGETED BY MOSHITA MARO — let him take their quirk for two minutes and let it be a genuine problem. Then have him grin and thank them for it afterwards. Every minute of screen time he gets here is worth double later.
• IF THE FIGHT SPRAWLS — run it in three four-minute phases with a scoreboard between each, and narrate everything outside the PCs' immediate reach. Do not track twenty-four individual initiatives.
• IF YOU ARE RUNNING SHORT ON TIME — cut this event to a single phase and a scoreboard. Day Three is the one that matters.
sections.heading: Day Two — The Cavalry Battle

aside.body: Agency scouts are everywhere at the festival, openly, with notebooks and tablets, cataloguing quirks and taking notes on weaknesses. This is completely normal, entirely legitimate, and the reason nobody notices one more man doing exactly the same thing.
aside.label: Scouts

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — teams of four, headbands, twelve minutes → phase one → scoreboard → phase two → scoreboard → the last thirty seconds → one sentence about a man in the third tier who is watching the screen instead of the field.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one phase and a scoreboard. Keep the Moshita Maro commentary in full; it is the reason Chapter 4 hurts.

• Twelve minutes, teams of three or four, top eight advance. This is where 1-A and 1-B mix properly for the first time and where the rivalries in the roster get their airing.
• Run it in three phases of four minutes with a scoreboard between each. Keep the whole field in play — call out what other teams are doing constantly.
• 1-B highlights: Achi Homei echolocating through the scrum and calling positions for his whole team; Hatashi Hamba being consistently, unglamorously better than everyone at everything; Moshita Maro touching an opponent and wearing their quirk for two minutes, which the booth explains in detail and with enthusiasm; Isosato Sari building solid-air platforms that reshape the field twice.
• Kakita Keiko locks on to Ando Iorai early and does not stop. Their rivalry is scales versus a thrown weapon that cannot miss, and she has been studying his exam footage.
• Let the PCs be brilliant here. This is the last unambiguous win in the campaign.
• THE BOOTH keeps working. Moshita Maro's Copy gets four separate explanatory segments because it is the most televisually interesting quirk in the year. Write at least one of those lines out loud, in full, in a warm and admiring voice.
• Between phases, cut once to the stands: a tall thin man in the upper tier, not watching the field. Watching the screen. One sentence. Do not describe his teeth.
• MOSHITA MARO IS THE INVESTMENT AND THIS IS WHERE YOU MAKE IT. He is earnest, he is friendly, he is a bit funny, and he is quietly ashamed that his quirk is other people's. Give him four things across this session: one moment of real skill, one self-deprecating joke about borrowing, one exchange with a PC that ends with him grinning, and the full commentary segment as written. Everything Chapter 4 costs is priced here.
• THE FIELD IS LOUD AND SHOULD BE NARRATED WIDE. Call out what three other teams are doing every round, by name, whether or not it affects the PCs. Achi Homei calling positions through smoke. Hatashi Hamba quietly being better than everybody. Isosato Sari rebuilding the middle of the field out of solid air, twice.
• HIRO AND RAKUKA ARE ON A SCRATCH TEAM with two General Studies students and come nineteenth of twenty-four, and the booth does not mention them once. If a PC is on their team, Rakuka narrates his own manoeuvres continuously and Hiro spends the whole twelve minutes as the horse, at the front, taking every hit aimed at the rider.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Teams of four. Headbands worth points. Twelve minutes.

The field is a hundred metres square and contains twenty-four teenagers who have all decided, independently and simultaneously, that this is the most important thing that has ever happened.

Somewhere in the middle of it Masahata Shikoji is standing on someone's shoulders shouting about rankings.

▶ COMMENTARY ON MOSHITA MARO — use this one, in full, warmly. It matters in nine sessions.

"And there it is — Moshita of 1-B, and that is Copy. He touches you, he gets your quirk, two minutes. Two minutes exactly.

"What I love about this lad is he's never once hidden behind it. Ask him and he'll tell you straight: it's borrowed, all of it, every time. And he still walks into a scrum of eleven people to get a hand on somebody.

"That takes something the quirk doesn't give you."

▶ THE LAST THIRTY SECONDS

The clock is on the big screen and everyone on the field can see it and nobody is looking at it, because looking at it costs you a second.

▶ BETWEEN PHASES — one sentence, then move straight on

Up in the third tier there is a tall, thin man who is not watching the field. He is watching the screen, and writing something down.
sections.treasure:
A place in the final eight, and — for whoever performs best — the first approach from a professional agency. Play the scout as friendly, slightly slick, and genuinely impressed.

Agency interest is a reward the class will re-evaluate completely in Chapter 4.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Eight pairs. One arena. Medical on standby, which they say every year and which is starting to sound different now you can see how big the arena is.

Forge is in the booth. Bose is at the barrier. Entoss has laid a cement perimeter that he keeps calling "the good fence" and Yanami is in the air above it with three rings turning slowly.

"PAIRS," says the announcer, to a stadium. "For the first time in the history of this competition."

▶ BEFORE A PC MATCH

The arena floor is closer than it looked from the stands and the stands are much, much higher.

Across from you, two people you have trained with all year are checking each other's straps and not looking over.

▶ THE POST-MATCH INTERVIEW — play this as a reward, because it is one

She is warm and quick and good at her job, and the microphone is already up.

"Brilliant work out there. Tell me honestly — what's the hardest part of your quirk? What do you have to work around?"

She waits. Eleven million people wait with her. And the honest, self-aware answer is the one that is going to play beautifully.

▶ SOMEWHERE IN THE LAST HOUR — throw this away completely

A floor manager frowns at her clipboard, looks at a credentialed medical contractor on the third tier who is not on her roster, decides it is a badge error, and fixes it in the system.

▶ THE MEDICAL TENT, BETWEEN ROUNDS — throw this away completely

The tent behind the competitors' entrance has eleven beds in it and all of them are full, because full contact means full contact and there are only so many ways a first-year comes off an arena floor.

Everybody gets looked at. That is the rule and nobody argues with it, not even Bose.

Outside the tent flap, Hiro is holding two people's bags and waiting.
sections.treasure:
Podium places, medals, photographs, and a stack of agency approach letters that arrive at the school over the following week.

Also: a permanent, public, searchable archive entry for every student, with their name, quirk, classification, and eleven hours of footage. Present it as the prize. It is presented as the prize.
sections.dmNote:
The peak. Give the players their trophy, their photographs and their moment, and mean it — this is a victory and the campaign is not being sarcastic about it.

The post-match interview is the trap and it should feel like a reward. A journalist asks a PC, warmly, what the hardest thing about their quirk is, and a good answer is candid and self-aware and plays extremely well. Let it play extremely well. Let the player enjoy giving it.

The floor manager's badge correction is a single sentence delivered to nobody. It is the only thing in this session that matters and it should be completely unremarkable.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC ANSWERS THE INTERVIEW HONESTLY — let it play brilliantly. Compliments, clips, agency interest. Reward it fully and sincerely. Do not hint that it was a mistake.
• IF A PC REFUSES OR DEFLECTS THE INTERVIEW — note it. In Chapter 5, give that character one moment where Sylar has misjudged them and it saves someone. That is the payoff and it should be explicit at the table.
• IF A PC PAIR IS ELIMINATED EARLY — they watch the rest from the competitor's box with 1-B, which is a better scene than winning. Play Yamaru offering commentary and Hatashi Hamba being quietly generous about their performance.
• IF A MATCH RUNS LONG — call it on points. Forge will do it from the booth without ceremony and nobody will consider it unfair.
• IF PLAYERS TRY TO INVESTIGATE THE THIRD-TIER MAN — Sugitsu's Search says the venue is clean, because it is, because the man's biological registration belongs to somebody else. Give them the honest negative result. This is not them failing; it is the quirk working exactly as documented.
sections.heading: Day Three — The Paired Tournament
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — eight pairs, one arena → two or three matches in full, the rest narrated → the post-match interview, played as the reward it looks like → the podium, with classifications read aloud → a floor manager fixes a badge error → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — run the one match with the deepest rivalry in it, then the podium and the interview. The interview is the trap and it is not optional.

• Eight pairs, single elimination, full contact. The format exists because Forge's class bracket impressed the committee, which means Class 1-A are the reason the festival is like this and everybody knows it.
• The 1-A/1-B matchups draw on the existing rivalries — Kakita Keiko against Ando Iorai, Domoto Fumiju against Izuto Kutsu, Yamaru Todao against Kazama Kenji, Tateta Fumira against Ren Suzuki, Hashige Tataka against Setaka Toko, Isosato Sari against Chozen Tadachi, and Moshita Maro against whoever he has already managed to touch.
• YAMARU vs KAZAMA is the match of the tournament: a man who does not stop against a man with a hard cap on how much he can absorb. Kazama's Steel takes five times his level in damage before it shatters, and Yamaru simply keeps going. Play the whole thing as a clock.
• REN vs TATETA is two precision shooters at range with nowhere to hide, and Kazama standing in the open being a mirror.
• Run two or three matches in full and narrate the rest. Whoever wins, win or lose, the class comes out of this bracket ranked, named and nationally known.
• THE PODIUM — first, second and third are announced with quirk classifications read aloud. Photographs. Interviews. At least one PC is asked, live, to explain their own limits, and the honest answer is the one that makes them look good.
• Somewhere in the last hour, a floor manager notices that a credentialed medical contractor on the third tier is not on the roster she has, decides it is a badge error, and fixes it in the system.
• CLUE FIVE — everybody comes off that arena floor and goes through the medical tent, because full contact means full contact and it is the rule. Hiro waits outside it holding other people's bags. One sentence, once, in passing.
• CLUE SIX — the post-match interviews. The journalist is warm, quick and good at her job, and she works down the line of competitors, and she does not stop at Hiro. Not unkindly. There are eleven million people watching and the producer in her ear is choosing, and a boy who came twenty-second is not the choice. He does not appear to mind and does not appear to have expected anything else.
• THE PODIUM IS THE PEAK OF THE CAMPAIGN. Names, quirks, classifications read aloud to forty thousand people and eleven million more. Photographs. A medal that is heavier than it looks. Play it entirely straight and let the players have every second of it.
• THE ARENA IS SMALLER THAN THE STANDS SUGGEST and the stands are much higher than they look from the floor. A student standing on that concrete can see individual faces in the first eight rows and nothing at all above that — just a wall of noise going up.

aside.label: If the players are cautious
aside.body: Some tables will have clocked the pattern by now and start guarding what they say. Excellent — let them. A PC who refuses to explain their weakness on camera has genuinely made themselves harder to take, and you should honour that in Chapter 4 by making Sylar's read on them wrong in one specific, survivable way.

sections.tag: Sports Festival · bracket · 1–2 sessions · full contact

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — six thousand people on stopped escalators → a nine-foot man starts growing → put the civilian clock on the table out loud → the class fights, Entoss routes, Yanami lifts → deny him room and he comes down → then Sugitsu, alone, at eleven at night, running the scan again.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the concourse, the clock, and the fight. Skip the arrests and go straight to Sugitsu in the operations room, which is the actual end of the chapter.

• Kuma. Gigantification, 9'5" at rest, up to twenty-five feet at peak, with strength, durability and reach scaling as he grows. Overconfident, loud, tactically hopeless, genuinely enjoying himself, and carrying no particular malice — this is a job and he is good at it.
• THE ENCOUNTER'S REAL PROBLEM is not Kuma, it is six thousand civilians on stopped escalators in an enclosed concourse. Every round the class spends fighting is a round they are not evacuating. Make that explicit and put it on a clock.
• DENY HIM ROOM. At full size in an enclosed space he is a natural disaster; the concourse ceiling is his enemy as much as theirs. Smart play is to force him into a stairwell, or bring the ceiling low, or simply not let him finish growing. Reward every attempt to control his size over damaging him.
• FRED ENTOSS arrives fast and turns the concourse into a maze — Cement Wall gives twenty feet of three-quarters cover, and he uses it to route civilians rather than to attack. He is sarcastic the entire time and he is also visibly rationing: his uses are capped by his Constitution modifier and going past them costs him force damage and a level of exhaustion he cannot reduce.
• YANAMI MAHO is overhead moving civilians with Energy Rings, and Momentum Lock stops Kuma's arm mid-swing once, spectacularly, in front of a live camera. She will later describe the whole incident in a way that gives her more of it than she had.
• Kuma loses. He is meant to lose. He is furious and humiliated and says so continuously while being restrained, and complains that he wasn't even told what it was for.
• Nobody dies. Forty-one injuries, none critical. It reads, on every news broadcast that evening, as a triumph.
• SUGITSU JARVICHI was tracking the perimeter, the gates and the service tunnels throughout. He caught Kuma the moment he entered and dispatched staff correctly and quickly. He did not catch the credentialed medical contractor on the third tier, because that man's biological markers were registered to somebody else — a known limit of Search that is written into its own file and that somebody had read.
• PUT A NUMBER ON THE CLOCK AND SAY IT EVERY ROUND. Start at six thousand people in the concourse and take three or four hundred off it for every round the class spends on evacuation, routing or crowd control, and none off it for a round spent doing damage. Say the number out loud. The party will start solving the right problem inside two rounds and they will have worked it out themselves.
• KUMA IS FUNNY AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. He apologises for the shop front. He asks a student their name and then says not to tell him. He is having the time of his life and he is standing on an escalator full of civilians, and holding both of those in the same scene is the whole tonal exercise of this campaign in one fight.
• THE CEILING IS HIS ENEMY. Past about twenty feet the struts are on his shoulders and he is fighting the building as much as the class. Any player who works this out and starts forcing him upward instead of hitting him has solved the encounter — reward it heavily and let it be the winning move.
sections.heading: Kuma at the North Concourse

aside.label: Kuma in custody
aside.body: He talks freely and knows nothing. He was paid, told where to stand and when to start, and given no reason. He is honest about all of it and mildly offended that nobody has asked him about the fight itself. He is a genuinely useful recurring NPC from here — an incarcerated man with no loyalty to anybody who will answer any question he actually knows the answer to, which is almost none of them.

sections.dmNote:
The chapter's climax, and it is a lie. Run it as a proper boss fight — big, loud, funny, dangerous — and let the class win it in front of the country.

Then end the session on Sugitsu Jarvichi in an empty operations room at eleven at night, running the scan again. He is not celebrating. He knows exactly how good his quirk is and he knows what a clean sweep costs, and something about the shape of tonight is wrong in a way he cannot yet name.

Do not explain the badge, the contractor, or the biological marker. The players have been given every piece and the arithmetic is theirs to do, in Chapter 4, at the worst possible moment.
sections.developments:
• THE REAL PROBLEM IS THE CIVILIANS. Put six thousand people on stopped escalators and make it explicit: every round spent fighting is a round not spent evacuating. Track it out loud. A party that solves the crowd and lets the teachers handle Kuma has played this correctly.
• IF PLAYERS TRY TO STOP HIM GROWING — reward it heavily. Anything that denies him room, breaks his footing, or interrupts the growth is worth more than damage. Say yes to improvised ideas here.
• IF THE FIGHT IS GOING BADLY — Entoss and Yanami are on scene and are extremely capable. Have them take pressure off without taking the win. A beginner DM should feel free to use teachers as a difficulty dial in either direction.
• IF THE PLAYERS ASK WHY HE'S HERE — he does not know, and says so, repeatedly, while being restrained. He is not being cagey. He was paid and told where to stand.
• IF THE PLAYERS SUSPECT A DISTRACTION — they are right, and there is nothing they can do about it tonight. Let them be right and let it not help. Sugitsu will confirm the perimeter was clean, honestly, because it was.
sections.treasure:
Public credit, on every channel, that evening. The class beat a named villain in front of the country and nobody died — forty-one injuries, none critical.

And a prisoner. Kuma in custody is the campaign's most useful recurring asset and the players earned him here.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The north concourse is four storeys of glass, escalators and food stalls, and it is full of about six thousand people trying to get to their seats.

The noise it makes when a nine-foot man begins growing in the middle of it is not a scream. It is a sort of collective inhale, and then the escalators stop.

"RIGHT!" says Kuma, delighted, at fifteen feet and rising. "WHO'S IN CHARGE HERE?"

▶ AS HE GROWS

Eighteen feet. The handrail of the second-floor balcony comes up to his hip. He puts a hand through a shop front without meaning to and looks briefly apologetic about it.

Twenty-two. His shoulders are into the ceiling struts and there is dust coming down in sheets.

▶ WHEN THE CLASS ENGAGES HIM

"Oh, students! Brilliant. No, genuinely — brilliant. I've never done students."

He is enjoying this enormously. That is the horrible part.

▶ WHEN HE GOES DOWN

He hits the floor at about eleven feet and shrinks the rest of the way on the way down, and by the time anyone reaches him he is a very large man lying on a smashed escalator complaining bitterly.

"Kids. I got done by kids. Don't tell me who you are. I don't want to know."

▶ THE CLOCK — say a version of this out loud at the top of every round

Second floor, north side: about eleven hundred people, and the escalator they are standing on is not moving.

Third floor: worse.

Somebody's grandmother has sat down on the floor because she cannot do the stairs, and the crowd is going round her, and she is completely calm about it, which is somehow the thing you cannot stop looking at.
sections.tag: Sports Festival · boss encounter · the distraction

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the archive goes live Monday → a genuinely lovely week, played warm and at length → Okuma arrives and disagrees with Sugitsu, politely → Friday morning, Rawagi asks who gave interviews → "Right" → he teaches the lesson → out on the archive page.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the good week in five minutes, then Rawagi's question. Do not cut the good week entirely; the question needs something to land on.

• A short session to bank the win and turn the corner. Agency interest, scouting letters, phone calls home, a genuinely lovely week.
• Rawagi Chiso (Instinct) finally becomes a real presence. Dry, poor at conversation, strict because he believes he has to be, and openly bad at hiding which students he prefers. He has been on the Case 9 investigation since April and he has just seen four of five victims' festival footage lined up next to the depth of their post-match interviews.
• He does not tell the class any of that. He asks who gave interviews, notes the answers, and leaves. It is the single most alarming thing an adult has done all year, precisely because he offers no explanation.
• INSPECTOR OKUMA SHIZUKA of the Commission's Serious Incidents division arrives on campus the same week and is politely, immovably at odds with Sugitsu Jarvichi about whether a school is a suitable environment for an active investigation. She thinks it is not. He thinks she is underestimating his quirk. They are both right and neither will move.
• If the players go looking, the Case 9 material is publicly available in outline: five victims, all Rare-class or above, all found with the cranium opened and nothing else disturbed. What is not public, and what Rawagi has, is that four of the five competed in a Sports Festival.
• End on the archive page. Whatever the PCs' placements were, they are on it, with their names, their quirks, their classifications, and eleven hours of searchable footage explaining exactly how they work.
• PLAY THE GOOD WEEK AT LENGTH AND MEAN IT. Letters. Phone calls home, and let players narrate those. A second-year who has never spoken to them says well done in a corridor and keeps walking. Somebody's mother has printed the bracket out and laminated it, which Masahata regards as vindication of a principle.
• AGENCY LETTERS ARRIVE BY NAME. Read two of them out. They are flattering, slightly template, and specific enough about a student's performance to prove somebody watched the footage properly.
