• RAWAGI'S QUESTION IS THE HINGE AND IT NEEDS SILENCE. Come in late, do not sit down, ask it flatly, and then actually wait at the table until a player answers. Count the hands. Look at each of them for slightly too long. Say "Right." Then teach the lesson and do not refer to it again.
• HIRO PUTS HIS HAND UP FOR NOTHING, because he gave no interviews and placed nowhere, and Rawagi's eyes go past him the way everyone's do. He is the only student in the room who is not on any of the lists being drawn up that week, and this is the last time that will be a small thing.
sections.heading: The Results
sections.developments:
• IF PLAYERS CHASE RAWAGI DOWN THE CORRIDOR — he says he is not able to discuss it and that they should not give any more interviews. Both true. Both useless. He will not budge and he is visibly unhappy about not budging.
• IF PLAYERS RESEARCH CASE 9 NOW — give them the public record in full: six victims, all Rare or above, all found with the cranium opened. The festival connection is NOT public. Rawagi has it. Okuma has it. Nobody else does.
• IF YOUR TABLE WORKS IT OUT THIS SESSION — completely fine, and it does not spoil anything. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene forward and let them be the ones who tell the staff. The chapter works just as well with the class ahead of the adults.
• IF NOBODY GAVE AN INTERVIEW — Rawagi asks who placed in the top eight instead, which produces the same list and the same silence.
• END THE SESSION ON THE ARCHIVE PAGE open on somebody's phone, with the ticker running in the background. Then stop. Do not add a sting.
sections.treasure:
Agency approach letters, a trophy, a corridor photograph, and a national profile.

Every one of these is a genuine reward and every one of them is also a line in somebody's file. Do not tip the second half. The players should re-read this list in Chapter 4 themselves.
sections.dmNote:
The turn. Play the whole session warm — this is a good week and the class have earned it — and put the cold at the very end.

Rawagi's question is the hinge of the campaign. He asks it flatly, gets his answer, says "Right," and goes. No explanation, no reassurance, no follow-up. If a player chases him down the corridor he says that he is not able to discuss it and that they should not give any more interviews, which is both entirely correct and completely useless.

The last image of the chapter should be the archive page itself, open on somebody's phone in the common room, with the ticker running in the background.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The festival archive goes live on Monday. Full footage, all three days, every match, with commentary, searchable by student and by quirk.

By Wednesday, Class 1-A's placements are on the fridge in Heights Alliance, under Masahata's original prediction, which he has annotated with the words "BROADLY CORRECT" in red.

▶ THE GOOD WEEK

Letters. Phone calls home. A second-year you have never spoken to says well done in a corridor and keeps walking. Somebody's mother has printed the bracket out.

It is, without qualification, the best week any of you have ever had.

▶ RAWAGI CHISO, FRIDAY MORNING — flat, no preamble, no explanation

He comes in late, which he never does, and he does not sit down.

"Before we start. Which of you gave interviews?"

Nobody says anything, so he waits, and one by one you put your hands up, and he looks at each of them for slightly too long.

"Right," he says.

And then he teaches the lesson.

▶ THE ARCHIVE, THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY OPENS IT — read this warmly, because it is a good thing

It is genuinely well made. Somebody has done a proper job.

Every student has a page. Name, class, quirk, classification, height. Eleven hours of footage indexed by event and by round, with the commentary track on by default, and a little search box at the top that works properly.

Masahata has already found his own page and is reading the view count out loud to a room that has asked him twice to stop.

aside.label: What is actually on the archive
aside.body:
Worth being concrete, because the players are going to re-read this page in Chapter 4 and you want it to have been real.

Every first-year has a page. Name, class, quirk name, classification, height, and eleven hours of indexed footage across three days — every heat, every scrum, every match, with the professional commentary track on by default and a search box that works.

It is free. It requires no account. It is archived indefinitely, as every year's is, because taking it down would be strange and nobody has ever had a reason to want it gone.

The commentary is the part that matters, and it is good commentary, which is exactly the problem. Eleven million people had the mechanism and the limit of forty teenagers explained to them by a professional, warmly, at length, with examples.

Four of the five Case 9 victims are in an archive exactly like this one.

chapters.intro: Six weeks of training and three days of the biggest broadcast in Japan. The obstacle course, the cavalry battle, and — for the first time in the competition's history, because Forge's class bracket impressed the committee — a paired tournament, with every 1-A and 1-B rivalry in the roster getting its match. Forty thousand people in the stands and eleven million watching a professional commentary team explain, helpfully and accurately and at length, exactly how every student's quirk works and exactly where it fails. Halfway through the third day a nine-foot man starts growing in the north concourse and the class beat him in front of the entire country. Nobody dies. It reads as a triumph on every channel that evening. The archive goes live on Monday, searchable, free, and permanent.
chapters.dmNote:
Run this chapter for joy and do not undercut it. The victory is real, the class earned it, and the campaign's entire second half depends on the table having genuinely enjoyed this week.

The commentary booth is the most important prop you will use all campaign. Write two lines for every notable moment and deliver them in a different voice, warmly and admiringly, always explaining the mechanism and always explaining the limit. Good sports commentary does exactly this. When the class rewatch their own footage in Chapter 4, every one of those lines becomes a page in somebody's file, and you will not have to say so.

Kuma's attack is a genuine boss fight and a genuine distraction, and both halves need to be true. Let them win it properly. Then end on Sugitsu Jarvichi alone in an operations room at eleven at night, running a clean scan for the fourth time, unable to say what is wrong with it.

The class end this chapter ranked, photographed, interviewed, nationally known, and catalogued. Only the last of those is a problem, and none of them can tell which is which.
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 4 at the end of "Six Weeks," so the training benefits and the new tier arrive together and the festival is played by people who feel upgraded.
LEVEL 5 after Kuma goes down in the north concourse. They beat a named villain in front of the country; give it to them on the night, in front of everybody, before the chapter turns cold.

chapters.dmNote:
Everything in this chapter is a bill for Chapter 3, and it collects in the same currency the class was so pleased with: their own footage, their own interviews, their own placements.

The most important craft instruction is that you have already written the horror. Re-read your Chapter 3 commentary verbatim, in the same warm voice, in a silent common room. Nothing you invent now will be as effective as something admiring you wrote when everyone was happy.

Do not let adults solve anything the class can solve, and do not let the class solve anything only an adult can. Sugitsu is right about lockdown. Okuma is right that a school is the wrong place for this. Rawagi is right about the profile and breaks the rules to say so. The students are right that sitting on campus is unbearable. Nobody in this chapter is stupid and that is why it hurts.

Keep the two registers strictly separated. The dorm kitchen argument about whose milk it is happens in the session after somebody dies, played completely straight, because that is what actually happens to people. Super panda is exactly as silly in Chapter 4 as he was in Chapter 2 and he is also the reason a girl gets home.

The chapter ends with a teacher standing in front of a 100-foot detonation and a 1-B student not coming back. Play the roll call.
chapters.intro: A sixth pro hero is found in a stairwell in Ota, and this time somebody in the common room says the quiet thing: wasn't he at ours? Twenty minutes later Class 1-A have the archive open and are listening to a warm, admiring, professional voice explain to eleven million people exactly how each of them fails. The campus goes into lockdown, the principal puts all ten of his permanent Search slots on students and tells them so, and a man with no nose comes over the fence at nine at night to find out which of them answers a question. Students start disappearing. The class fight a man who tears off his own hand to throw at them and a woman who quietly puts him back together, and they spend an entire session attacking the wrong one of the two.

closing.body:
Powder is dead, properly this time, and the crater in the loading yard will be fenced off for a year. Saki Hiyori is out of hit dice and in a bed he will not stay in. Touch up got away, or didn't, depending on how fast the class worked it out. Three students were taken; one came home and cannot say what happened.

And Moshita Maro is not on the roll. Copy — a quirk that borrowed other people's, belonging to a boy who was quietly ashamed of that and determined not to let it define him. He got four separate segments of admiring commentary during the cavalry battle. It was the best television of the week.
closing.label: Chapter Note — What it cost

aside.body: If a player asks who the ten are, Sugitsu answers honestly and immediately, and the list is not flattering — it is the ten with the most broadcast footage, which is to say the ten who did best. Winning put them on his list for the same reason it put them on the other one.
aside.label: Which ten

sections.heading: Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth
sections.dmNote:
The chapter's opening should be the coldest twenty minutes of the campaign, and almost all of it is a room full of teenagers watching television.

The rule here is that you have already done the work. Every line of commentary you wrote in Chapter 3 is now evidence, and re-reading it verbatim is more effective than any new description you could write. If you skipped the commentary earlier, this is where that decision costs you, so bank it now if you have not.

Do not let an adult solve the puzzle. The class must be the ones to open the archive, because the horror is specifically that the shop window was theirs and they built it enthusiastically.

Sugitsu's ten permanent Search slots is the line to land hardest. He is doing exactly the right thing. He is also a man who has decided which ten children he can guarantee, out of four hundred, and he says it out loud without appearing to notice what he has said.
sections.developments:
• LET THE CLASS SOLVE THIS THEMSELVES. Do not have a teacher explain it. The horror is that the shop window was theirs and they built it enthusiastically, and that only lands if they open the archive.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHO THE TEN ARE — Sugitsu answers immediately and honestly, and the list is the ten students with the most broadcast footage. Which is the ten who did best. Say it plainly and let the table do the arithmetic.
• IF THE CLASS DEMANDS TO BE LET OUT — no. Sugitsu is immovable and correct. Okuma wants them dispersed off-campus entirely and Sugitsu is refusing that too. Let the players hear the adults disagree in front of them.
• IF A PLAYER SPOTS THE ONDO KASUMI EXCEPTION — victim two never competed. Excellent catch, and there is no answer yet. Rawagi does not have one either and says so. It resolves in Chapter 5: Sylar wanted that quirk enough to do the work without a manual.
• IF YOUR TABLE IS SHAKEN AND WANTS TO STOP — that is a good moment to check in out of character. See the "Safety, and the horror dial" appendix. Nothing in this campaign is worth pushing a table through.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the sixth one is on the news before school → somebody says "wasn't he at ours?" → the class opens the archive themselves → twenty minutes to confirm five of six → then they scroll to this year → read your own Chapter 3 commentary back, word for word → Sugitsu closes the campus that afternoon.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the news, the archive, and your own commentary read back. That is the whole session and it does not need the rest.

• The class works it out themselves. Do not have an adult explain it. Six victims, and somebody remembers that one of them competed at a Sports Festival, and then somebody opens the archive.
• Within twenty minutes they have five of six confirmed as festival competitors. It takes them another ten to find the commentary segments. It takes Chozen Tadachi about ninety seconds after that to say the thing nobody wants said, because he has been running this arithmetic since Rawagi asked who gave interviews.
• Play the archive scene properly. Put their own footage on. Read back the commentary you wrote in Chapter 3 — the same warm, admiring, accurate lines — in the same voice, in this room, in this silence.
• Ondo Kasumi, victim two, is the exception: never competed. This is the hole in the theory and the class will worry at it. The answer, which they will not get until Chapter 5, is that he wanted her quirk badly enough to do the work without a manual.
• RAWAGI CHISO confirms it when asked directly, because lying to them now would be worse. He is not authorised to and does it anyway, and it visibly costs him something. He also tells them the part that matters: the Commission's profile says the killer selects for power, and the profile is wrong, and he has been saying so since June.
• SUGITSU JARVICHI's response is immediate and correct: campus lockdown, no student off-site unaccompanied, his own Search running permanently on every one of them. He stores ten individuals permanently and he uses all ten slots on students. He tells them this. It is meant to be reassuring and it is the most frightening thing they have ever heard a teacher say.
• INSPECTOR OKUMA argues, again, that the students should be moved off-campus and dispersed. Sugitsu refuses. This time the argument happens in front of the class.
• DO NOT LET AN ADULT SOLVE THIS. If the table stalls, have an NPC classmate say the obvious thing — Ichitaka Shijime, who will have got there and be waiting to see whether anyone else does. Never a teacher.
• READ THE COMMENTARY BACK VERBATIM. Find the lines you wrote in Chapter 3 and read them again, in the same warm voice, at the same pace, into this silence. Do not add a sting, do not slow down, do not change a word. If you deliver them exactly as you did when everybody was pleased, the scene works on its own and you can simply stop talking afterwards.
• LET THE AUTOPLAY DO THE WORK. One clip ends and the next one starts by itself, because that is what archives do, and now it is somebody else's turn to have their weakness explained to eleven million people. Nobody in the room reaches for the remote for a while.
• SUGITSU'S ANNOUNCEMENT THAT AFTERNOON is delivered as a comfort and it is the most frightening thing a teacher says all campaign. He is not being ominous. He is a man telling four hundred children that he has personally guaranteed ten of them, and he does not appear to notice what he has said, and no adult in the hall corrects him.
sections.treasure:
Information, and it is the worst kind. The class now have the pattern, and the pattern is a list they are on.

Give them a physical prop: the six victims written out, with festival placements next to five of them. Add their own placements underneath in the same handwriting.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The sixth one is on the news before school.

A pro called Backdraft — combustion, Rare, thirty-four — found in a stairwell in Ota. The report is careful and the photographs are not shown and the phrasing is the same phrasing as the other five.

In the common room somebody says, without thinking about it, "Wasn't he at ours? Like, years ago?"

And then the room goes quiet, because everyone has had the same thought at the same time, and it takes about four seconds.

▶ WHEN SOMEBODY OPENS THE ARCHIVE

It takes twenty minutes to confirm five of the six. It takes another ten to find the commentary segments.

Then somebody scrolls, without really deciding to, to this year.

▶ PLAY BACK YOUR OWN CHAPTER 3 COMMENTARY — same warm voice, word for word

"Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his stance, he's rationing. That quirk costs him. Every shot is stamina he doesn't get back."

The room does not say anything.

The clip autoplays into the next one.

▶ SUGITSU JARVICHI, IN THE HALL, THAT AFTERNOON

"Campus is closed. Nobody off-site unaccompanied. That is not a discussion.

"My quirk holds ten people permanently. Locations, condition, weaknesses, all of it, all the time, no matter where they are. I have moved all ten slots onto students as of this morning."

He means it as a comfort. You can tell he means it as a comfort.

▶ THE FOUR SECONDS — this is the most important pause in the campaign, so actually take it

Somebody says "wasn't he at ours?" and then keeps talking, because it was a throwaway remark and they have already moved on.

And then they stop talking, halfway through the next sentence.

It takes about four seconds to go round the room. You can watch it happen. It gets to Chozen Tadachi first and it gets to him fastest, and he does not say anything for another minute and a half, which for him is unheard of.

▶ WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE — the room, not the screen

Twenty people around one phone is not enough, so somebody puts it on the common room television, which means the archive is now the size of a wall.

Nobody sits down. That is the detail. There are two sofas in this room and everybody is standing.

sections.heading: Lockdown
sections.tag: The quiet register · half a session · no combat
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST MORNING — flat, ordinary, and no music

The gates are shut and there is a man on them who is not Bose, in a Commission jacket, checking a tablet against faces he already recognises.

Lessons run. That is the part nobody was ready for. There is a serial killer with a documented interest in this year group and there is also a double period of maths, and Super panda is delighted to see everybody, and the double period of maths happens.

▶ THE KITCHEN, THAT EVENING — play this completely straight

"That's my milk."

"It's got no name on it."

"It's got no name on it because it's mine—"

It runs for four minutes. It is the same argument it has always been, in the same kitchen, with the same people, and nobody at any point acknowledges that anything is different, and about halfway through it stops being funny and nobody is able to say why.

▶ SUGITSU JARVICHI, WHEN THE CLASS ASKS WHO THE TEN ARE

"I'll tell you, because you'll work it out anyway and I would rather you had it from me."

He reads ten names off no list at all, because he does not need one.

They are the ten with the most broadcast footage. Which is to say, they are the ten who did best.

▶ AND THEN SOMEBODY COUNTS — this is the beat, so do not rush it

"That's not everyone."

"No," says Sugitsu. "It's ten."

Somebody works down the class list, and gets to the end of it, and stops.

"Hiro's not on there."

"No," says Sugitsu. "There's nothing there for me to hold on to. I've never needed a slot for Hiro."

And then, because he has been asked a question and he answers questions:

"I have one on Otowa Suzume. She hasn't left that room since the start of term."

▶ AND NOBODY IN THE ROOM KNOWS WHO THAT IS — let the silence run

Somebody says the name back to him, as a question, because it does not belong to anybody.

Sugitsu looks at them, and then at Hiro, and works out — about a second and a half too late — what he has just done.

"Ah," he says.

▶ AND THEN HIRO — same voice they have been listening to since April

He has not moved. He is standing exactly where he has been standing this whole time, in the uniform, with the tie done properly.

"Yeah," he says. "That's me."

A pause. Not a hurt one.

"It's on my file. It's been on my file since April. Nobody's asked."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the gates shut and lessons run anyway → one ordinary domestic scene played entirely straight → 1-B in the corridor → Sugitsu names his ten → somebody counts → a name nobody recognises → out, without resolving it.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the milk argument and the ten names. Half an hour, and it does more for Chapter 5 than an encounter would.

• RUN THIS DIRECTLY AFTER THE ARCHIVE SESSION, in the same evening or the next one. It is half a session, it has no combat, and it is where the chapter's second register lives — the one the chapter DM note asks for and that the campaign otherwise never writes down.
• THE RULE IS THAT NOTHING IS HEIGHTENED. The lessons happen. The kettle is broken again. Samitsu cooks. Aikawa reorganises the store cupboard nobody asked her to reorganise. Two students have a genuine falling-out about something trivial and it is not a metaphor for anything.
• CLASS 1-B ARE ON THE SAME CAMPUS AND THE TWO CLASSES DO NOT KNOW HOW TO BE AROUND EACH OTHER. Nothing has happened to 1-B yet. That is precisely why it is awkward: everyone can feel that 1-A are the ones on the list and nobody has a way to say so.
• LOCKDOWN AS A SET OF RULES, so the players feel it as a structure rather than a mood — no student off-site unaccompanied; bags checked at the gate; phones on and answered within the hour; a staff member sleeps in the Heights Alliance common room, on the sofa, badly, and it is a different one each night and none of them will admit it is a rota.
• SUGITSU'S TEN. He answers honestly and immediately when asked, and the list is the ten students with the most broadcast footage, which is the ten who did best. Say it plainly and let the table do the arithmetic in front of you.
• AND THEN THE COUNT. Somebody works down the register and finds that Hiro is not on the principal's list, and that a student none of them has ever heard of is. Sugitsu answers the question he was asked, in two flat sentences, and realises about a second and a half too late what he has just told a room of teenagers.
• WHAT ACTUALLY COMES OUT is not that Hiro is a doll. The class has known that since April; it is on his sheet and nobody finds it remarkable. What comes out is that there is nobody in it — that the body is a frame, that it is driven from a ground-floor room a corridor away by a girl called Otowa Suzume who has never once been in the building, and that the voice they have been listening to all year is hers.
• PLAY HIM ENTIRELY UNBOTHERED. He does not apologise, does not explain himself unprompted, and is not embarrassed. He answers what he is asked, completely, and stops. "Nobody's asked" is said without any edge on it at all, which is what makes it land.
• THE NAME IS THE WORST PART. Nobody in Class 1-A knew it. They have lived with him for a term and the register has been sitting in an office the whole time.
• DO NOT RESOLVE IT IN THIS SCENE. Nobody apologises. Nobody makes a speech about having failed to notice her. The class sits with it, badly, and the session ends.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PLAYERS WORKED HIRO OUT IN CHAPTER 2 OR 3 — excellent, and it costs the campaign nothing. Skip the reveal and give them the scene instead: they are the ones who tell the rest of the class, or they are the ones who already knew and said nothing, and either is a better version of this beat than the surprise was.
• IF NOBODY EVER ASKS HIM ANYTHING — that is a legitimate and quietly devastating outcome, and you should let it stand. Do not have an NPC ask on the table's behalf. In Chapter 5, when he is the one who cannot come, it will be worth exactly as much as it cost.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS TO SEE THE ROOM — he says yes straight away, without hesitating, because he has never had a reason to say no. Whether you play that scene is your call and the campaign does not need it. If you do: a ground-floor room, a bed, a chair, a window, a great many books, and a girl who looks nothing like the frame and sounds exactly like it. Keep it short and do not make it sad. She is not sad.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHAT TO CALL HIM NOW — that is the best question anybody asks all chapter and there is no correct answer. He says he does not mind, which is true and is also not much help. Let the table decide and let different players land differently.
• IF PLAYERS DEMAND SUGITSU ADD HIM TO THE TEN — he already has, in the only way that means anything: the slot is on the girl in the room, and it has been since April. He points out, correctly and horribly, that a Search slot is for finding somebody who might be moved, and that he can see that door from the road.
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO DO SOMETHING ABOUT ANY OF IT — they cannot, and the whole session is about that. Give them small things they can actually do: sit with 1-B, walk somebody to a lesson, take the fridge chart down.
• IF THE SESSION FEELS AIMLESS — good. Cut it at forty minutes and go straight into "Riddle at the Perimeter" the same evening. A quiet scene followed immediately by a man on the wrong side of the fence is the best running order this chapter has.
sections.treasure:
Nothing, and deliberately.

What the class gain is the shape of the list — theirs, the principal's, and the one name on neither — and the knowledge that being good at the Sports Festival put them on both.

If a player does ask Hiro a direct question and waits for the answer, give that player something real for it in Chapter 5: he is the one who tells them what he can hear through the frame, and he is right, and it saves somebody.
sections.dmNote:
This is the chapter's second register and it is the harder one to run, because nothing happens in it.

The instruction from the appendix applies here more than anywhere: U.A. never stops being funny and Appetite is never funny. The milk argument goes exactly as it always has. Somebody makes a joke and it lands. The maths lesson is good. Play all of it entirely straight and let the contrast do the work — that is what actually happens to people, and a table that has laughed in this session will be in far worse shape for the next one.

The Hiro reveal is the only piece of plot in the scene and it should be delivered as paperwork. Sugitsu is not making a revelation; he is answering a question about slot allocation, and he does not realise what he has said until it is out. Hiro is not making a confession; he is confirming something that has been on a file since April.

The thing to keep hold of is what is actually revealed. Not that he is a doll — the class has always known that, and if you play the scene as though it were that, it will land as nothing. What is revealed is that the doll is empty, that it is driven from a room down the corridor, and that there is a girl in this school whose name none of them has ever heard. The horror is entirely the class's, and it is not about the quirk. It is that they lived with him for a term and nobody thought to ask him anything.

Then let it be unresolved, and end the session. Somebody will want to apologise to her. Do not let them do it well.

aside.label: If your table finds the quiet sessions hard
aside.body:
Some tables do, and it is not a failing. If the room goes flat rather than heavy, you have two clean outs.

Cut it to a single scene — the milk argument, then Sugitsu's ten, then stop. Fifteen minutes, both beats intact, nothing lost.

Or fold it into another session entirely: run the ten names at the end of the archive scene, and the kitchen at the top of "Riddle at the Perimeter." The chapter works exactly as well.

What you should not do is replace it with an encounter. Chapter 4 has three fights in it already, and the reason the last one costs anything is that the class had an ordinary Tuesday in between.

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — nine at night, the fence line, near-total darkness → he is already inside and already bleeding → the question, given to the player and then silence → whatever they choose, play it straight → he leaves when he is finished, not when he is losing → Sugitsu, two minutes late, at a smear of somebody else's blood.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the question and the silence. Everything else in this scene is staging for one decision.

• Riddle. Question One has a 40-foot range and needs only that the target can hear him. Anyone who attempts an answer is braindead for five rounds or until they succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence check. Answering correctly ends the effect and instantly reveals his location to the answerer.
• THE MECHANICAL TRAP, and it is a good one: the correct play is to refuse to engage. Any character who does not attempt an answer is unaffected. Players will want to answer — the questions are easy, they are fair, and the quirk explicitly cannot ask something unanswerable. That is what makes it work.
• CHOZEN TADACHI is the target. Not by accident. Riddle has watched him and picked the student who cannot leave a problem alone, and the question is a genuinely interesting one that Chozen will want to solve. His player should be given the question straight, with no metagame warning, and allowed to make the choice.
• If Chozen answers: five rounds down, in the dark, with his pair standing over him. If he refuses: it costs him something real to walk away and he should be visibly worse for it — his sheet says he has thought about forty contingencies and none of them were this.
• Question Two only works at 5 feet. If anyone closes to melee while a Question One is active, Riddle asks it: "What would hurt more?" A wrong answer comes true within twenty-four hours. Use this once in the campaign and use it here.
• He is not a fight and does not want one. HP is low, he has no defensive options, and the moment the class organises he leaves. If they hurt him, he lets them; he is not there to win and he never was.
• What he was there for: he now knows which students move first, which ones freeze, and which one answers. That is the entire purpose of the visit and he has it inside ninety seconds.
• SUGITSU is on him within two minutes. Riddle is gone. Sugitsu's Search can be defeated by presented biological material — blood, tissue — and there is a smear of somebody else's blood on the fence.
• RUN IT DARK AND RUN IT SLOWLY. The fence line behind the Battle Centres is the worst-lit part of campus and the lamps are further apart than they should be. He is inside the fence this time, standing on grass, in school grounds, and the difference between this and the gate is the entire reason the scene is frightening.
• GIVE THE QUESTION TO THE PLAYER, NOT THE CHARACTER. Say it out loud at the table and then stop talking. Do not prompt, do not roll anything, do not offer a hint. The best version of this scene is thirty seconds of a real person deciding whether to answer a riddle.
• HE IS NEVER THEATRICAL. Level voice, ordinary volume, unhurried. He says "ah, good" the way a man does when the bus arrives. He is disappointed when someone walks past and slightly impressed, and he says so, and he means both.
• AFTERWARDS, THE FENCE. There is a smear of blood on the wire at about chest height and it is not his and it is not any student's. Sugitsu will not say whose it is for two days, and when he does say, he says it to Okuma and not to the class, and a player who is in the corridor hears the number rather than the name.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING — run this in near-darkness and keep his voice level throughout

Nine at night. The dorm side of the campus, the fence line, the long stretch behind the Battle Centres where the lights are further apart than they should be.

He is on the wrong side of the fence this time. Inside.

And he is bleeding from the mouth already, which means he has been here a while, and it means he has already asked somebody something.

▶ THE QUESTION — give this to the player, out loud, and then stop talking

"Ah. Good." He does not raise his voice. He does not need to.

"Three switches outside a sealed room. One of them works a bulb inside it. You can flip whatever you like, as often as you like — but you can open the door once, and only once, and then you have to tell me which switch it was."

A pause. Pleasant. Interested.

"How do you do it?"

And then he waits, and so do you.

▶ IF SOMEONE ANSWERS

Whatever they were going to say, they get about half of it out.

Then nothing. Standing, breathing, eyes open, gone — and the fence line is very dark, and it is a long way back to the dorms, and there are four of you left.

▶ IF THEY WALK PAST HIM WITHOUT ANSWERING

"No?" He sounds genuinely disappointed, and a little impressed, and he lets you go.

"Someone will."

▶ WHEN HE LEAVES

He wipes his chin with the back of his hand, looks at it, and seems mildly irritated — the way you would be about a spill, not a wound.
sections.heading: Riddle at the Perimeter

aside.body: Make it fair, mild and genuinely interesting — a lateral-thinking puzzle a clever fifteen-year-old would enjoy. Something like: a man is found dead in a locked room with forty-eight puddles of water and no other trace. The cruelty is entirely in the fact that it is a nice question.
aside.label: The question

sections.dmNote:
A short, sharp, low-HP encounter that is genuinely dangerous without being a combat. Run it in near-total darkness and keep his voice conversational throughout — he is never theatrical, never wry, and never raises his voice.

Give the question to the player, not the character. Say it out loud, at the table, and wait. The best version of this scene is a real silence while a person decides whether to answer a riddle.

If the party's instinct is to kill him, let them try and let him not care. He bleeds from the mouth after every question and does not wipe it, he takes damage without commenting on it, and he leaves when he is finished rather than when he is losing. Nothing about him is invested in the outcome of a fight.
sections.developments:
• THE CORRECT PLAY IS TO NOT ANSWER. Anyone who does not attempt an answer is completely unaffected. Do not warn the players of this in character. Give them the question and let them decide.
• IF A PLAYER ANSWERS AND FAILS THE DC 14 INT CHECK — five rounds. Ask that player to sit out and watch, in real time, and run the rest of the scene without them. Do not narrate what their character experiences, because there is nothing to narrate.
• IF A PLAYER ANSWERS CORRECTLY — the effect ends instantly and they know exactly where he is. Honour it fully. (The answer: flip the first switch, wait, turn it off, flip the second, open the door — lit is the second, warm and dark is the first, cold and dark is the third.)
• IF THE PARTY ATTACKS — he has almost no hit points and no defences and he does not care. He takes it, keeps talking, and leaves when he is finished rather than when he is losing. If they close to melee he asks Question Two.
• IF A PC ANSWERS QUESTION TWO WRONG — write down exactly what they said. It comes true within twenty-four hours, precisely as described, and you use it in the Chapter 5 epilogue. Do not soften it and do not make it fatal.
• IF CHOZEN'S PLAYER REFUSES BOTH — that is the best outcome in the scene and should visibly cost him. He is shaking afterwards. Say so.
sections.treasure:
Nothing, except a location for the blood on the fence — which is not his. Sugitsu's Search can be defeated by presented biological material, and somebody has been feeding it other people's.

That is the first hard evidence that the killer has read the principal's own quirk file.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

He is laughing before you get there. You can hear it from the far end of the street, over the alarm, over everything.

He is in a white button-up shirt and smart black trousers and he has already torn his own left hand off at the wrist and is holding it in his right, thoughtfully, the way you'd hold a stone you were about to skim.

Behind him, a woman kneels and puts her palm flat against the stump, and the hand grows back while you're watching.

▶ WHEN HE THROWS

"Catch."

▶ THE FIRST TIME THEY DROP HIM

He goes down hard and he is still laughing when he lands, and there is a moment — half a second, maybe — where you think that is the end of it.

Then she is already there, on her knees beside him, both hands flat on his chest, not looking at any of you at all.

And he sits up.

▶ WHEN HE THREATENS BURST — do not use it this session

He stops laughing, which is worse, and he puts a hand on the top button of his shirt.

"You know what I am, don't you? Someone's told you." He is almost gentle about it. "Ask them how far it goes. Go on. Ask them and then have a look around."

He does up the button again.

"Not today. You've not annoyed me enough."
sections.developments:
• THE CLASS WILL ATTACK POWDER. This is wrong and you should let it be wrong for most of a session. Every point of damage they put into him is undone by a woman nobody has looked at once.
• THE MOMENT SOMEONE SAYS "KILL THE HEALER" — that is the encounter being solved. Reward it immediately and let the fight turn.
• THE FAIR WAY OUT is her own limit: healing a creature five times in a minute inflicts a rank of exhaustion, plus one for every two further uses, to a maximum of five. Powder is being healed constantly. So is she, in effect. Count it out loud once the players start paying attention to her.
• IF NOBODY WORKS IT OUT — Help Woman will explain cellular fatigue in four blunt sentences to anyone who asks her afterwards. The class have a nurse on staff and are allowed to use her.
• IF THE PLAYERS KILL POWDER HERE — excellent. He detonates something small going down, she drags him out, and he is back next session in a fresh body and the same shirt. Discovering that killing him achieves nothing is worth more than a clean win.
• IF THE PLAYERS ARE SLOW — Powder and Touch up take a student and leave. That is a legitimate outcome and a better story than a win. Do not fudge it.
sections.treasure:
If they take Touch up alive she is silent, cooperative, and completely uninformative. She will confirm anything they already know and volunteer nothing.

The real prize is the exhaustion clock — once the class understand it, they have the tool that kills Powder in the chapter's climax.
sections.tag: Encounter · the pair that cannot be finished · 1–2 sessions

aside.label: If they kill Powder here
aside.body: Excellent. He detonates something small on the way down, she gets him out, and he is back in the next session with a fresh body and the same shirt. The class discovering that killing him achieves nothing is worth more than any win.

sections.dmNote:
The encounter that establishes the campaign's real problem: an enemy who dies and comes back, held together by somebody standing behind him.

Run the first session as a losing fight. The class will focus Powder because Powder is loud, and every point of damage they put into him is undone by a woman they have not looked at once. Let them feel that. When somebody finally says "kill the healer," it should be a genuine table moment.

The exhaustion clock is the fair way out and it is discoverable — the class have a nurse on staff, and Help Woman will explain cellular fatigue in four blunt sentences if anyone thinks to ask her.

Play Powder as delighted throughout and Touch up as almost silent. She heals him, she watches, she says nothing. Her sheet is nearly empty and you should keep her that way; she is more frightening as a function than as a person.
sections.heading: Powder and Touch up
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — he is laughing before you get there → he throws his own hand → the class focuses him → she puts him back together → let that cycle run and be infuriating → somebody says "kill the healer" → the fight turns → Burst is threatened and not used.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — two rounds of the cycle, then let a player notice her. Do not stretch the wrong-target phase past the point of frustration.

• POWDER (Yutaki Yusuzen) — Destruction lets him tear off parts of his own body and detonate them at 30 feet for 4d6, and he does it constantly, cheerfully, laughing. He plays from range and sets traps. He is loud and violent and will laugh in the face of anyone in his way. His backstory — he once ripped out his own eye and used it to kill his own parents — should never be spoken aloud by him. It comes from the Commission file, flatly, in a briefing.
• TOUCH UP (Fuchiguchi Yuko) — the reason he is a recurring problem. Healing Touch restores 3d6 and mends specific limbs. Regenerative Kiss grants 5 HP a round for a minute and strips a rank of bleeding, queasy and concussed each turn.
• THE CLOCK, and it is the only one the class has: healing a creature five times within one minute gives them a rank of exhaustion, plus one more for every two further uses, to a maximum of five. Powder is being healed constantly. Powder is accumulating exhaustion. So, at a different rate, is she.
• The class will spend most of the first session attacking Powder. This is wrong and should be allowed to be wrong. The correct target is Touch up and working that out is the encounter.
• BURST is in his back pocket the entire time: 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, 100-foot radius, Strength save at disadvantage, five ranks of bleed, five ranks of concussed, knocked back to the edge of the radius. It ignores resistance, treats immunity as resistance, ignores all damage reduction. It kills him. Touch up brings him back. He has done this before.
• DO NOT USE BURST YET. He threatens it, he enjoys threatening it, and the threat is what makes him terrifying. Save the detonation for the section below.
• They are here to take a student. If the class is slow, they succeed and leave, and the campaign is better for it than for a clean win.
• PLAY TOUCH UP AS FURNITURE UNTIL SHE IS NOT. She does not speak, does not attack, does not look at the students, and does not react to anything they do to him. Describe her once at the start, and then only ever as a thing that happens to Powder — "he sits up again" — until a player asks a question about her. The moment they do, describe her properly, and let that be the turn.
• COUNT THE HEALS OUT LOUD once the players start watching her. "That's four." "That's five." You are not hinting; you are giving them the clock the rules already contain, and a table that hears you counting will work out what the number means.
• POWDER ENJOYS THIS ENORMOUSLY and never stops talking. He compliments people. He asks a student where they trained. He tells them, cheerfully and accurately, which of them is going to be a problem, and he is right, and he does not care.
• THE STREET IS FULL OF THINGS TO HIDE BEHIND AND HE HAS ALREADY BEEN ROUND IT. He sets his own hands as traps before the class arrives — a finger in a doorway, a thumb under a car. Two or three of those going off in the first three rounds establishes that the ground here is his.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Three students missing in nine days. Two from 1-B, one from General Studies. Nobody saw anything and Sugitsu's Search has nothing, because Sugitsu's Search needs a biological marker and somebody has been feeding it other people's.

The staff room has been arguing for two hours when the maths teacher, who has been asleep in the corner throughout, sits up and says:

"Have we asked the birds?"

▶ WHEN HE ASKS THEM

He goes out into the car park in his slippers and makes a noise that is not a word, and about forty crows come off the roofline at once.

Then he has a conversation. An actual conversation, with pauses in it, where he says "mm" and "oh, that's not good" and "no, you're quite right."

He is very polite to them. He thanks each one.

▶ WHAT THE ANIMALS GIVE YOU — deliver these as fragments, in the wrong order

A crow remembers a tall man who does not smell right. Not bad. Wrong.

A cat remembers a white van that was outside the laundrette on Tuesday and outside the shuttered bank on Tuesday night, and is very clear about the difference.

A dog remembers a woman who crouched down and was kind to it and scratched behind its ear for a while, and the dog liked her a lot.

▶ WHEN THEY FIND THE GIRL

She is sitting on a stack of pallets with her knees up, and she is completely unhurt, and the first thing she says is:

"Sorry. Sorry — I know I should remember. I'm really sorry."
sections.heading: The Crows

aside.label: The most powerful quirk in the campaign has been teaching maths
aside.body:
Anivoice comprehends and speaks with any animal within 120 feet, can command them, and can have them act on his initiative. Animals report what they have perceived within the past day. The only limit is the animal's own intelligence.

That is, by a distance, the best investigative tool anyone in this campaign has access to, and it has spent two chapters in a classroom being ignored by a school with a serial abduction problem, because it belongs to a panda who wants to talk about maths.

Do not treat this as a joke that turns serious. It is a joke and it is serious and neither one wins. He asks the birds in his slippers. He is delighted that Nomi Igisa did the reading. He finds a missing child. He goes back to maths.

If a player asks, later, why nobody thought of this sooner, let an adult answer honestly: they did think of it, three days ago, and Sugitsu asked him, and he has been out every night since, and nobody put it on a briefing slide because it is not the sort of thing that goes on a briefing slide.

sections.treasure:
One student home alive. That is the reward and it should feel like one.

Also a white van, a location, and a witness who cannot remember being asked a question — which is the first time the class connect Riddle to the disappearances rather than to a school gate.
sections.developments:
• THIS IS A WINNABLE PUZZLE and the table needs one. After two hard sessions, give them a real investigation they can actually solve, with a tool they overlooked for two chapters.
• RUN IT AS THREE PARALLEL SEARCHES — split the class into pairs, each with a teacher and a radius of animals, and cut between them. Pairs are the campaign's whole structure; use them here too.
• IF PLAYERS ASK BETTER QUESTIONS, GIVE BETTER ANSWERS. Animal information is limited by animal intelligence, not by your plot. A player who thinks to ask about smell, or routine, or which direction something left in, should get something real.
• THEY FIND ONE OF THREE. Decide that before the session and hold to it. The other two are found in Chapter 5, or they are not, depending on how the finale goes.
• DO NOT MAKE SUPER PANDA SOLEMN. He is exactly as ridiculous in this session as he was in Chapter 2. He asks politely, thanks the crows, and goes back to being pleased that Nomi did the reading. He is also the reason a girl gets home. Both are true and the contrast is the point.
• IF A PLAYER TRIES TO THANK YANAMI FOR THE EXTRACTION — she accepts the thanks warmly and completely, including for the parts she did not do. Play it straight. It is funny and then it is a bit sad.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — three missing in nine days and the staff room has been arguing for two hours → the maths teacher wakes up → he asks the birds → split the class into pairs, each with a teacher and a radius of animals → cut between them → fragments, in the wrong order → they find the girl.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one crow, one cat, one dog, three fragments, and the girl on the pallets. It works fine compressed and the last beat is what matters.

• SUPER PANDA (pasta man, Anivoice) — comprehends and speaks with animals within 120 feet, and can command them; they act on his initiative. Animals can report what they have perceived within the past day, and their usefulness is limited only by their intelligence. This is the single most powerful investigative tool in the campaign and it has been sitting in a maths classroom for two chapters being ignored.
• Run this as a genuine investigation session with the class fanning out across three wards, each pair with a teacher and a radius of animals. Crows in Adachi. Cats in Ota. A very large number of pigeons.
• The information comes in fragmentary and animal-shaped: a crow remembers a tall man who does not smell right; a cat remembers a van that was in one place on Tuesday and a different place on Tuesday night; a dog remembers a woman who was kind to it, which is Touch up, and which is worse than if she hadn't been.
• They find one of the three alive. Choose a General Studies student — unnamed until now, badly frightened, physically unharmed, and completely unable to say what happened after somebody asked her something.
• They find where the other two were held. They do not find the other two.
• Play Super panda exactly as written throughout: happy, sleepy, never angry, passionate about maths and nothing else. He is not solemn about any of this. He asks the crows politely, thanks them, and goes back to being pleased that Nomi Igisa did the reading. It is the least funny thing that happens all session and he is not doing a single thing differently.
• YANAMI MAHO handles extraction with Energy Rings and takes the credit in the debrief, warmly and without malice, in front of the students who did the work. Let it sit.
• ASK BETTER, GET BETTER. A player who asks a crow what the man smelled like, or which way the van turned, or whether the woman came back, gets a real and specific answer, because animal information is limited by animal intelligence and not by your plot. Reward the good question every time; this session exists to be solvable.
• THE FRAGMENTS SHOULD ARRIVE IN THE WRONG ORDER AND NOT LINE UP AT FIRST. Give the table four or five and let them do the assembly. The van on Tuesday and the van on Tuesday night are the same van, and the cat is very clear about the difference, and that is the whole break in the case.
• THE DOG IS THE ONE THAT LANDS. A woman crouched down and was kind to it and scratched behind its ear for a while, and the dog liked her a lot and would like to see her again. Deliver it warmly, exactly as the animal means it, and do not comment.
• SUPER PANDA THANKS EVERY SINGLE BIRD. Individually. It takes a while. He is not being solemn and he is not doing a bit; this is simply how he talks to animals, and it is how he talks to students, and it is how he will talk to the crows again next time.
sections.dmNote:
A change of pace and the chapter's most humane session. After two sessions of horror, give the table a puzzle they can actually solve, with a tool they overlooked, delivered by the silliest character in the campaign.

The tonal instruction from the appendix applies hardest here: U.A. never stops being funny and Appetite is never funny. Super panda is exactly as ridiculous in this session as he was in Chapter 2. He is also the reason a girl gets home. Do not have him become grave — the whole point is that he doesn't, and it works anyway.

End on the student they found. She is fine. She cannot remember. Riddle asked her something and everything after that is missing, and she keeps apologising for not being more helpful.

sections.heading: Kuma, Interviewed

aside.label: Do not make him sympathetic by softening him
aside.body: He took money to endanger six thousand people in an enclosed concourse and he is unbothered by that. He is likeable and he is not a good man, and the campaign does not need to resolve the tension between those two things.

sections.treasure:
The carpet line — which connects the man at the school gate to the man who hired the distraction, and tells the class that the festival attack and the disappearances are one operation.

And Kuma himself, as an ongoing source, if they were decent to him.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

They have him in a reinforced interview room in Kosuge because there is nowhere else in Tokyo that will take him, and he has been in it for six weeks, and he is bored out of his mind.

He brightens up considerably when he sees the uniforms.

"Oh, brilliant," says Kuma. "You're the ones from the stairs. Sit down. Nobody's asked me about the fight. Six weeks and not one of them has asked me about the actual fight."

▶ ON THE FIGHT — let him do this at length

"Right, so — your mistake, and I say this with respect, was going for the legs. Everyone goes for the legs. I'm nine foot before I even start, I've got legs like a bridge.

"What you should have done is not let me stand up. That's it. That's the whole thing. I'm rubbish on the floor.

"Anyway. Kids. Beaten by kids. I'll never hear the end of it."

▶ ON THE JOB — he is completely honest and knows almost nothing

"Bloke with a scar. Down his whole face, like this. Never gave a name and I never asked, because you don't.

"Cash up front. He told me a date, a gate, and to be loud. That's it. Didn't say why. Wasn't my business."

▶ THE LINE THAT MATTERS — throw it away entirely, as an aside about something else

"Nice enough, actually. Bit odd. He bled on my carpet the whole time we were talking — kept dabbing at it and apologising, honestly more bothered about the carpet than I was."

He shrugs.

"Anyway. Where was I. Oh — your other mistake was—"
sections.developments:
• HE WILL ANSWER ANYTHING and knows almost nothing. Do not make players roll to get information out of him. He is bored and he likes them.
• HIS TACTICAL COACHING IS REAL. Whatever the players actually did wrong in the concourse, have him identify it accurately. He has thought about nothing else for six weeks. It is genuinely the best combat advice in the campaign and it comes from a man relitigating a loss.
• IF PLAYERS MISS THE CARPET LINE — that is fine. Have Okuma raise it in the debrief: a man who bleeds from the mouth. Do not leave the connection on the floor for more than a session.
• IF PLAYERS TREAT HIM BADLY — he shuts down, sulks, and gives them the job details only. They lose the carpet line and the coaching. This is a real consequence and you should apply it.
• IF PLAYERS TREAT HIM WELL — he becomes a recurring asset for the rest of the campaign and will confirm or deny anything they bring him. He has no loyalty to anyone and resents being used as a distraction far more than he resents losing.
• DO NOT SOFTEN HIM. He took money to endanger six thousand people in an enclosed concourse and is unbothered by that. He is likeable and he is not a good man.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a reinforced room in Kosuge and a man who is bored out of his mind → let him relitigate the fight at length, and be right → the job, which he is honest about and knows nothing of → the carpet line, thrown away → Okuma says one thing on the way out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the coaching and the carpet line. If you are very short, Okuma delivers the carpet detail in a briefing instead and you skip the visit entirely.

• Kuma is the campaign's most useful and least informed source, and the joke is that he will answer absolutely anything and knows almost nothing.
• WHAT HE ACTUALLY KNOWS: he was paid in cash by a man with a scar down his face who never gave a name. He was told a date, a time, an entrance, and to be loud. He was not told why and did not ask. He never met a tall thin man and has never heard the word Appetite except on the news, where he was annoyed to find he was not mentioned by name.
• WHAT HE WILL TALK ABOUT AT LENGTH: the fight. He has thought about it constantly for six weeks. He will tell any PC who asks exactly what they did wrong, and he is right, and it is genuinely the best tactical coaching in the campaign. He is not being generous — he is relitigating a loss.
• He is overconfident, loud, not strategically inclined, and carries no particular malice toward anybody. Getting beaten by a class of first-years was extremely embarrassing and he brings this up roughly every ninety seconds without being asked.
• THE ONE THING HE SAYS THAT MATTERS, and he says it as small talk: the man with the scar bled from the mouth the entire time they were negotiating, and apologised for it, and seemed embarrassed about the carpet.
• If the class treat him decently he becomes a genuine recurring asset. He has no loyalty to anyone, resents being used as a distraction far more than he resents losing, and will confirm or deny anything they bring him for the rest of the campaign.
• INSPECTOR OKUMA sits in on the interview and says nothing at all. Afterwards she tells the class, without warmth and without criticism, that they got more out of him in forty minutes than her people did in six weeks, and that this is because he likes them, and that she would like them to think carefully about what that is worth.
• HIS COACHING MUST BE ABOUT WHAT THE PLAYERS ACTUALLY DID. Think back to the concourse, find the genuine mistake, and have him name it. He has thought about nothing else for six weeks and he is right, and being corrected by a man who lost is a specific and excellent flavour of humiliating.
• THE ROOM IS BUILT FOR HIM AND IT IS STILL TOO SMALL. Reinforced, high-ceilinged, and he is sitting on a bench that is bolted down because the first one was not. He is at his resting nine foot five throughout, which in an interview room is its own kind of pressure, and he is entirely unaware of this.
• LET HIM TALK PAST THE POINT OF USEFULNESS. The carpet line has to arrive in the middle of a digression about something else, on its way to a third thing, and he must not pause after it. If your players do not react, keep going. Okuma will pick it up in the debrief.
• IF THEY BRING HIM SOMETHING LATER — a photograph, a name, a description — he will look at it properly and tell them the truth, including when the truth is that he does not know. He is the only source in the campaign who has never once shaded an answer.
sections.dmNote:
A deliberate breather between two heavy encounters, and the campaign's best comic scene since the bracket.

Play Kuma exactly as written: he genuinely enjoyed the fight, he holds no grudge, and he is desperate to talk to somebody who understands what happened in that concourse. Let the players enjoy him. Let him be right about their tactics.

The carpet line is the whole point of the scene and should be thrown away completely — a large man complaining about a stain, in the middle of a story about something else. Riddle bleeds from the mouth after every question. He was asking Kuma questions the entire negotiation, and Kuma, who has no reason to think anything of it, has just handed the class the connection.

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Powder knows he has lost and it makes him happy → give the party one round to see it coming → Saki Hiyori gets in front → roll 15d12 in the open, slowly → the crater → he gets up four times → then roll call.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the telegraph round, the detonation rolled in the open, and roll call. Nothing else in this session is required.

• BURST: 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, 100-foot radius. Every creature in the radius makes a Strength save at disadvantage against his Quirk save DC or takes full damage, five ranks of bleed, five ranks of concussed, and is knocked back to the edge. Success is half damage, no knockback, half the conditions. It ignores resistance, treats immunity as resistance, and ignores all damage reduction. It collapses structures, breaks terrain and throws debris a hundred feet. It leaves a crater.
• SAKI HIYORI (Creed, Deathly Endurance) — Constitution up to 24, and Death's Standing: at 0 hit points he can spend hit dice equal to his maximum hit dice to stabilise and regain consciousness, and can keep doing it as long as he has dice left. He is the one member of staff that damage alone cannot finish, and he is standing in the only place that matters.
• Run the detonation. Roll it in the open. Let the players watch 15d12 come up.
• The class survive because he is between them and it and because Fred Entoss got a cement wall up in the round before, and both of those things need to be earned in play — give the party a round to see it coming and let their choices decide how many of them are behind the wall.
• Saki Hiyori goes down. He gets up. He goes down again. Play the hit dice honestly and out loud, and let the table watch the resource drain.
• Touch up does not recover Powder this time, because she is nine ranks deep in cellular fatigue from a fortnight of putting him back together, and because the class finally, belatedly, went for her first. If they did not, she gets him out and the campaign gets one more Powder encounter in Chapter 5, which is a fine outcome.
• THE COST: Powder is gone. So, from the loading yard, is Moshita Maro of Class 1-B — Copy, earnest, quietly hungry to prove himself, painfully aware that his quirk is always somebody else's. He was taken during the detonation, in the smoke, while everyone who could have stopped it was behind a wall.
• THE TELEGRAPH ROUND IS A REAL DECISION AND YOU SHOULD RUN IT PROPERLY. Go round the table and ask each player what their character does with that one round. Who runs for the wall, who runs for a classmate, who does not move. Whatever they choose decides who is behind Entoss's cement when it goes, and you should hold to it exactly.
• ROLL THE DICE WHERE EVERYONE CAN SEE THEM AND ROLL THEM SLOWLY. Fifteen d12 takes real time to gather and real time to read, and that time is the scene. Do not use an app. Do not total it in your head. Let the table hear it.
• SAKI HIYORI DOES NOT MAKE A SPEECH. Six words, an arm across a student's chest, and his back to them. He gets up four times afterwards, and each time he gets up you say the number of hit dice he has left, out loud, until the number is nothing.
• ROLL CALL IS THE END OF THE SESSION. Somebody starts counting because that is what you do after something like this, and they lose their place, and they start again from the beginning, and everyone knows before anybody says it. Then stop. Do not add anything after roll call.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

He knows he's lost. That's the thing you'll remember afterwards — that Powder knew, and that knowing made him happy.

He stops laughing, which is worse, and he looks around the loading yard at all of you and does a small mental sum, and then he opens his shirt.

▶ SAKI HIYORI

And Saki Hiyori — who teaches endurance, who has a passion for teaching, whose hair gets spikier the more damage he takes and whose entire body is a collection of scars from things exactly like this — puts a hand on Kazama's chest and moves him backwards and says, without turning round:

"Get behind me. All of you. Now."

▶ ROLL THE DAMAGE IN THE OPEN — fifteen d12, slowly, where everyone can see

There is no sound for a moment. There is just a change in the air pressure, like a door opening somewhere very large.

▶ AFTERWARDS

The loading yard is a crater and the crater is still moving — dust coming down in slow sheets, something metal ticking as it cools.

He is on his knees at the lip of it with nothing in front of him any more, and he is getting up.

He gets up four times.

▶ ROLL CALL

Somebody starts counting, because that is what you do, and they get most of the way through and then stop and start again from the beginning, which is how everybody knows before anybody says it.

Moshita Maro is not there.

▶ THE TELEGRAPH ROUND — say this and then ask, going round the table, what each of them does

He stops laughing.

His hand goes to the top button of his shirt and this time he does not talk, and the loading yard is about a hundred and ten feet across, and you are all in it.

Somewhere behind you Fred Entoss says a word you have never heard a teacher say.

You have one round.

▶ THE INFIRMARY, AT THE END — close the session on this

Help Woman puts him in a bed and he does not stay in it, and she puts him back, and he does not stay in it.

The third time she simply stands in front of him with her hands in her cardigan pockets until he sits down.

"You have no hit dice," she says. "You have nothing. You are a man-shaped bruise with opinions."

He says something about the students.

"They're alive," she says. "One of them isn't. I'm not going to tell you that's the same as all of them, because it isn't."

She writes something on the chart and goes to see the next one.

aside.label: Say his name
aside.body: Somebody has to tell Class 1-B. Do not skip this. Ebina's students are in the corridor and one of the PCs has to walk past them, and the campaign is better if you play the walk.

sections.heading: Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It
sections.treasure:
Powder is dead, properly, and the class worked out how. That is the win and it is worth naming out loud.

The cost is on the roll call. Put the class photograph from Chapter 2 back on the table at the end of this session and say nothing about it.
sections.developments:
• GIVE THE PARTY ONE ROUND TO SEE IT COMING. Powder opening his shirt is a telegraph, not a surprise. What the players do with that round decides how many of them are behind Entoss's wall, and that is a real decision with real consequences.
• PLAY SAKI HIYORI'S HIT DICE OUT LOUD. He drops, spends dice, stands, drops again. Let the table watch the resource drain. When he runs out, he stays down.
• IF THE CLASS WENT FOR TOUCH UP EARLIER — she is too exhausted to recover Powder and he is gone for good. If they did not, she drags him out and you get one more Powder encounter in Chapter 5. Both are fine; play whichever they earned.
• DO NOT SHOW MOSHITA MARO BEING TAKEN. It happens in the smoke, during the detonation, while everyone who could have stopped it was behind a wall. The players discover it at roll call.
• IF A PLAYER TRIES TO SAVE HIM — they cannot see, cannot hear, and are prone at the edge of a hundred-foot radius. Say no, clearly, once. This is the one moment in the campaign where the answer is simply no.
• SOMEBODY HAS TO TELL CLASS 1-B. Play the walk down the corridor. Do not skip it and do not narrate past it.
sections.dmNote:
The campaign's biggest single moment and it belongs to a teacher, not the players. That is deliberate. Class 1-A have been the protagonists of every scene for eleven sessions, and this is the one where an adult stands in front of them and takes it, and they can only watch.

Roll the damage in the open and slowly. Fifteen d12 is a lot of dice and the sound of them is the scene.

The loss of Moshita Maro should be discovered afterwards, in the quiet, by roll call — not shown, not narrated in the moment. He is the 1-B student the table have been enjoying since the cavalry battle, the one whose quirk got four separate segments of admiring commentary, and he is gone because he was the most interesting thing on television that week.

End the chapter in Help Woman's infirmary with Saki Hiyori conscious, out of hit dice, and refusing to lie down. She tells him he is an idiot. She tells the class the truth about how close it was, because she tells no lies even when they would help.

chapters.title: Question One
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 6 after "The Crows" — the chapter's one clean win, and the right place to hand out something good.
LEVEL 7 at the end of "Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It," and do it quietly. Roll call first. Level after. Do not let a level-up be the thing that closes that session.

chapters.title: Keepsake

closing.body:
Sylar is dead or in a cell. Riddle bled out asking questions. Powder is a fenced-off crater and Kuma is doing eleven years and complaining about the food.

The Sports Festival archive is still online. Eleven hours, forty first-years, every quirk demonstrated under pressure with professional commentary explaining the mechanism and the weakness. It has not been taken down, because taking it down would be an admission, and because next year's first-years would like to watch it.

Forge has a new board with twenty names on it and will not explain her pairings.
closing.label: Chapter Note — What's still up

chapters.dmNote:
Everything in this chapter is a payoff and almost nothing in it is new, which is how it should feel. Three chapters of setup are now due: the pairs, the archive, the headache, the binder, the permission slip, and an empty training room in the small hours with two people in it.

Play Sylar as an anticlimax as a person and a catastrophe as an opponent. No philosophy, no monologue, no interest in the class at all. He selects for documentation because documentation is convenient. The most he ever gives them is one line to Ren Suzuki and then nothing.

Build every mechanical decision in the finale around pairs. Sylar's whole method is separating one person from a room; the campaign's whole argument since session one is that these twenty people are components that have finally been assembled. Reward proximity to a bracket partner, and make Maw escapable by an ally rather than by its victim.

And hold the Kinji Hamakida reveal until the exact moment Carlos Might points at her. If the setup has been played straight — a teacher who is never in the building, a training room nobody books, a girl who says nothing because nobody asks — the table will understand what has been happening since April in the same second she does.

Then finish in the infirmary, keep it short, and give the last line to the boy with the ranking chart.
chapters.intro: Nine days of nothing, and Class 1-B still coming to school every morning because the alternative is sitting at home. Rawagi Chiso burns himself down to nothing running Foresight over surveillance footage frame by frame and finds eleven seconds the principal's quirk was never going to catch. The Commission finally wins the argument and tells Class 1-A they are not part of what happens next. And then a man with no nose asks two last questions in a corridor, and behind him is a tall thin man with a permanent headache who is wearing a classmate's quirk and does not know he is wearing it badly. The finale is the 2v2 bracket with the safety off, it ends with a quirkless girl and a teacher in a sombrero, and it does not get everybody back.

sections.dmNote:
A quiet, procedural, miserable session that sets up the finale. Let the class be angry at being sidelined and let the adults be right to sideline them.

Rawagi's condition is the emotional content. He is dry, bad at conversation, strict because he believes he has to be, and openly has favourites — and he has burned himself out on frame-by-frame footage for nine days for a boy in the other class. He will not accept a single word of thanks and gets visibly uncomfortable when anyone tries.

The Carlos Might beat is four lines long and should be played completely flat. Three chapters of a running joke about a teacher who never turns up, and here he is, in a corridor, checking that the quirkless student has been training. Do not underline it.

aside.label: Where he's been
aside.body: If a player pushes, Carlos Might says he has been looking, which is true, and says nothing about how or where, which is also deliberate. He has been eating his way across six wards asking questions in restaurants. It is an absurd method. It has produced two of the four leads the Commission is working from.

sections.developments:
• LET THEM BE SIDELINED AND LET THE ADULTS BE RIGHT. Okuma finally wins the argument and Class 1-A are told they are not part of what happens next. The players will hate this. That is correct and you should not undercut it.
• HOW THEY GET INVOLVED ANYWAY is up to them — sneaking out, being present when something happens, or simply being asked once the location is found and nobody else can get inside. Say yes to a reasonable plan. Do not require a specific one.
• IF PLAYERS TRY TO THANK RAWAGI — he becomes visibly uncomfortable and changes the subject. He will not accept a word of it. He is dry, bad at conversation, and has burned himself down to nothing over nine days for a boy in the other class.
• IF PLAYERS PUSH CARLOS MIGHT ON WHERE HE'S BEEN — he says he has been looking. That is true. He has been eating his way across six wards asking questions in restaurants, which is an absurd method that has produced two of the four leads the Commission is working from. He will not explain the training room.
• IF THE SESSION FEELS FLAT — that is the intended texture. Nine days of nothing. Keep it short and get to the cold store.
• IF A PLAYER THINKS OF MOVING HER — say yes, and make it cost something. She has to be asked, in the room, in person, and somebody has to be the one who carries her. Forge volunteers before anyone else can. Play the asking honestly: she says yes immediately, and then says "you'll have to actually look at me," which is the only time in the campaign she asks anybody for anything.
• IF NOBODY THINKS OF IT — Hiro stays on campus, in a corridor, a mile away, and is the only member of Class 1-A who is not at the finale. Do not fix this for them. It is the correct consequence of four chapters of nobody asking him anything, and the campaign is completely willing to charge it.
sections.treasure:
Eleven seconds of footage: a tall thin man, third tier, credentialed under someone else's biological registration.

And, from Rawagi, the thing that actually matters — the killer read the principal's own quirk file. That is how the party works out that the cold store was chosen, not found.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Moshita Maro has been missing for nine days.

Class 1-B are still coming to school. That is the detail nobody is handling well — Ebina brings them in every morning, and they sit in their room, and they do the work, because the alternative is sitting at home doing nothing.

Somebody has taken the fridge chart down. Nobody will admit to it and nobody wants it back up.

▶ RAWAGI CHISO, WHEN THEY FIND HIM

The staff room is dark except for one screen, and he is four inches from it, and he has been for a while.

He does not look well. His eyes are doing something that eyes should not do and there is a mug of tea beside him with a skin on it.

"Third tier. North stand. Day three." He does not turn round. "Eleven seconds. I've got him for eleven seconds and then a stanchion and then he's gone."

▶ SUGITSU JARVICHI WATCHING IT BACK

He asks Rawagi to run it again. Then again. Then twice more.

He does not say anything at all, which from him is very loud.

▶ CARLOS MIGHT IN THE CORRIDOR — play this completely flat

He has not been in the building for a month and he is standing in the corridor like he never left.

He does not ask how anyone is. He looks past all of you at Kinji Hamakida and says: "You been keeping it up?"

"Yes."

"Good," says Carlos Might, and that is the whole conversation.

▶ THE MAP ON THE WALL — when the location comes in

Somebody has put a pin in a map of the ward, and somebody else has drawn a circle around U.A. with a compass, and the circle is one mile across.

The Shirahige cold store is on the Sumida side.

It is not close. It is not anything like close.

▶ HIRO, WHEN SOMEBODY WORKS THAT OUT

"Yeah," he says. "I know. I did it on Tuesday."

He has not asked anyone for anything all term and he does not ask now. He just says the number and lets it sit there, which is worse.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — nine days of nothing, played slowly → the fridge chart is gone and nobody admits to it → Rawagi in a dark staff room, four inches from a screen → eleven seconds of footage → Sugitsu watches it back four times and says nothing → Okuma finally wins her argument → Carlos Might in the corridor, four lines, flat.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — Rawagi and the eleven seconds, then Okuma sidelining them. The Carlos Might beat is four lines and you should keep it.

• Open on the wait. Nine days of nothing is the correct pace and the session should be allowed to be slow and unpleasant before it turns.
• What the class have: Kuma, in custody, cheerfully useless. A General Studies student who cannot remember. A crater in a loading yard. Touch up, either dead or in the wind. And an archive.
• WHAT BREAKS IT OPEN is Rawagi Chiso and it costs him. Foresight requires uninterrupted vision and taxes the mind — after every use, a DC 14 Constitution save or a level of Concussed, and a DC 13 Perception check at the start of each turn or he cannot use it again for three rounds. He has been using it on surveillance footage, frame by frame, for nine days, and he is in a state Help Woman describes bluntly as 'stupid.'
• What he has: a tall thin man, third tier, north stand, day three, credentialed as a medical contractor under somebody else's biological registration. Sugitsu's Search was never going to catch him. It is a documented limit of the quirk, written in its own file, and someone read that file.
• SUGITSU JARVICHI takes this badly and quietly. He is a man whose entire professional identity is that he sees everything, being shown the eleven seconds he did not see. He does not make a speech. He asks Rawagi to run it again and watches it four more times.
• OKUMA SHIZUKA finally wins her argument and it does not help anybody: the students are to be dispersed off-campus in supervised groups. Class 1-A are told they are not part of what happens next.
• CARLOS MIGHT is in the corridor when they come out. He has not been in the building for a month. He does not explain where he has been and he does not say anything reassuring; he asks Kinji Hamakida if she has been keeping it up, and she says yes, and he says good, and that is the whole conversation.
• THE MILE. When the cold store's location comes in, somebody will notice what it means. Hiro runs from a room in Heights Alliance and the leash is one mile; the Shirahige is on the other side of Tokyo. He is not coming, and he worked this out days ago, and said nothing to anybody about it.
• AND THEN THE CLASS CAN ASK. Otowa Suzume can be moved. She has been moved before — a chair, a van, and somebody willing to carry her, which is not a small thing to ask a fifteen-year-old to consent to and is not a small thing to ask an adult to do. Forge will do it if she says yes. Sugitsu will hate it and will not forbid it. Do not raise this yourself; let a player think of it. If nobody does, Hiro stays on campus, and that is its own ending.
• THE FRIDGE CHART IS GONE and this should be the first thing they notice in the common room, before anybody mentions Moshita Maro. Somebody took it down at some point over the nine days. Nobody will admit to it and nobody wants it back up, and there is a rectangle on the fridge door where it was.
• NINE DAYS OF NOTHING MEANS PLAYING SOME OF THE NOTHING. Cut across the week: 1-B arriving every morning; a Commission press conference that says nothing; the Case 9 board in a room the students are not allowed into; somebody's parents ringing to ask, again, whether they should take their child out of the school.
sections.heading: Nine Days

sections.developments:
• HE DOES NOT MONOLOGUE. He has no philosophy, makes no speeches, does not threaten, does not gloat, and has no interest in the class as people. If players try to engage him in conversation, he waits for them to finish and then attacks. That absence is the character.
