• IF PLAYERS ASK WHY HE DOES IT — the honest answer is about nine words and he will give it if cornered: quirks are useful and brains are where they are kept. He does not think this needs defending.
• THE HEADACHE IS AN EXPLOITABLE MECHANIC. Play it openly: recent acquisitions are unreliable and he misjudges them; the old ones are lethal. Let players work out that forcing him to switch is how they win, and reward it when they do.
• IF RAWAGI IS PRESENT — Foresight forces Sylar to declare movement, action and reaction in advance and gives the party his HP, AC and initiative. It costs Rawagi a Concussed level each use. Let him do it repeatedly, past the point of sense, and take him off the board before the end.
• IF THE PARTY FLEES — entirely legitimate. He does not pursue committed opposition; he goes and finds somebody on their own instead. Losing ground to him should always be possible.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING — do not build this up. Play it small and wrong.

He is six foot eight and he is thin in a way that makes the height worse, and he is sitting down when you find him, which somehow does not help.

He looks up. He has a headache — you can see it, in the way people who are always in pain hold their faces — and he looks at you for a moment with something that is almost, but is not, interest.

Then his jaw comes open, further than it should, and further, and the teeth are the last thing you notice because they are the only thing there is.

▶ IF THEY TRY TO TALK TO HIM

He waits until they have finished. He does not interrupt and he is not being polite; he is waiting.

Then he says nothing at all and moves.

▶ THE ONE LINE HE GIVES THEM — to Ren Suzuki, once, and never again

He stops. He actually stops, and looks at Ren for slightly too long, and something almost moves in his face.

"You've got a good one," says Sylar. "And you don't want it."

Then the moment is over and he is not interested any more.

▶ THE HEADACHE

Somewhere in the middle of a fight he stops, and puts the heel of his hand against his temple, and stands there for a full second doing nothing at all.

Then he carries on.

aside.label: The one student he has nothing on
aside.body:
Sylar builds from documentation. Eleven hours of indexed footage, a commentary track, a post-match interview, a classification read out on a podium.

On Hiro he has one sentence, from a pundit with four seconds and a name, and it is a guess.

He placed twenty-second. He gave no interview. The booth mentioned him once all week. There is no segment explaining his mechanism, because nobody in that box understood it well enough to try, because it did not look like anything worth a segment.

If he is at the cold store, this matters twice. Sylar does not know what he is — and the first time Maw closes on him, he finds out in the worst possible way, with his teeth already through it and nothing inside. Give him a full turn of doing nothing. He has been eating brains for nine years and he has never once been wrong about what he was biting.

If Hiro is not there, it still matters, and you should say so out loud in the epilogue: of the twenty students in Class 1-A, the file he could not build was on the one nobody in the country thought was interesting.

sections.dmNote:
The campaign's antagonist should be a disappointment as a person and a catastrophe as an opponent, and both of those are deliberate.

Resist every instinct to give him a philosophy. He is not making a point about hero society. He selects for documentation because documentation is convenient, and he would tell the class that if they asked, in about nine words, and then be finished talking.

The headache is the humanising detail and it is not sympathetic — it is the sound of a man who has eaten too much and cannot stop. Let it make him worse at his job in ways the players can exploit.

Have him recognise Ren Suzuki. Not warmly and not at length: a man made entirely of other people's abilities, looking at a boy raised to believe a hero should never need one. One line, no follow-up, and let Ren's player sit with it.
sections.heading: Sylar
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — do not build him up → he is sitting down when they find him → the jaw → he does not talk → name every quirk he uses, and how long he has had it → the headache costs him something visible → he disengages the moment it becomes a fight.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — this is a reference section, not a scene. Read it before the finale and use it during "Keepsake."

• SYLAR (Ken Reed) — Transfer. 6'8", slim, black hair well kept, an enormous pair of indestructible metal teeth, and a jaw he can dislocate at will. Cold, sociopathic, cannot hold a conversation without succumbing to the urge to chew on somebody's brain.
• MAW (Action, melee, 3d12 slashing) — on a hit he grabs the victim, forces them to the floor and begins working through the skull. The target is restrained and he must succeed on a DC 12 check at the start of each of his turns to maintain it.
• KEEPSAKE (Passive) — if he consumes a brain, he immediately gains that person's quirk.
• HIS WEAKNESS IS HIS COLLECTION. The more quirks he holds, the worse the headache. By now it is permanent and severe and it makes him imprecise with anything he has not practised — he is genuinely dangerous with three or four quirks he has had for years, and clumsy with the recent ones. Play this openly at the table: he misjudges a range, he over-commits, he uses the wrong thing.
• HE DOES NOT MONOLOGUE. He has nothing to say to the class. He does not explain himself, does not threaten, does not gloat, and does not acknowledge that they beat Kuma or won a tournament. The absence of any interest in them as people is the character.
• The one thing that makes him legible is Foresight. Rawagi Chiso can force him to declare his movement, action and reaction in advance, and grants the party his HP, AC and initiative. It costs Rawagi a level of Concussed each time and he will do it anyway, repeatedly, past the point of sense.
• WHAT HE IS WEARING: quirks taken from six professional heroes and, now, from students. Give him three or four in play, named, and let the class recognise at least one.
• NAME EVERY QUIRK AND SAY HOW LONG HE HAS HAD IT. "That's Falsework — he's had that since April, and he is very good with it." "That one he's had nine days." Two sentences per ability, every time, and the table will have the mechanic worked out inside three rounds without you ever explaining it.
• HE IS NOT FAST TO START AND HE IS APPALLING ONCE HE IS MOVING. He walks. He does not run at anybody. Then a round happens in which he crosses a room, takes somebody down and is working on them, and the pace change is the horror.
• HE HAS FILES AND HE HAS READ THEM. He knows Kazama's Steel has a cap, because a professional explained it on television. He knows Izuto runs on fluid. He does not know any of it perfectly, because he learned it the way anybody learns from a broadcast, and where the class has trained since then he is out of date by six weeks.

sections.developments:
• ENFORCE THE SILENCE EVERY TIME. No shouting between floors, no hearing a fight two rooms away, no coordinating without line of sight. This is the rule that makes the location work and it is the easiest one to forget.
• IF THE PARTY SPLITS — let them, and run the halves in alternating scenes. Not knowing whether the other half is alive is the entire reason the finale is set here.
• IZUTO LOSES OUTPUT IN THE COLD and his reserve does not last. Warn his player once, in character, through the hum. Then hold to it.
• CHOZEN'S BINDER FINALLY WORKS. Identical floors mean mapping one maps all eleven. Give real mechanical benefit for notes the players actually take — this is the payoff for four chapters of a running joke.
• IF THE PARTY GETS COMPLETELY LOST — that is a legitimate and interesting outcome, not a failure state. Have them come out on a floor they have already cleared and let them realise it from their own map.
sections.heading: The Shirahige Cold Store
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING — give the players a hand-drawn plan of ONE floor and tell them it is all eleven

Eleven storeys of nothing, on the Sumida side, condemned since before any of you were born.

It was a refrigerated warehouse and the insulation is still in the walls, which means it is silent inside — properly silent, the kind that makes your own pulse audible. Every floor is the same floor. Every corridor is the same corridor. There are no windows above the second storey because a cold store does not need any.

The lifts don't work. The stairwells do. There are four of them and they do not connect to each other.

▶ THE FIRST TIME SOMEONE SHOUTS

Nothing comes back. Not an echo, not a muffle — nothing. The insulation takes it out of the air about four feet from your mouth.

Whoever is one floor up did not hear that. Whoever is one floor up is not going to hear anything.

▶ ON THE COLD FLOORS

Three, seven and nine still hold temperature, and you feel it in the doorway before you feel it anywhere else.

Izuto's engines note it first. The hum drops a tone and does not come back up.

▶ IF REN FIRES IN THE DARK

For a quarter of a second the corridor is the brightest place any of you have ever been, and you can see all the way to the far end of it, and there is nothing there.

Then it is dark again, and everything in the building knows which floor you are on.

▶ SUGITSU, OUTSIDE, ON THE ROAD

"Steel shell, sealed cavity, refrigerant lining. I can see the doors. I cannot see one metre past them and I have not been able to for the last forty minutes.

"Whoever picked this building knew that before they picked it."

▶ THE SMELL, AND THE FLOOR — first thing, before anything happens

Ammonia, faintly, everywhere, the way it is in a building that held refrigerant for forty years.

The floors are painted concrete with drainage channels cut into them, running to a grate every twenty feet, because this is a building that was designed to be hosed down.

Everything in here was built to be cleaned easily. Try not to think about that.

▶ THE STAIRWELLS

Four of them, one at each corner, and they do not connect to each other at any point.

Whichever one you are in is the one you are committed to. If you want to be in another stairwell you go back down to the ground floor and walk across the building, in the dark, past every door you have not opened yet.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — hand them a plan of one floor and tell them it is all eleven → the silence, enforced from the first shout → four stairwells that do not connect → the cold floors → they split, because they will → alternate between the halves.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the plan, the silence rule, and the split. The building does the work if you hold those three.

• The finale site, and it is chosen to do one job: separate people. Sylar's entire method is getting a person on their own, and this building is a machine for it.
• THE INSULATION kills sound. Shouting does not carry between floors. A fight two rooms away is inaudible. Rule this hard — no calling for help, no hearing a scream, no coordinating between groups without line of sight.
• FOUR STAIRWELLS, none connecting. A party that splits does not easily un-split. Let them split. They will.
• NO WINDOWS above the second floor. No natural light, no orientation, no rooftop exit, and no way for anyone outside to see in. Eleven identical floors give nobody a landmark to steer by, and no one outside can see in — this is the one location in the campaign built specifically to take the party's bearings away, and they should feel it.
• THE COLD ROOMS on floors three, seven and nine still hold temperature. Izuto Kutsu's Engine loses output in the cold and his fluid reserve does not last. Fred Entoss's cement sets slowly. Ren Suzuki's beam lights a room up like a flare and tells everything in the building exactly where he is.
• WHAT IS ALREADY IN HERE: Riddle, in a second-floor corridor, waiting. Two of the three missing students, on nine. Sylar, wherever the class are not.
• THE ONE ADVANTAGE THE CLASS HAVE is that the building is genuinely, dumbly simple. Every floor is identical, which means once they have mapped one they have mapped all eleven. Chozen Tadachi's binder is finally useful in the way he always wanted it to be.
• Sugitsu Jarvichi cannot see inside. He is outside on the road with his Search running and he has been telling anyone who will listen for an hour that a refrigerated building with steel-shell insulation is the one structure in Tokyo his quirk is useless against, and that whoever chose it knew that.
• IF HIRO IS HERE, HE IS THE ANSWER TO THIS BUILDING and the players should get to discover that. He can walk a corridor alone, in the dark, ahead of everybody, with a man who eats brains somewhere in it — and if it goes wrong the class loses a frame and not a classmate. He is the only person in the campaign who can be separated safely, in the one location built entirely around separating people.
• AND IT SHOULD COST SOMETHING. He feels nothing. He will not know he is badly damaged until a limb stops answering, and he will keep walking into things because there is no part of him that flinches. A player who works out that they have started sending him first every single time, and says so out loud, has found the best scene available in this location.
• MAKE THEM DRAW ON THE PLAN. Hand over one floor, hand over a pencil, and let them mark what they clear. When they come out of a stairwell onto a floor they have already been on, do not tell them — let them work it out from their own map, and let it land.
• ENFORCE THE SILENCE THE FIRST TIME AND THEY WILL BELIEVE IT ALL SESSION. Somebody will shout. Nothing comes back — not an echo, not a muffle. The insulation takes it out of the air about four feet from their mouth. Say that once, properly, and then hold the rule without ever softening it.
sections.treasure:
Two of the three missing students are on floor nine, alive.

Whether they get out depends entirely on how the finale goes, and you should decide the answer honestly rather than in advance.
sections.dmNote:
Give the players a floor plan on paper — one floor, hand-drawn, and tell them it is all eleven. The identical-floors gimmick turns a dungeon crawl into an orientation problem and rewards note-taking enormously.

The silence is the most important feature and the easiest to forget. Enforce it every time somebody shouts. A party that gets separated in here is properly separated and the tension of not knowing whether the other half is alive is the whole reason the finale is set here rather than anywhere with windows.

Every environmental detail above is targeted at a specific PC. That is deliberate and it is what a location for a finale should do — Izuto is throttled, Ren is a lighthouse, Kazama is the only thing holding a corridor, and Chozen is, for once, in exactly the kind of problem he has spent four chapters preparing for.

aside.body: If anyone asks how Sylar found an eleven-storey building that defeats the principal's quirk: he did not. Riddle did, by asking somebody who used to work for the Commission a perfectly ordinary question about the limits of Search, and then not letting them remember being asked.
aside.label: Why here

sections.dmNote:
Structurally this is a puzzle in the shape of a boss fight and you should not let it become a real one. Keep it in a corridor, keep it dark, keep his voice level and conversational.

Give the questions to the players out loud, as questions, and wait. That is the encounter. A table sitting in silence deciding whether to answer a riddle while the clock runs is worth more than any amount of damage.

Make Question Two count. If someone answers it wrong, write down what they said, and use it in the epilogue.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

He is waiting for you, and he has been for some time, and there is blood down his chin and the front of his shirt because he has been practising.

"You came," he says. "Good. I've got two."

And he smiles, and the scar moves in a way that a face should not.

▶ QUESTION ONE — give it to the table and wait, however long that takes

"A woman gives birth to two boys. Same hour, same day, same mother, same father."

He tilts his head.

"They are not twins. How?"

▶ IF THEY START TO WALK PAST HIM

"Ah — no, that's clever. That's genuinely clever." He sounds pleased for them.

Then, to their backs, conversationally: "He's on nine. I'd hurry."

And you will never know whether that was true.

▶ QUESTION TWO — only at five feet

He leans in, close enough that you can smell the blood, and he asks it almost kindly.

"Last one. What would hurt more?"

▶ THE END OF HIM

He asks one too many and it comes out of him all at once — mouth, nose, the corners of his eyes — and he sits down against the wall quite carefully, as though he had been expecting this for a while and wanted to do it tidily.

He does not seem to mind.
sections.heading: The Question You Don't Answer
sections.treasure:
If they take him alive, he answers questions honestly and at length, because being asked is the thing he enjoys.

He gives them the ninth floor, the layout, and Sylar's condition. He will not tell them anything about himself and there is nothing to tell.

aside.label: Chozen's out
aside.body: If Chozen's player refuses both questions and drags the party past him, give it weight — he should be shaking, and he should be no use for the next scene, and it should be the best thing he does in the campaign.

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — he has been waiting and he has been practising → question one, given to the table, and then silence for as long as it takes → whatever they do, make the cost explicit → "he's on nine, I'd hurry" → question two if anyone closes → he bleeds out tidily.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — both questions and the choice to walk past. Do not let this become a fight and do not shorten the silence.

• Riddle's last stand and the campaign's final moral beat. He is between the class and Sylar and he knows exactly what he is for.
• QUESTION ONE — 40 feet, must be heard, one target at a time. Anyone who attempts an answer is braindead for five rounds or until they succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence check. Correct answers end it and reveal his location.
• QUESTION TWO — 5 feet. "What would hurt more?" A wrong answer comes true within twenty-four hours. He asks this of whoever reaches him first.
• THE SHAPE OF THE ENCOUNTER: he cannot be beaten quickly and he cannot beat them at all. He is low-HP, has no defences, and every question costs him blood. What he can do is take five rounds off one PC at a time, in a corridor, while something with metal teeth is somewhere ahead of them. He is a delay and he is a very good one.
• THE CORRECT PLAY is still to refuse to engage — but this time refusing means walking past him, leaving him alive and behind you, with a party member down on the floor. Make that cost explicit.
• If a PC answers Question Two wrong, honour it. Within twenty-four hours, the thing they named happens. Do not soften it and do not make it fatal; make it exactly what they said.
• Riddle does not survive the campaign, but the class do not necessarily kill him. He bleeds out from his own quirk if he is made to ask enough questions, which is an ending he seems to have expected and does not appear to mind.
• CHOZEN TADACHI's arc lands here. Every contingency in the binder assumes a problem worth solving. This is a problem whose only correct answer is to walk away from it, and he has never once done that.
• THE SILENCE IS THE ENCOUNTER. Ask the question out loud, put your hands down, and wait. Do not fill it. Do not offer a check. However long the table takes is how long the scene is supposed to be, and a minute of five people not speaking is worth more than any amount of damage in this campaign.
• MAKE THE COST OF WALKING PAST EXPLICIT BEFORE THEY CHOOSE. Leaving him alive means leaving him behind them, in a corridor, in a building where sound does not carry, with a classmate on the floor for five rounds and something with metal teeth somewhere ahead. Say all of that, plainly, and then let them decide.
• HE HAS BEEN PRACTISING and it shows. There is blood down his chin and the whole front of his shirt, dried in layers, and he has clearly been asking questions of somebody for some time in order to be ready for this. Do not say who. The players will supply somebody worse than anything you would have named.
• THE END OF HIM IS TIDY AND HE DOES NOT MIND. He asks one too many, it comes out of him all at once, and he sits down against the wall carefully, the way a man does when he has been expecting this and would rather not make a mess of it. If a PC stays with him, he will answer any question they ask, accurately, until he stops.
sections.developments:
• THE CORRECT PLAY IS STILL TO WALK PAST — but this time it means leaving him alive behind them, with a party member on the floor, and something with metal teeth somewhere ahead. Make that cost explicit before they choose.
• DO NOT LET THIS BECOME A REAL FIGHT. He is low-HP with no defences. He is a delay, and a very good one: five rounds off one PC at a time while the clock runs.
• IF A PC ANSWERS QUESTION TWO WRONG — write down exactly what they said. It happens within twenty-four hours, precisely as described. Do not soften it, do not make it fatal, and use it in the epilogue.
• IF THE PARTY KILLS HIM OUTRIGHT — fine. He does not resist. But make them spend the actions on it while a PC is down and the clock is running.
• THE "HE'S ON NINE" LINE IS TRUE. Two students are on floor nine. Riddle said it to hurry them into splitting up. Both of those things are true at once and the players should never be certain.
• ANSWER TO QUESTION ONE, if you need it: they are two of a set of triplets.

• BUILD EVERY MECHANIC AROUND PAIRS. Give advantage, a bonus, or a reroll to any PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner, and rule that Maw's restraint is broken by an ALLY rather than by the victim. Sylar's whole method is separating one person from a room; the campaign's answer is that these twenty are components that have finally been assembled.
• FORCE HIM TO SWITCH QUIRKS. Anything that denies him his fluent, old abilities pushes him onto the recent clumsy ones. Reward players who notice and exploit this.
• GIVE KINJI THE FINISHING BLOW. Not a beam, not a portal, not steel — a quirkless fifteen-year-old with two terms of private coaching. Hold the reveal until Carlos Might points at her. If the setup has been played straight since Chapter 2, the table will understand what has been happening in that gym in the same second she does.
• AND THEN DO NOT LET ANYONE MAKE A SPEECH ABOUT IT.
• IF THE PARTY WOULD RATHER TAKE HIM ALIVE — a legitimate and arguably worse ending for him: permanent pain, a cell, nothing new to take. Okuma prefers this outcome. Rawagi will not say what he prefers.
• MOSHITA MARO DOES NOT COME HOME. Decide before the session whether the other two students do, and be honest either way. Do not decide it with a die roll at the table.
• IF THE FIGHT IS OVERWHELMING THEM — Rawagi's Foresight, Entoss's walls, and Carlos Might are all difficulty dials. Use them. A beginner DM should feel free to adjust mid-fight and nobody at the table will ever know.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The first thing he does is a Copy.

He touches Kazama, and for two minutes he is wearing Steel, and it is not Kazama's steel — it is dull, grey, ordinary, the way everyone else's is. He does not notice. He has never seen it done properly.

He is using Moshita Maro's quirk. He learned it nine days ago.

▶ NAME EVERY QUIRK OUT LOUD AS HE USES IT

"That's Falsework. That's a construction quirk, and he's had it since April, and he is very, very good with it."

"That one he's had nine days."

▶ WHEN THE HEADACHE COSTS HIM

He reaches for something and gets the wrong one. A wall goes up where he wanted a wall to come down.

For a second he looks less like a monster and more like a man carrying too much.

Then he shakes it off.

▶ CARLOS MIGHT ARRIVES — badly timed, unannounced, absurd

There is no dramatic entrance. There is a fire door going off its hinges and a very large man in a sombrero standing in it, out of breath, holding a paper bag.

"AH! Here! I have found it! I asked at four restaurants!"

▶ DURANGO SMASH

The corridor fills with beans. All of it. Everyone. Enemy, students, the floor, the ceiling, Rawagi Chiso.

It is, unarguably, extremely effective.

▶ ESTADOS UNIDOS DE SMASH

He hits him hard enough that the sound arrives after the movement.

And then Carlos Might, breathing hard, covered in beans, turns and points across the room at the one student in this school who has no quirk at all, and who has been in an empty training room with him at six in the morning since April.

"¡Ahora es tu turno!"

And Kinji Hamakida steps forward.

▶ IF HIRO IS IN THE BUILDING — the first time Maw closes on him

He takes him the way he has taken everybody: down, fast, one hand across the chest, and then the jaw comes open.

And then he stops.

He is knelt over a fifteen-year-old boy with his teeth through the back of his skull and there is nothing in there. Ceramic. Wiring. A hollow the shape of a thought that was never in it.

He has been doing this for nine years and he has never once been wrong about what he was biting.

He does not say anything. He does not have anything to say. He just kneels there, for a whole turn, with his mouth full of somebody else's engineering.

▶ AND FROM ACROSS THE ROOM, IN THE SAME VOICE AS ALWAYS, PERFECTLY LEVEL

"Sorry. There's nobody home."

▶ KINJI HAMAKIDA — hold everything, and give this its own silence

There is no music for this. Do not describe her doing anything impressive on the way in.

A fifteen-year-old girl walks past a teacher covered in beans, and she has no quirk, and she has never had one, and she has been in an empty training room at six in the morning since April with a man nobody could find.

Nobody in the room knows what is about to happen except two people, and one of them is her.
sections.dmNote:
The finale should feel like the 2v2 bracket with the safety off, and every mechanical decision should push toward pairs.

The Kinji Hamakida beat is the campaign's best card and it only works if you have played the setup exactly as written for three chapters: Carlos Might never in the building, always in the training room with her, never explained; Rob Joestar's permission slip as a running joke; Kinji saying nothing about any of it because nobody ever asks her. If you have done that, the moment he points at the quirkless girl and the whole table realises what has been happening in an empty gym since April is the payoff for the entire campaign.

Give her the kill. Not a beam, not a portal, not steel. A quirkless fifteen-year-old with two terms of private coaching from a man in a sombrero.

And then do not have anyone make a speech about it.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — he opens with a Copy and it is Moshita's → name every quirk as he uses it → build every ruling around bracket pairs → force him onto the recent ones → Rawagi burns out → a fire door comes off its hinges → beans → and then he points at Kinji.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the quirk rotation, the pairs rule, and the ending. If the fight is running long, bring Carlos Might in early — he is a difficulty dial as well as a punchline.

• The finale, and the mechanical premise is cruel: Sylar fights the class using their classmates' abilities. Give him three or four in rotation and name every one out loud when he uses it.
• Suggested loadout — Copy (Moshita Maro, 1-B), taken nine days ago and his newest and clumsiest; a construction quirk from Tsuzuri Hane, taken in April and fluent; a perception quirk from Habara Jun; and combustion from Ikari Tomonobu. Plus Maw, always, which is the only thing he is actually good at.
• THE HEADACHE IS THE MECHANIC. Every quirk he holds worsens it. Rule it openly: the recent acquisitions are unreliable — he misjudges ranges, over-commits, and picks the wrong tool. The old ones are lethal. Let the players work out that the way to beat him is to force him to keep switching.
• RAWAGI CHISO burns himself out running Foresight and should be genuinely, visibly ruined by it. Each use is a DC 14 Constitution save or a level of Concussed; he fails several. He keeps doing it. Take him off the board before the end.
• THE PAIRS ARE THE POINT. Every fight in this campaign since session one has been two people covering each other, and the finale should reward that structurally — Sylar's entire method is separating a person from a room. Give mechanical benefit to PCs fighting within reach of their bracket partner, and make Maw's restraint escapable by an ally rather than by the victim.
• REN SUZUKI is the one the campaign has been aiming at. His father taught him a blade and a doctrine, and here is a man who is nothing but other people's quirks. Ren's answer should not be his beam. Give him the moment with the katana and give it to him without comment.
• CARLOS MIGHT arrives. Not at the start — near the end, badly timed, entirely uncoordinated, having found the place by asking in restaurants. Durango Smash does 6d6 and covers everyone present in beans, including the class, including the enemy, including the floor. It is genuinely useful and completely absurd and both of those are true at once.
• ESTADOS UNIDOS DE SMASH — 7d12, and then he points at Kinji Hamakida and says "Ahora es tu turno." She has been training with him privately for two terms. She has no quirk. She has been waiting for this since Chapter 2 and nobody at the table knew it was coming, and she should get the finishing blow.
• ROB JOESTAR is here too and this is where the comedy curdles: he loses his temper properly for the first time on screen, enters the rage, and it is not funny. Acid Pressure builds every time he fires. He does not stop.
• MOSHITA MARO does not come home. Decide before the session whether the class can save the other two, and be honest about it either way.
• BUILD THE RULINGS AROUND PAIRS AND SAY SO AT THE TABLE. Any PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner has advantage on the roll. Maw's restraint is broken by an ALLY, never by the victim. Say both rules out loud at the top of the fight — this is the campaign's thesis and it should be a mechanic the players can see, not a theme they infer.
• THE ROTATION IS THE FIGHT. Give him four abilities, name each one as it comes out, and say how long he has had it. When the class denies him the old fluent ones he is forced onto the nine-day-old Copy and the six-month-old combustion, and he starts getting things wrong — a wall where he wanted a hole, a range misjudged by twenty feet. Let them win by making him reach.
• HIRO, IF HE IS HERE, IS WORTH ONE ENORMOUS MOMENT AND NOT MORE. Maw closes on him and finds nothing, and Sylar loses a full turn to it, and that turn is the party's window. Do not give him the kill and do not give him a speech. He says one flat sentence from across the room and the fight carries on.
• CARLOS MIGHT'S ARRIVAL IS BADLY TIMED ON PURPOSE. Not the cavalry — a fire door off its hinges, a man in a sombrero out of breath holding a paper bag, announcing that he asked at four restaurants. The corridor fills with beans. It is absurd and it is genuinely, mechanically effective and both of those are true at the same time.
• AND THEN HE POINTS AT KINJI. Hold it exactly there. No music, no slow motion, no speech from anybody. He says four words in Spanish and steps out of the way.
sections.heading: Keepsake
sections.treasure:
The two students from floor nine, if the party got there. Sylar's collection, ended.

And the thing that is not a reward: they were right about everything and it still cost them a classmate. Let the win be a real win and let the cost stand.

aside.body: Sylar in custody is a legitimate ending and arguably a worse one for him — a man in permanent pain who cannot stop collecting, in a cell, with nothing new to take. Okuma will prefer this outcome. Rawagi will not say what he prefers.
aside.label: If your table would rather not kill him

sections.heading: Help Woman's Office
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the infirmary, nine of them in six beds → Help Woman down the line, softening nothing → a closing beat for every PC, round the table → 1-B in the corridor and somebody has to go out → the fridge chart goes back up → Masahata gets the last line → Monday, and a new board.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the beats round the table and Forge's board. Twenty minutes, warm, and then stop.

• Close in the infirmary. Every chapter has ended here and this one should too.
• HELP WOMAN — straight to the point, tells no lies even where a lie would help. She gives each PC an honest assessment of their injuries and, if asked, an honest assessment of anything else. She is the only adult in the campaign who has never once managed a student's feelings and the class have come to rely on that enormously.
• Go round the table and give every PC a closing beat:

  — REN SUZUKI: the man who was nothing but borrowed quirks is gone, and Ren's own is still the thing his father was afraid of. Nothing resolves. He is calmer about it than he was.
  — KAZAMA KENJI: the scar, at last, if his player wants it. He has never refused a direct question and by now somebody has finally asked one.
  — CHOZEN TADACHI: the binder gets a new page and it is one line long, and it is about walking away.
  — IZUTO KUTSU: he ran dry, in front of people, and was carried. He should say thank you, badly, to exactly one person.

• 1-B are in the corridor. Ebina Chikara is with them and has been for nine days. Somebody has to go out there.
• If a PC answered Question Two wrong, this is where it comes true. Exactly as they described it. No worse and no better.
• The fridge chart goes back up. Somebody puts it back up. Do not say who.
• FORGE has already started on next term's equipment and has a new board with twenty names on it, and she is eating, and she will not explain her pairings.
• GO ROUND THE TABLE AND ASK EACH PLAYER WHAT THEIR CHARACTER DOES IN THE WEEK AFTERWARDS, and take whatever they give you as true without adjusting it. This is the last thing that happens in the campaign and it should belong to them.
• THE NPC CLASSMATES GET ONE LINE EACH and you should give them out loud, quickly, going round the class — Aikawa organising something nobody asked her to organise, Samitsu cooking for a room that is too quiet, Nomi Igisa saying one sentence that stops the room, Tazato helping somebody and constructing a reason it was efficient. Twenty seconds each. The class survives, and the players should hear all of them survive.
• HIRO gets a beat either way. If he was at the cold store, somebody has to go and collect what is left of him, and Forge does it, and does not want help. If he was not, he is on the sofa in the morning asking who is hurt, by name, one at a time — which is the first time all campaign anyone has done to him what he is doing to them.
• AND IF A PLAYER GOES DOWN THE CORRIDOR AND KNOCKS ON THE GROUND-FLOOR DOOR, give them the scene and keep it to four lines. She is reading. She says come in. She is not sad and you should not play her as sad.
• HELP WOMAN TELLS THE TRUTH ABOUT HOW CLOSE IT WAS, because she tells no lies even where a lie would help, and the class have come to rely on that more than any comfort anyone else has offered them.

aside.body: Give it to Masahata Shikoji, at the fridge, arguing that his original bracket prediction was broadly correct. He is wrong. Nobody corrects him. It is the first time anyone has laughed in three weeks.
aside.label: The last line

sections.developments:
• GO ROUND THE TABLE AND GIVE EVERY PC A CLOSING BEAT. Ask each player what their character does in the week afterwards and take whatever they give you as true. This is the last thing that happens; make it theirs.
• IF A PC ANSWERED QUESTION TWO WRONG — this is where it comes true. Exactly as they described it. No worse, no better.
• IF PLAYERS WANT TO VISIT MOSHITA MARO'S FAMILY, OR 1-B, OR KUMA — say yes to all of it and play the scenes. There is no clock any more.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS A SECOND SEASON — the hook needs no invention. Sylar selected for documentation, and nothing about the archive has changed. It is still free, still searchable, still up. Next year's first-years would like to watch it.
• KEEP IT SHORT AND WARM. The campaign has been cold for two chapters and the last twenty minutes belong to the school.
sections.treasure:
Whatever the class earned publicly — and it will be considerable, because six professional heroes died before anyone caught this and a first-year class is what caught it.

The real reward is Forge's new board. Same handwriting, twenty names, no explanation. Class 1-A go back to being fifteen.
sections.dmNote:
Keep it short and keep it warm. The campaign has been cold for two chapters and the last twenty minutes belong to the school.

The final image is Forge's board. New pairs, no explanation, the same handwriting. Class 1-A go back to being fifteen.

If your table wants a second season, the hook is already in the file and needs no invention: Sylar selected for documentation, and there is nothing about the Sports Festival archive that has changed. It is still free, still searchable, and still up.
sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

The infirmary has six beds and there are nine of you in it, so three are sitting on the floor against the radiator, which she has already told you not to do twice.

She goes down the line. She does not soften anything. When she gets to the end she stands there for a second with her hands in her cardigan pockets and says:

"You did what you could. It wasn't enough for everyone. That's usually how it goes."

Which is not comfort. But it is true, and she has never once said anything to you that wasn't.

▶ THE CORRIDOR

Class 1-B are outside. They have been for a while. Ebina Chikara is with them and has been for nine days.

Somebody has to go out there.

▶ THE FRIDGE

At some point over the weekend the chart goes back up.

Nobody says who did it. Nobody takes it down again.

▶ THE LAST BEAT — give it to Masahata

"— which is what I said. Look at it. Look at the original. Broadly correct."

It is not. It is nowhere near correct. Ichitaka opens his mouth and then closes it again, and Aikawa makes a noise into her sleeve, and then the whole room goes, all at once.

It is the first time anybody has laughed in three weeks.

▶ AND THEN, MONDAY

Forge is at the board with a marker and a bento the size of a briefcase.

There are twenty names on it. They are already in pairs.

"Right," she says. "Nobody's swapping. Don't ask."

▶ IF HIRO WAS NEVER THERE — the morning after, and give it four lines

He is on the sofa in the common room when they come back, in the uniform, with the tie done properly.

He has been there all night. The television has been off the whole time.

"I couldn't hear anything," he says. "That's all. I want you to know it wasn't that I heard it and couldn't do anything. There was just nothing there."

Then he asks who is hurt, and he asks it about each of them separately, by name, in order, which is not something anybody has ever done for him.

chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 8 before the party goes into the Shirahige cold store, not after. They need it for the finale and the finale is not a place to be doing arithmetic.
If your table prefers XP to milestones, the same points work — hand out a level's worth at each of them and stop counting.

campaigns.title: The Shortlist

appendix.body:
If you have never done this before, run session one exactly like this.

BEFORE — read Chapter 1. All three sections, start to finish; it is the shortest chapter in the module and it has no combat, no dice and no antagonist. Write the four PC names down the side of a piece of paper. That is your notes page. Total prep: fifteen minutes.

AT THE TABLE

• Ask each player to say their character's name, quirk, and one thing they are like. Two minutes each, no more.
• Read the ▶ OPENING block of "The Letter" to one player, properly, in full. Then summarise it for the others — it is funnier once.
• Go round the table: what room were you standing in when it arrived, and who else was in the house?
• Ask the two exam questions. What did you do that you are proud of, and what did you do that you have not told anybody? Write down both answers for all four players. Do not skip this; it is the most useful twenty minutes in the campaign.
• Give each PC one short scene at home during the six weeks, then read the kit list.
• Finish with First Morning — the gate, the corridor, three classmates, and a woman in the doorway eating.

THAT IS A FULL SESSION. It has no combat and no dice, and it is the right way to start this campaign.

IF YOU FINISH EARLY — go straight into "Ten Names on the Board" in Chapter 2. The two are one continuous morning and were written to be run back to back. If you run out of time — stop anyway; the board keeps.

AFTERWARDS, ASK ONE QUESTION: "anything you want more of next time?" Then give them that. It is the single most useful thing a new DM can do and it takes thirty seconds.
appendix.heading: Your First Session, Step By Step
Running A Fight Without Panicking
appendix.body:
Combat is where new DMs freeze. Here is the minimum that works.

THE LOOP — go round the table in initiative order. On each turn ask "what do you do?", let them do one thing and move, roll to see if it lands, describe the result in one sentence, next person. That is combat.

IF YOU DO NOT KNOW WHETHER SOMETHING WORKS — pick a number between 10 and 18, ask for a d20 roll plus whatever ability seems right, and go with it. Nobody will check. Consistency matters more than correctness.

2v2 IS DIFFERENT AND EASIER. Fewer combatants, faster rounds, and every action visibly affects one specific ally. Lean into it: ask players to describe what their partner is doing while they act.

REWARD COMBINATION PLAY WITH ADVANTAGE. When two players coordinate, give the roll advantage rather than inventing a new rule. This is the whole mechanical spine of the campaign and advantage is enough to carry it.

END FIGHTS EARLY. When the outcome is obvious, narrate the last thirty seconds and stop rolling. A fight that has been decided but is still being rolled out is the most common way a good session goes flat.

IF THE PARTY IS LOSING AND YOU DID NOT MEAN THEM TO — a teacher arrives. This campaign has eleven of them and several are explicitly written as difficulty dials. Nobody at the table will ever know you adjusted it.

IF THE PARTY IS WINNING TOO EASILY — do not add hit points mid-fight. Add a complication instead: a civilian in the way, a floor giving, a second thing happening elsewhere.

They will. Every time. It is not a problem and it is not your fault.

THE FOUR-STEP FIX
1. Say "give me a second" out loud. Genuinely. Take the second.
2. Ask them what they are hoping to find. Their answer is usually a better idea than yours would have been.
3. Give them a version of it, plus one complication.
4. Steer back by having something happen — Ame-style: a phone call, a teacher looking for them, a classmate at the door.

WHAT THIS CAMPAIGN GUARANTEES — no scene is load-bearing. If the players skip the archive, Rawagi tells them. If they skip Kuma's interview, Okuma raises the carpet detail. If they never fight Powder in Chapter 4, he is at the cold store in Chapter 5. Every thread has at least two ways to reach the players and the Developments boxes list them.

IF THEY WANT TO INVESTIGATE SOMETHING THAT ISN'T THERE — say so, gently, in the fiction. A dead end that is confirmed as a dead end costs five minutes. A dead end you improvise into a plot costs you three sessions.

IF THEY SOLVE THE MYSTERY EARLY — let them, and skip forward. This campaign is not damaged by players being ahead of it; the threat does not depend on secrecy. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene up and carry on.
appendix.heading: When The Players Go Somewhere You Didn't Prepare
Pacing — What To Cut And When
appendix.body:
Seventeen to nineteen sessions is a guideline, not a target. Here is where the slack is.

SAFE TO CUT ENTIRELY

• The Common Room Ticker as its own scene — fold the lines into other sessions.
• Day Two of the festival, down to a single phase and a scoreboard.
• Kuma's interview, if Okuma delivers the carpet detail in a briefing instead.
• Any bracket match with no PC in it.

SAFE TO COMPRESS

• Chapter 1 entire — take one sentence per PC about the exam and the wait, then open at the classroom door.
• Six Weeks — twenty minutes of everyone naming two training focuses.
• The obstacle course — three obstacles and a finish line.
• Nine Days — a single scene with Rawagi, then straight to the cold store.

DO NOT CUT

• A Question at the Gate.
• The archive scene in Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth.
• Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It.
• The Kinji Hamakida moment in Keepsake.

These four are the campaign. Everything else is support.

SIGNS A SCENE HAS GONE ON TOO LONG — players checking phones, the same suggestion being made twice, or you narrating for more than about ninety seconds without a question. Cut to the next named beat. You do not have to resolve the current one.

A SHORT CAMPAIGN VERSION exists if you want one: compress Chapter 1 into the first twenty minutes of session one; run Chapter 2 sections 1, 2 and 6; all of Chapter 3; Chapter 4 sections 1, 3 and 6; and all of Chapter 5. That is roughly ten sessions and loses nothing structural.

appendix.heading: Safety, And The Horror Dial
appendix.body:
This campaign contains a man who eats brains, a student who does not come home, and a suicide detonation. It is also a school story with a panda in it. Both need managing.

BEFORE SESSION ONE, say this or something like it: "This one gets darker as it goes — there's body horror and characters we like get hurt. If anything lands badly, say so and we'll move past it, no explanation needed. That goes for me too." Thirty seconds, once, and it makes the rest of the campaign easier to run.

GIVE EVERYONE A WAY TO STOP A SCENE. The simplest version: anybody at the table can say "let's cut away from this" and you cut, immediately, without discussion or negotiation. Use it yourself early on so it is clearly not a big deal.

THE DIAL IS THE DESCRIPTION, NOT THE PLOT. Every beat in this campaign works with the camera pointed away. Sylar's method can be a closed door and a Commission report rather than anything on screen. Riddle's victims can go quiet rather than anything worse. Powder's self-mutilation can be entirely off-camera. None of that changes a single event.

THE ONE THING NOT TO SOFTEN is the cost. Moshita Maro not being at roll call is the campaign's spine. You can make it bloodless. Do not make it reversible.

IF A PLAYER IS UPSET RATHER THAN THRILLED — take a break, out of character, and ask. Being frightened by a story you chose is fun; being upset is not, and the difference is not always visible from the DM's chair.

appendix.heading: Improvising An NPC Or A Stat Block In Thirty Seconds
appendix.body:
You will need a person or a monster you have not prepared. Here is the fast version.

A PERSON — a job, a want, and one physical detail. "Floor manager, wants her shift to end, keeps losing her pen." That is a complete NPC and it will hold up for an entire scene.

A VOICE — you do not need to act. Change one thing: speak slower, speak quieter, be blunter, use shorter sentences. Rawagi is short sentences. Kuma is too many. Help Woman never softens anything. That is enough to tell people apart.

A STAT BLOCK — pick a difficulty and use these:

• Minor threat: AC 13, 25 HP, +4 to hit, 2d6 damage.
• Real threat: AC 15, 60 HP, +6 to hit, 3d8 damage.
• Serious threat: AC 17, 120 HP, +8 to hit, 4d10 damage, one special move.

Give it one interesting thing it can do and nothing else. Nobody needs a full sheet.

A QUIRK ON THE SPOT — name it, say what it does in one sentence, and say what it cannot do. The limit is what makes it feel real. Every quirk in this campaign is written that way and players will match the pattern without being asked.

IF A PLAYER ASKS SOMETHING ABOUT THE WORLD YOU HAVE NOT DECIDED — the honest answer, "I don't know yet, what do you think?", works far more often than it has any right to.

Ten pairs, assigned by Forge, no substitutions, no negotiation. Two play-in matches cut the field to eight, then quarters, semis, final — nine matches in total. Play three or four at the table and narrate the rest.

PLAY-IN
· Aikawa Sakume + Samitsu Hinsei  vs  Setaka Toko + Nakaya Emari
· Rakuka Rizo + Hiro  vs  Masahata Shikoji + Ichitaka Shijime

QUARTER-FINALS
· Ren Suzuki + Kazama Kenji  vs  Tazato Tadamaki + Ando Iorai
· Kinji Hamakida + Kibi Kankei  vs  Yoshibara Hiyoko + Nomi Igisa
· Chozen Tadachi + Toragi Kayo  vs  second play-in winner
· Izuto Kutsu + Isokono Yoromu  vs  first play-in winner

WHY THESE PAIRS
Ren + Kazama — Kazama's hardened skin is mirror-bright rather than the dull grey most Steel users show. They work out they can bounce the beam in round one and spend the rest of the bracket refining it.
Kinji + Kibi — the two quietest students in the class, one with vines and one with no quirk at all. In a format where a partner covers your reach, Kinji is suddenly not a liability, and Kibi is the only person who noticed that before the draw.
Chozen + Toragi — two escalating strikers who both get better the longer they survive. Enormous ceiling, catastrophic first two rounds.
Izuto + Isokono — speed and grapple. Izuto cannot win this alone and the whole exercise knows it.
Masahata + Ichitaka — the two most arrogant people in the class, who are also, infuriatingly, effective together. Being made to fight a play-in when his own laminated chart has him winning the tournament is the funniest thing that happens to Masahata all term, and he does not find it funny.
Yoshibara + Nomi — best friends. A clone and a poltergeist is four bodies and every loose object in the arena.
Setaka + Nakaya — iron balls and lightning. Conductive artillery, and a genuine safety briefing beforehand.
Tazato + Ando — a cranky dragon and a lizard who is far more frightened than he admits.
Aikawa + Samitsu — a loud striker behind a wall with six arms.
Rakuka + Hiro — a boy who announces every move to a crowd, and a boy the crowd does not look at twice. Rakuka treats the whole bracket as theatre and Hiro lets him, and somewhere in round one they find out that a partner willing to stand in the worst place on the floor is worth more than either of them expected. Forge will not say what she was thinking. Forge never does.
appendix.heading: The 2v2 bracket — Class 1-A

appendix.body:
DAY ONE · THE OBSTACLE COURSE — all forty first-years, four kilometres, open campus. Top twenty-four advance. Terrain is Forge's and it is unkind. Run as a skill challenge with three or four set-piece obstacles rather than a full initiative track.

DAY TWO · CAVALRY BATTLE — teams of three or four, headbands worth points, twelve minutes. Top eight teams advance. This is where 1-A and 1-B genuinely mix, and where the commentary booth starts explaining everyone's mechanics to a national audience in helpful, ruinous detail.

DAY THREE · THE PAIRED TOURNAMENT — eight pairs, single elimination, full contact, medical on standby. The format that exists only because Forge's bracket impressed the committee.

1-A versus 1-B matchups, drawn from the existing rivalries — Kakita Keiko against Ando Iorai, Domoto Fumiju against Izuto Kutsu, Moshita Maro against whichever 1-A student he has already touched, Yamaru Todao against Kazama Kenji, Tateta Fumira against Ren Suzuki, Hashige Tataka against Setaka Toko, Isosato Sari against Chozen Tadachi.

THE COMMENTARY — write two or three lines of broadcast commentary for every match you run. It is the single most important prop in the campaign. Every line that explains how a quirk works is a line Sylar is listening to, and when the class rewatches the footage in Chapter 4 they should recognise their own highlights.
appendix.heading: Sports Festival — event format
Appetite — tactics
appendix.body:
SYLAR (Ken Reed) — Transfer. Never opens a fight and never fights fair. Maw is a melee attack that on a hit grabs the target, forces them prone and begins working through the skull; the target is restrained and Sylar must make a DC 12 check each turn to maintain it. Keepsake is passive — a consumed brain gives him the quirk permanently. Play him as patient, quiet and appallingly fast, and have him disengage the moment a fight becomes a fight. His weakness is the collection: every quirk he holds worsens a permanent headache, and by Chapter 5 he is in constant pain and increasingly imprecise with abilities he has not practised.

RIDDLE (Makochi Clue) — Question One targets one creature within 40 feet who can hear him; anyone who attempts an answer is braindead for five rounds or until they pass a DC 14 Intelligence check, and on answering correctly they instantly know where he is. Question Two, at 5 feet, asks 'what would hurt more?' — a wrong answer comes true within twenty-four hours. He bleeds from the mouth after every question and never hides it. One target at a time; the questions cannot be unanswerable. Play him as cruel and unhurried. He does not want to win, he wants you to participate.

POWDER (Yutaki Yusuzen) — Destruction lets him tear off parts of his own body and detonate them at 30 feet for 4d6, which he does constantly and cheerfully. Burst is the endgame: 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, in a 100-foot radius, Strength save at disadvantage, five ranks of bleed, five ranks of concussed, knockback to the edge. It kills him. It has killed him before. A third party can trigger it if he is incapacitated, which is the detail that should make the table stop breathing.

TOUCH UP (Fuchiguchi Yuko) — the reason Powder is a recurring enemy instead of a one-off. Healing Touch mends 3d6 and repairs specific limbs; Regenerative Kiss grants 5 HP a round for a minute and strips ranks of bleeding, queasy and concussed. Heal a target five times in a minute and they gain exhaustion, which is the only clock the class has against her. She is the correct target and it takes the class an embarrassingly long time to work that out.

KUMA — Gigantification, 9'5" at rest, up to 25 feet at peak, strength and reach scaling with size. Overconfident, loud, no strategy, and no particular malice — this is a job and he is good at it. Deny him room to grow and he is manageable; give him a stadium concourse and he is a natural disaster. Getting beaten by a class of first-years is going to be very embarrassing for him, and he will say so, at length, while it happens.

NOBARA FORGE (Creation) — 1-A homeroom. Builds the class's paired gear out of her own caloric budget. Ten pounds of food a day, minimum, and she will eat during a lesson without apologising. Chapter 2 is hers.

SUGITSU JARVICHI (Search) — Principal. Scans a one-mile radius as a bonus action, tracks up to a hundred targets across five miles by 5th level, and permanently stores ten individuals. Strict, funny once you know him, avoids combat and flees after hitting. He is the reason the school is safe and the reason the failure at the festival is unbearable — his quirk can be fooled by presented biological material, and someone knew that.

RAWAGI CHISO, Instinct (Foresight) — seconded to the Case 9 investigation and visibly worse at his job for it. Foresight makes visible creatures declare movement, action and reaction in advance and gives him their HP, AC and initiative. Dry, poor at conversation, denies having favourites while obviously having them. He is the only person who can make Sylar predictable, and it costs him a level of Concussed every time.

SAKI HIYORI, Creed (Deathly Endurance) — Constitution up to 24, and Death's Standing lets him spend hit dice at 0 HP to stand back up as long as he has dice left. Extreme passion for teaching, and does not hold back when someone gets between him and his students. He is the answer to Powder and the campaign's best single image.

CARLOS MIGHT (Calos over wall) — barely attends. Turns up in the canteen eating Mexican food, or in the training room with Kinji Hamakida, and nowhere else. Durango Smash does 6d6 and covers everyone present in beans. Estados Unidos de Smash does 7d12 and ends with him pointing at Kinji and saying 'Ahora es tu turno.' Play the absence as a running joke for three chapters and then do not play it as a joke.

ROB JOESTAR (Acid) — English. Chill until he isn't; short temper, and at full wind-up he enters the rage and summons Whitesnake. Strict, gets the lesson done, and holds a written permission slip to beat Kinji and only Kinji if she is naughty, which he waves at people. Acid Pressure Points accumulate every time he fires and reset on a rest.

ADITYA BOSE, Bad Touch Bose (Rifle) — drill sergeant, always precisely on time, shouts at minor inconveniences. Standard Shot is 4d12 piercing at 120 feet and ignores resistance; ammunition costs an inch of his own hair, one hundred inches maximum, regrowing an inch an hour. Despite the range he prefers to close and beat people with no quirk at all. Festival training is his.

FRED ENTOSS, Fridas (Cement) — sarcastic, enjoys banter, on the students' side. Cement Wall builds twenty feet of three-quarters cover or a fifteen-foot restraining trap; Cement Spike Rush is 4d10 in a cone. Limited uses, and going past them costs him force damage and exhaustion. Stadium containment is his.

YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — rescue specialist. Energy Rings grant flight or halve movement; Momentum Lock freezes a creature mid-air as a reaction. Concentration-dependent, useless above 500 pounds. Enjoys being alone, and accepts the majority of the credit for things she did not do — play this honestly, it is funny and then it is a little sad.

SUPER PANDA, pasta man (Anivoice) — maths, passionately, and nothing else. Talks to and commands animals within 120 feet; Hitchcock Birds blinds a cone and restrains. Happy, sleepy, never angry. In Chapter 4 he finds three missing students by asking the crows, and it is the least funny thing that happens that session.

HELP WOMAN (Heal) — school nurse. Short, hunched, grey. Straight to the point and tells no lies, including the ones that would help. Every chapter ends in her office.
appendix.heading: The staff, and what each is for

appendix.body:
Kept as a physical prop. Add to it in front of the players.

1 · Tsuzuri Hane, 'Falsework' — Rare, construction. Adachi car park, spring. Competed in the Sports Festival, eleven years ago, placed fourth.
2 · Ondo Kasumi, 'Kelvin' — Very Rare, thermal. Nerima, summer. Never competed. The outlier, and the one that made the Commission's power-based profile look right for a while.
3 · Habara Jun, 'Sightline' — Rare, perception. Itabashi, autumn. Competed. Placed second. Extensive broadcast commentary explaining exactly how his quirk was limited.
4 · Meguro Sanae, 'Trellis' — Rare, growth. Suginami, autumn. Competed, placed sixth, and gave a post-match interview about her own weakness because she was proud of having worked around it.
5 · Ikari Tomonobu, 'Backdraft' — Rare, combustion. Ota, winter. Competed. Placed ninth.

The pattern the Commission missed and Rawagi did not: four of five have festival footage, and the depth of the commentary tracks with how cleanly they were taken. Ondo Kasumi is the exception — a quirk he wanted enough to work for without a manual.
appendix.heading: Case 9 — the victim list
Per-PC threads
appendix.body:
REN SUZUKI — raised by a father who taught him a blade and the doctrine that a hero should never need a quirk, then disowned him the day his quirk arrived. Sylar is a man who is nothing but other people's quirks, worn badly. Ren is the only student in the class who looks at him and understands what he is looking at, and that recognition is not comfortable.

KAZAMA KENJI — his sheet says the scar is a story about a moment he did not act, or could not, or chose wrong. Chapter 4 offers that moment again, in almost the same shape. His Steel has a hard damage cap and finite daily uses, and the campaign should make him spend them on other people until he has none left at the wrong time.

CHOZEN TADACHI — the binder has forty contingencies and none of them cover a question you must not answer. Riddle is written for him specifically: a threat that punishes preparation, because the more thoroughly Chozen engages with the question the worse the outcome. His growth is learning to walk away from a problem, which he has never once done.

IZUTO KUTSU — his growth arc is accepting help, and the 2v2 format is that arc rendered as a rule. Engine burns fluid and shuts down entirely at zero; give him a Chapter 4 sequence where he runs dry and has to be carried, in front of people, and let him hate it.

appendix.heading: Running the horror without breaking the school
appendix.body:
The tonal risk is obvious: a maths teacher who is a panda, and a man who eats brains. The two have to live in the same campaign for sixteen sessions.

The rule that makes it work is that Appetite is never funny and U.A. never stops being funny. Do not have Rob Joestar make a joke about Case 9. Do not have Riddle say anything wry. Keep the two registers in separate scenes and let the contrast do the work — the dorm kitchen argument about whose milk it is should be played completely straight, in the session after somebody dies, because that is what actually happens to people.

Second rule: Appetite is quiet. No monologues, no theatrics, no announcements. Sylar has nothing to say to the class. Riddle only ever asks. The loudest thing any of them do is Kuma, and Kuma is a decoy.

Third rule: nobody dies off-screen to make a point. If a named student is taken, the table sees the room afterwards.

TSUZURI HANE, 'Falsework' — the first victim, and the campaign's only ghost. A mid-ranked pro with a construction quirk and a genuinely nice reputation, twenty-nine, eleven years on the boards, a fourth place at his own Sports Festival that he never stopped mentioning. He appears only in archive footage, in a commentary clip, and in the fact that Rawagi Chiso knew him.

INSPECTOR OKUMA SHIZUKA — Hero Public Safety Commission, Serious Incidents. Forties, unhurried, entirely without warmth and entirely without malice. She thinks a school is the worst possible place to run an investigation and she is correct. She and Sugitsu Jarvichi disagree in a formal, polite, escalating way across three chapters, and neither of them is wrong.
appendix.heading: Two new faces
Stat blocks — Appetite
appendix.body:
Numbers for the five members of Appetite, pitched at the level the party will be when they meet them. They use the same three-tier scale as "Improvising An NPC Or A Stat Block In Thirty Seconds" above, so the two agree; adjust anything freely and nothing here will break.

RIDDLE (Makochi Clue) — Chapters 2, 4 and 5 · not a fight
AC 12 · HP 30 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Quirk save DC 14
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 10 · INT 16 · WIS 14 · CHA 12
Unarmed +2, 1d4 bludgeoning. That is his entire offensive capability and it is not a mistake.
· QUESTION ONE (Action) — one creature within 40 feet who can hear him. The target chooses whether to attempt an answer; a creature that does not attempt one is entirely unaffected. A creature that does is braindead for 5 rounds, or until it succeeds on a DC 14 Intelligence check at the end of each of its turns. A correct answer ends the effect instantly and the answerer knows exactly where he is standing. One target at a time. The question cannot be unanswerable.
· QUESTION TWO (Action) — 5 feet, and only against a creature currently engaged with Question One. 2d6 psychic. "What would hurt more?" A wrong answer comes true within 24 hours, exactly as described.
· HAEMORRHAGE (Passive) — every question costs him 3 hit points, ignoring everything. He does not stop asking. Ten questions kills him and he knows the number.
· HOW TO RUN HIM — he never raises his voice, never gloats, never fights back, and leaves when he is finished rather than when he is losing. If the party attacks, he lets them, and keeps talking. He is a delay, and the delay is measured in five-round blocks off one PC at a time.

KUMA — Chapter 3 · a genuine boss fight
AC 15 · HP 160 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +2 · Quirk save DC 15
STR 20 · DEX 10 · CON 18 · INT 8 · WIS 10 · CHA 14
· GIGANTIFICATION (Bonus action) — one size step per round, from 9'5" to 15 feet to 25 feet. He starts small and grows, and the fight is a race against that clock.
· AT 9'5" — +6 to hit, 2d10+5 bludgeoning, reach 10 ft.
· AT 15 FEET — +7 to hit, 3d10+6, reach 15 ft, advantage on Strength checks and saves.
· AT 25 FEET — +8 to hit, 4d10+7, reach 20 ft. In any enclosed space he takes 2d6 at the start of each of his turns from the structure he is wearing, and attacks at disadvantage against anything smaller than a car.
· HE IS RUBBISH ON THE FLOOR and says so afterwards. Prone, he cannot grow, attacks at disadvantage, and needs his whole movement to stand. Anything that takes his footing is worth more than damage and the encounter is built to be won that way.
· NOT A KILLER. He has no interest in casualties and will not pursue a fleeing civilian. The danger in this fight is the building and the six thousand people in it.

POWDER (Yutaki Yusuzen) — Chapter 4
AC 14 · HP 75 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Quirk save DC 15
STR 12 · DEX 16 · CON 16 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 14
· DESTRUCTION (Action) — tears off a part of himself and detonates it at 30 feet. 4d6 fire, DC 15 Dexterity save for half. He takes 1d6 doing it and does not appear to notice.
· LEFT HAND, THUMB, TWO FINGERS (Trap) — he sets pieces of himself around the ground before the party arrives. 4d6 in a 10-foot radius, DC 15 Dexterity for half, triggered when he chooses. Three of them, and using one in the first round establishes that the street is his.
· BURST (Action or Reaction, once, and it kills him) — 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, 100-foot radius. Strength save at disadvantage against DC 15 or full damage, 5 ranks of bleed, 5 ranks of Concussed, and knocked back to the edge of the radius; success is half damage, no knockback and half the conditions. Ignores resistance, treats immunity as resistance, ignores all damage reduction. Collapses structures and leaves a crater. A third party can trigger it if he is incapacitated.
· DO NOT USE BURST IN HIS FIRST APPEARANCE. He threatens it, enjoys threatening it, and does up his shirt button again.

TOUCH UP (Fuchiguchi Yuko) — Chapter 4 · the actual problem
AC 12 · HP 40 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · Quirk save DC 13
STR 8 · DEX 12 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 16 · CHA 10
· HEALING TOUCH (Action) — 5 feet, restores 3d6 and mends a named limb, fracture or burn. Cannot regrow what is missing.
· REGENERATIVE KISS (Action, 3/long rest) — 5 hit points at the start of each of the target's turns for 1 minute, and strips a rank of Bleeding, Queasy and Concussed each turn.
· CELLULAR FATIGUE — this is the encounter. Heal a creature 5 times within one minute and it gains a rank of exhaustion, plus one more for every 2 further uses, to a maximum of 5. Powder is being healed constantly. Count it out loud once the players start watching her.
· SHE DOES NOT FIGHT, does not speak, and does not look at the students. She is more frightening as a function than as a person and her sheet should stay this empty.

SYLAR (Ken Reed) — Chapter 5
AC 17 · HP 190 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +5 · Quirk save DC 16
STR 18 · DEX 16 · CON 18 · INT 14 · WIS 12 · CHA 6
· MAW (Action, melee +9) — 3d12 slashing. On a hit the target is grabbed, forced prone and restrained, and he begins working through the skull. At the start of each of his turns he must succeed on a DC 12 check to maintain it; while maintained the target takes 2d12 at the start of each of his turns. THE RESTRAINT IS BROKEN BY AN ALLY, not by the victim — DC 16 Strength or Dexterity check by any creature within 5 feet. This is the campaign's whole argument expressed as a rule and you should say it out loud at the table.
· KEEPSAKE (Passive) — a consumed brain gives him that quirk, permanently.
· BORROWED QUIRKS — give him three or four, name each one aloud, and say how long he has had it. Old acquisitions (Falsework's construction quirk, April) attack at +9 and roll full damage. Recent ones (Moshita Maro's Copy, nine days) attack at +5, roll half the damage dice rounded down, and on an attack roll of 5 or less he has reached for the wrong one entirely — describe the mistake and lose him the action.
· THE HEADACHE (Passive) — the first time he drops below half hit points he stops, puts the heel of his hand against his temple, and loses his entire turn. Once per fight, free, and the players should see it happen.
· HE DISENGAGES the moment a fight becomes a fight. He does not pursue committed opposition; he goes and finds somebody on their own instead.

appendix.heading: Stat blocks — the staff, as difficulty dials
appendix.body:
You will need numbers for teachers twice: when the party is losing and you want to take pressure off, and when a teacher is the scene. Keep them vague in play and precise on your own sheet.

SAKI HIYORI, Creed (Deathly Endurance) — the answer to Powder
AC 16 · HP 140 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · CON 24 (+7)
· DEATH'S STANDING — at 0 hit points he may spend hit dice to stabilise and regain consciousness, and may keep doing it as long as he has dice left. He has 12d12. Spend them out loud, one at a time, and say the number remaining each time he stands up. When they are gone, he stays down.
· Unarmed +8, 2d8+7. He is not there to deal damage.

FRED ENTOSS, Fridas (Cement) — containment, and rationed
· CEMENT WALL (Action) — 20 feet of three-quarters cover, or a 15-foot restraining trap, DC 15 Strength to break out. Uses equal to his Constitution modifier (4) per day.
· CEMENT SPIKE RUSH (Action) — 4d10 in a 30-foot cone, DC 15 Dexterity for half.
· PAST HIS USES he can keep going, and each further use costs him 3d6 force damage and a level of exhaustion he cannot reduce. He will do this. He will be sarcastic about it.

RAWAGI CHISO, Instinct (Foresight) — the only thing that makes Sylar legible
· FORESIGHT (Action, concentration) — one visible creature must declare its movement, action and reaction in advance, and Rawagi learns its current hit points, AC and initiative. Requires uninterrupted vision.
· THE COST — after every use, DC 14 Constitution save or a level of Concussed, and at the start of each of his turns a DC 13 Perception check or he cannot use it again for 3 rounds.
· He will burn himself past the point of sense. Take him off the board before the end of the finale and let the party watch it happen.

SUGITSU JARVICHI (Search) — never in a fight
· Scans a one-mile radius as a bonus action; tracks up to a hundred targets across five miles; stores ten individuals permanently, wherever they are.
· DEFEATED BY presented biological material — blood or tissue belonging to somebody else — and by sealed refrigerated structures. Both limits are written in his own quirk file, and somebody has read it.
· He avoids combat and withdraws after striking. He is the reason the school is safe and the reason the failure is unbearable.

YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — rescue
· ENERGY RINGS — grant flight, or halve a creature's movement. Concentration. Useless above 500 pounds.
· MOMENTUM LOCK (Reaction) — freeze one creature mid-air. Once, spectacularly, and she will accept the credit for rather more than that.

ADITYA BOSE (Rifle) · ROB JOESTAR (Acid) · CARLOS MIGHT (Calos over wall)
· Bose: Standard Shot 4d12 piercing at 120 feet, ignores resistance, ammunition costs an inch of his own hair from a hundred, regrowing an inch an hour. He would rather close and hit you.
· Joestar: Acid Pressure Points accumulate on every shot and reset on a rest. At full wind-up he enters the rage and summons Whitesnake, and in Chapter 5 that stops being funny.
· Carlos Might: Durango Smash 6d6 and everyone present is covered in beans. Estados Unidos de Smash 7d12. Two moves, no defence worth writing down, and he is a plot device with a sombrero — use him exactly once.

appendix.heading: Class 1-A — twenty students at a glance
appendix.body:
Everything you need to voice the class without opening another page. Bracket partner in brackets. Full sheets are on the characters page.

THE FOUR PLAYER CHARACTERS
· REN SUZUKI — Beams From His Eyes (Rare). [Kazama Kenji] Quiet, respectful, steps into the scary thing first. Ranged pressure that punishes cover; every shot costs him stamina he does not get back. Disowned by a father who taught him a blade and the doctrine that a hero should never need a quirk.
· KAZAMA KENJI — Steel (Uncommon). [Ren Suzuki] Kind, a bit cocky about how much he can absorb for other people. His shell takes five times his level in damage and then shatters, and his uses reset only on a long rest. The scar on his left cheek is from before U.A. and he has never refused a direct question about it. Nobody has asked one.
· CHOZEN TADACHI — Stress (Very Rare). [Toragi Kayo] Overthinker with forty contingencies laminated. Gets physically stronger as the situation gets worse, which means bad situations put him in his best combat state and he has learned to enjoy that.
· IZUTO KUTSU — Engine (Rare). [Isokono Yoromu] Intelligent, self-reliant, terrible at accepting help. Engine burns fluid — about 32 cups of reserve; below 8 he has disadvantage on Constitution saves and drops a damage die, and at 0 the quirk shuts down entirely.

THE CLASS
· AIKAWA SAKUME — Iron Claws. [Samitsu Hinsei] Loud, proud, first to volunteer, organises things nobody asked her to organise. Gets in close and applies bleed.
· ANDO IORAI — Scales. [Tazato Tadamaki] Cocky, jokes constantly, far more frightened than he admits. The sunglasses come off only when he is genuinely shaken, which is rare.
· HIRO — Doll. [Rakuka Rizo] Dry, unhurried, always present and never eating. His body is constructed rather than grown, which the whole class knows and nobody finds remarkable. There is a second thing about him and it does not come out before Chapter 4; see "Hiro — the clues, in order."
· ICHITAKA SHIJIME — Hologram. [Masahata Shikoji] Genius, knows it, mildly superior to everyone equally. Creates false targets and splits attention. Gets to the answer first and waits to see if anybody else does.
· ISOKONO YOROMU — Tail. [Izuto Kutsu] Shy in groups, fiercely loyal, cries easily and does not hide it. Grapples one enemy and holds them where the heavy hitters can reach.
· KIBI KANKEI — Vines. [Kinji Hamakida] The most relaxed person in the class. Builds cover and chokepoints. His vine-hair flowers when he is content and he will not discuss this.
· MASAHATA SHIKOJI — Water Gun. [Ichitaka Shijime] Arrogant, loud, maintains the laminated ranking chart on the fridge. Annoying, and correct more often than is fair.
· NAKAYA EMARI — Element (Lightning). [Setaka Toko] Giggly, delighted by everything, no charge is too much charge. Chains current between conductive points.
· NOMI IGISA — Poltergeist. [Yoshibara Hiyoko] Timid, quiet, speaks perhaps twice a term and the room listens when she does. Moves enemies into bad positions.
· RAKUKA RIZO — Dying Flight. [Hiro] Theatrical, warm, announces every move and cannot stop. Flies in, gets somebody out, flies off.
· SAMITSU HINSEI — Dupli-Arms. [Aikawa Sakume] Cool exterior, easily offended, genuinely nice, extraordinary cook. Shields allies and attacks at the same time.
· SETAKA TOKO — Iron Ball. [Nakaya Emari] Respectful and honourable, writes actual thank-you notes, tallest in the class by several inches. The class's moral north.
· KINJI HAMAKIDA — Quirkless. [Kibi Kankei] Guarded, precise, says less than she knows. Everything she does is footwork and timing. Has been training privately with Carlos Might since April and nobody has asked her a second question about it.
· TAZATO TADAMAKI — Dragon. [Ando Iorai] Cranky as a resting state, not a bad mood. Helps people and constructs an efficiency-based reason for it every time.
· TORAGI KAYO — Twin Impact. [Chozen Tadachi] Intimidating, awkward, leaves small useful gifts on people's desks with no note. Can hit the same spot twice.
· YOSHIBARA HIYOKO — Double. [Nomi Igisa] Funny and friendly, then suddenly and completely furious, then fine. Her clone is exactly as much of all of that.

VOICES, IF YOU NEED THEM QUICKLY — Rakuka announces. Masahata ranks. Tazato is blunt and it is kindness. Setaka is formal. Ando jokes over the top of everything. Nomi says one sentence. Hiro answers exactly the question he was asked and stops.

appendix.heading: Class 1-B — the ones this campaign uses
appendix.body:
Ebina Chikara's class, twenty of them, and the campaign leans on nine. They are not the enemy; they are the other half of a year group, and by Chapter 5 they are in a corridor waiting for news.

· MOSHITA MARO — Copy. Touch someone, wear their quirk for two minutes exactly. Earnest, friendly, quietly ashamed that everything he has is borrowed, and he still walks into a scrum of eleven people to get a hand on somebody. He gets four separate segments of admiring commentary in the cavalry battle because his is the most televisually interesting quirk in the year. He is the student who does not come back. Every minute of screen time you give him in Chapter 3 is worth double in Chapter 4.
· YAMARU TODAO — Deathly Endurance. A man who does not stop, against Kazama Kenji, who has a hard cap on what he can absorb. The match of the tournament and you should run it as a clock.
· KAKITA KEIKO — Homing. A thrown weapon that cannot miss, locked onto Ando Iorai early and permanently. She has studied his exam footage.
· DOMOTO FUMIJU — Rabbit. Right behind Izuto Kutsu at the bottleneck and delighted about it.
· TATETA FUMIRA — Bullet Laser. Two precision shooters at range with nowhere to hide, against Ren Suzuki, with Kazama standing in the open being a mirror.
· HASHIGE TATAKA — Metal Manipulation. Against Setaka Toko, whose entire quirk is iron.
· ISOSATO SARI — Solid Air. Builds platforms that reshape the field twice in one event. Put one under a PC and you buy enormous goodwill for Chapter 4.
· ACHI HOMEI — Voice. Echolocates through a scrum and calls positions for his whole team.
· HATASHI HAMBA — High Specs. Consistently, unglamorously better than everyone at everything. Keeps a notebook of exact numbers.

THE OTHER ELEVEN — Naza Keiseki (Dark Shadow), Mawa Hisaya (Fire skin), Koto Kohomi (Gyrate), Chisano Tomose (Wave Motion), Asabira Magi (Weather Manipulation), Zabata Haho (Elasticity), Kagamo Akake (Air Cannon), Detsu Narumitsu (Beast Creation), Kukino Kaino (Clean Bubbler), Detsami Doki (Frog), Hama Kokao (Search). Use them as scenery, as cavalry-battle opposition, and as the faces in the corridor at the end.

EBINA CHIKARA brings his class in every morning for nine days after Moshita is taken, because the alternative is them sitting at home. He is in the corridor in the epilogue and he has been there the whole time.

appendix.heading: The session-by-session run sheet
appendix.body:
Twenty-nine sections across seventeen to nineteen sessions. Prep is what you actually need to read beforehand; the one thing is what the session fails without.

CHAPTER 1 — PROVISIONAL · Level 1
