1 · The Letter + The Weeks Between + First Morning — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: both exam questions, asked of every player, written down. Cut: the six weeks, to one sentence each.

CHAPTER 2 — TEN PAIRS · Levels 1-3
2 · Ten Names on the Board — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: read the ten pairs and then stop talking. Cut: the pair-by-pair introductions.
3 · Battle Centre III, first half — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: a PC pair discovers a combination nobody planned. Cut: every match with no PC in it.
4 · Battle Centre III, second half + Nobara Forge — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: each pair leaves the lab with one item written on both sheets. Cut: the Technology checks.
5 · Semis and the Final — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: the photograph. Cut: one of the two semi-finals.
6 · A Question at the Gate — prep 25 min. THE ONE THING: the class cannot legally act and has to stand there. Cut: nothing.
Heights Alliance and The Common Room Ticker are woven through all five and cost no session.

CHAPTER 3 — THE SHORTLIST · Levels 3-5
7 · Six Weeks — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: two named training benefits per PC, written on the sheet. Cut: to twenty minutes and run Day One after it.
8 · Day One, the Obstacle Course — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: the commentary. Cut: the fourth obstacle.
9 · Day Two, the Cavalry Battle — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: the Moshita Maro segment, in full, warmly. Cut: to one phase and a scoreboard.
10 · Day Three, the Paired Tournament — prep 25 min. THE ONE THING: a PC answers the interview honestly and it plays beautifully. Cut: to two matches and the podium.
11 · Kuma at the North Concourse — prep 30 min. THE ONE THING: six thousand civilians on a clock you say out loud. Cut: nothing; this is the chapter's climax.
12 · The Results — prep 10 min, short session. THE ONE THING: "Which of you gave interviews?" Cut: run it as the last twenty minutes of session 11.

CHAPTER 4 — QUESTION ONE · Levels 5-7
13 · Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth — prep 20 min, and re-read your own Chapter 3 commentary. THE ONE THING: the class opens the archive without adult help. Cut: nothing.
14 · Lockdown — prep 10 min, half a session. THE ONE THING: Sugitsu's ten names, and then somebody counts. Cut: to the kitchen and the ten names, fifteen minutes.
15 · Riddle at the Perimeter — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: give the question to the player and wait. Cut: run it straight after session 14, same evening.
16 · Powder and Touch up — prep 30 min, may run to two. THE ONE THING: somebody says "kill the healer." Cut: the trap phase.
17 · The Crows — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: they find the girl alive. Cut: two of the three parallel searches.
18 · Kuma, Interviewed — prep 10 min, half a session. THE ONE THING: the carpet line, thrown away. Cut: entirely — Okuma delivers it in a briefing.
19 · Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It — prep 30 min. THE ONE THING: roll 15d12 in the open, then roll call. Cut: nothing.

CHAPTER 5 — KEEPSAKE · Levels 7-8
20 · Nine Days — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: Rawagi's eleven seconds, and the class being told they are not part of what happens next. Cut: keep it short on purpose.
21 · The Shirahige Cold Store — prep 30 min, plus drawing one floor plan. THE ONE THING: enforce the silence the first time somebody shouts. Cut: floors, freely — eleven is a feeling, not a count.
22 · The Question You Don't Answer — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: the silence while they decide. Cut: nothing; it is twenty minutes long.
23 · Keepsake — prep 40 min, likely two sessions. THE ONE THING: Carlos Might points at Kinji Hamakida. Cut: two of Sylar's borrowed quirks.
24 · Help Woman's Office — prep 5 min, short session. THE ONE THING: a closing beat for every PC, round the table. Cut: nothing, and keep it under half an hour.

THE SHORT VERSION, if you want ten sessions: 1, 2, 3, 6, then all of Chapter 3, then 13, 15, 19, then all of Chapter 5. Nothing structural is lost.

appendix.heading: The table cheat sheet
appendix.body:
One page, for during play. Everything here is stated somewhere in the module; this is where you look when somebody is waiting for an answer.

THE PAIR RULE — the campaign's spine and the only house rule it needs. A PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner has advantage on the roll. Say it out loud in the first fight and use it in every fight after. In the finale it is the difference between winning and not.

RECURRING DCs
· Riddle's Question One — DC 14 Intelligence to break out, at the end of each of the target's turns. 5 rounds otherwise.
· Sylar's Maw — DC 12 for him to maintain the grab; DC 16 Strength or Dexterity for an ALLY to break it. The victim cannot.
· Touch up's exhaustion clock — 5 heals on one creature in a minute is a rank of exhaustion, plus one per 2 further uses, maximum 5.
· Powder's Burst — Strength save at disadvantage vs DC 15.
· Rawagi's Foresight — DC 14 Constitution or a level of Concussed, every single use.
· Forge building something complicated — Technology or Intelligence vs a DC you set. A failure still costs her the calories and makes something unstable: halved range, damage dice one step down, advantage on saves against it.

THE PCs' OWN CLOCKS — hold these honestly and the campaign runs itself
· Kazama's Steel absorbs 5 × level damage and then shatters; excess carries to his real hit points. Uses reset on a long rest, and after that he is just a guy.
· Izuto's Engine runs on about 32 cups of fluid. Under 8: disadvantage on Constitution saves, damage dice down one step. At 0: quirk off, one level of exhaustion until he drinks.
· Chozen's Stress needs a d20 of 12 or higher as a bonus action, decreasing by 1 per level, and only rises from actually taking damage. Calm removes it.
· Ren's beam costs stamina; sustained full-power use is a Constitution save or self-damage, and pushing past it stuns him until the end of his next turn.
· Toragi's Impact Echo, past level × proficiency uses in a day, is a DC 14 Constitution save or 1d12 true damage.

TRAINING BENEFITS — two per PC from Chapter 3, named, written on the sheet, and usable for the rest of the campaign. Be generous. In Chapters 4 and 5 these are frequently the only things still working.

WHEN YOU DO NOT KNOW — pick a number between 10 and 18, ask for a d20 plus whatever ability sounds right, and go. Consistency beats correctness and nobody will check.

WHEN THE PARTY IS LOSING AND YOU DID NOT MEAN IT — a teacher arrives. There are eleven of them and several are written as dials. Nobody at the table will ever know.

WHEN THE PARTY IS WINNING TOO EASILY — never add hit points mid-fight. Add a civilian, a floor giving way, or a second thing happening somewhere else.

appendix.heading: Hiro — the clues, in order
appendix.body:
The class knows Hiro's body is constructed. What comes out in Chapter 4 is that there is nobody in it. Everything before that is fair play: each of these is literally true, none is a trick, and all of them re-read cleanly afterwards. Plant three or four. Do not press any of them.

CHAPTER 2
1 · Forge measures the whole class for gear and does not use the tape on Hiro. "You I've got." She has the numbers because she built them.
2 · In the play-in he takes a hit that gets a wince out of the stands, does not react, does not check it, and gets up. Nobody calls medical over. This reads as his quirk, and it is not.
3 · A forearm on a bench in the support lab, unattached, wrist finished and fingers not. A third of what Forge builds in that room is a piece of somebody, so it is unremarkable. If asked, she says "spare."
4 · A ground-floor corridor in Heights Alliance with a laundry, a store cupboard and one door at the end. It is Hiro's room. He is upstairs on the sofa.

CHAPTER 3
5 · The booth gives him one line all week — "reinforced physiology of some sort, I'm told" — and it is a guess, and nobody corrects it.
6 · Everybody goes through the medical tent after full contact, because that is the rule. He waits outside it, holding other people's bags.
7 · The journalist works down the line of competitors after the tournament and does not stop at him. Not unkindly; he came twenty-second and there are eleven million people watching.
8 · He is at every meal, at the table, holding a cup, and has never once been seen to drink from it. This has been true since April.

THE ONE THAT IS NOT ABOUT HIM AT ALL
9 · Nobody in Class 1-A knows his family name, and nobody has ever needed to. It is not on the fridge chart, which lists him as "HIRO" in a column of nineteen full names, and Masahata — who is meticulous about this sort of thing — has simply never got round to asking.

CHAPTER 4 — the reveal, in "Lockdown"
10 · Sugitsu names his ten permanent Search slots. Somebody counts, works down the register, and finds that Hiro is not on the list and a student none of them has ever heard of is. He explains why in two flat sentences, in front of him.

IF THEY WORK IT OUT EARLY — let them, immediately, and give them the credit. The campaign loses nothing; the Chapter 5 payoff is entirely unaffected. A table that spotted it will be far more invested in him than a table that was surprised.

IF THEY NEVER ASK HIM ANYTHING — that is a real outcome and you should let it stand. It is the whole point of the character and the campaign is willing to charge for it in Chapter 5.

WHAT IS SAFE TO SHOW THEM — his character sheet, all of it. It says his body is constructed and says nothing else, and every word on it is true.

appendix.heading: Props to make before you start
appendix.body:
Five things, all of them paper, none of them taking more than ten minutes. This campaign is about documentation and it works considerably better when there is some on the table.

1 · THE CASE 9 VICTIM LIST — an index card or a sheet of A4 with five names, quirks, wards and dates. Add to it in front of the players when the sixth arrives. In Chapter 4, write the class's own festival placements underneath in the same handwriting and slide it across. That is the single most effective prop in the module and it costs one pen.

2 · THE FRIDGE CHART — Masahata's laminated bracket prediction, with himself winning. Print it, actually laminate it if you are that sort of person, and update it between sessions: annotated in week two, drawn on in week three, amended in red after the festival, gone in Chapter 4, back up in Chapter 5. Nobody says who put it back.

3 · RIDDLE'S INDEX CARD — after "A Question at the Gate," hand the players a card that says: tall, thin, white hair, scar forehead to chin, no nose, bleeds from the mouth. That is everything they have for two chapters, and they will produce it themselves in Chapter 4 when Kuma complains about a stain on his carpet.

4 · ONE FLOOR OF THE COLD STORE — hand-drawn, deliberately plain, on a sheet of paper. Give it to them at the door and tell them it is all eleven floors. Give them a pencil. Let them mark what they have cleared, and when they come out of a stairwell onto a floor they have already been on, say nothing and let them find it on their own map.

5 · THE CLASS PHOTOGRAPH — you do not need an image. You need four or five sentences describing it, written down and read out identically all three times you use it: on the steps in Chapter 2, on the table after roll call in Chapter 4, and in the epilogue. Same words every time. It has everybody in it.

AND ONE THING THAT IS NOT A PROP — the commentary. Write your lines down as you invent them in Chapter 3 and keep the sheet, because in Chapter 4 you are going to read them back word for word and there is no substitute for having actually said them when everyone was happy.

background.heading: Start Here — If You Have Never Run A Campaign Before
background.body:
This module is written so that you can run it having read one chapter, not all five. Here is the whole job.

WHAT A DM ACTUALLY DOES — you describe a situation, the players say what their characters do, and you tell them what happens. That is it. Everything below is support for those three steps.

WHAT TO READ BEFORE SESSION ONE — this page, the page after it, Chapter 1's intro, and all three of its sections. Chapter 1 is short and has no combat in it. That is about fifteen minutes of reading. Do not read Chapters 4 and 5 yet; they will make more sense after you have run the bracket, and there is nothing in them you need early.

WHAT TO DO IN THE SESSION — read the ▶ OPENING block out loud. Ask "what do you do?" Listen. Use the bullet points in the body as a list of things that are available, not a running order. When the players do something you did not expect, look at the 🔀 Developments box, which exists specifically for that.

THE THREE RULES THAT MATTER MOST
1. You are allowed to say yes. If a player has a good idea that is not in this document, let it work. Nothing here breaks.
2. You are allowed to cut. If a scene is dragging, end it and move to the next one. Every section in this campaign says where you can cut.
3. You are allowed to be wrong. If you forget a rule or contradict yourself, say so, pick an answer, and carry on. Nobody at the table minds nearly as much as you think.

WHAT YOU CANNOT GET WRONG — the plot. Appetite does what it does regardless of whether the players investigate well. The campaign has no puzzle that must be solved for the story to continue. If your table misses something, an adult raises it a session later. You will find that written into the Developments boxes throughout.

Every section of every chapter is built the same way, in the same order, and each coloured box has one job.

📖 READ ALOUD — text for the players. Read it out or paraphrase it; both are fine, and paraphrasing is often better. Blocks marked ▶ are separate moments, not one continuous speech. ▶ OPENING is how the scene starts. The others are for specific things that may or may not happen — read a block when the moment it names arrives, and skip the ones that do not. You will not use every block in every session and you are not supposed to.

📄 BODY — what is actually in the scene, as a list of available beats. This is not a script and not an order of events. Players will take these out of sequence. That is normal and nothing is lost by it.

🔀 DEVELOPMENTS — what to do when the players go off-plan. If you are ever stuck mid-session, this is the box to look at. It covers the obvious wrong turns, the clever ideas, the scene going too long, and the scene falling flat.

💰 TREASURE — what the players come away with. Often information, standing, or equipment rather than money. Several sections deliberately give nothing, and say so.

🎲 DM NOTE — why the scene is built this way and how to pitch it. Read this before the session, not during.

AND THE EXTRA CALLOUT at the bottom of some sections is a specific piece of setup, a running joke to plant, or a warning about a thing that is easy to get wrong.

The Appendix at the end of this module holds the reference material you will want at the table: the bracket, the festival format, the villains' tactics, the staff list, and a set of notes on running combat, pacing and safety.
background.heading: How To Read This Document
U.A. High School
background.body:
Japan's most prestigious hero-track school, sitting in its own walled campus on Tokyo's western edge. Entry is brutally competitive and the entrance exam is genuinely dangerous. Class 1-A is the flagship hero cohort — twenty students the rest of the country watches and resents a little.

Heights Alliance, the dorms — one room each, shared kitchen, shared living room, shared laundry, shared grievances. Most of this campaign's downtime happens on that sofa.

Battle Centres I through VII — numbered training grounds with different environments. City block, forest, industrial yard, interior combat. The 2v2 bracket runs in III and V.

The Support Lab — Nobara Forge's domain, currently full of half-finished paired equipment and a lot of empty food containers.

background.heading: Tokyo, and the thing in it
background.body:
The city is fine. That is worth saying plainly, because it stays fine for a long time in this campaign. Hero agencies have branded storefronts in Shibuya, the rankings run on the big screens between adverts, and being a hero is genuinely, uncomplicatedly cool.

In the spring before term, a mid-ranked pro called Tsuzuri Hane — hero name Falsework, a Rare-class construction quirk, twenty-nine years old, eleven years on the boards — was found in a car park in Adachi with the top of his skull removed and nothing else about him disturbed. His wallet was on him. His car was locked.

Four more followed over six months. All quirk users. All Rare or above. All found tidy.

The press called it Case 9 after the file number leaked. Then a tabloid ran the word Appetite across a front page and that stuck instead.

Not an organisation. There is no manifesto, no territory, no branding, no recruitment. There is a man who eats brains to take quirks, and there are four people around him because he needs four people around him.

Sylar — Ken Reed — is six foot eight and slim, with an enormous set of indestructible metal teeth and a jaw he can dislocate at will. He is cold in a way that does not perform coldness. He cannot hold a conversation for long without the urge overtaking him, so mostly he doesn't have them.

Riddle, Powder, Touch up and Kuma are not his equals and are not pretending to be. Riddle finds and holds. Powder opens. Touch up puts Powder back together. Kuma is loud somewhere else while it happens.

The Commission's working profile is four pages long and gets one thing badly wrong: it assumes he selects for power. He selects for *documentation*. He takes quirks he has seen used properly, repeatedly, on camera, with commentary explaining what they do.
background.heading: Appetite

background.body:
Three days, forty thousand seats, and the largest live audience for anything in Japan that isn't a New Year broadcast. Every first-year competes. Agencies scout from it. Careers begin at it.

It is also, and nobody has ever framed it this way before, a complete technical catalogue. Every student demonstrates their quirk repeatedly under pressure, at range, against varied opposition, with professional commentary explaining the mechanism, the limits, and the weakness — because good commentary explains the weakness. It is archived. It is searchable. It is free.

Sylar has watched it every year for nine years. Four of the five Case 9 victims competed in one.
background.heading: The Sports Festival

background.body:
Nobara Forge's assessment for the first term is a 2v2 bracket: ten pairs she assigns herself, single elimination, no substitutions, no negotiation.

Her stated reason is equipment. Gear built for a pair is not gear built for a person, and she cannot design for twenty students who all think they are the protagonist. Her unstated reason is that she has read the entrance exam footage the way a Creation user reads anything — as a materials problem — and concluded that Class 1-A is twenty excellent components that have never been assembled.

Ebina and the 1-B staff watch the bracket, argue about it for a fortnight, and push the festival committee to run the final tournament as pairs too. The committee agrees because it will look good on television.

Nobody involved in that decision knows they have just made the catalogue twice as informative.

One of her twenty is not, strictly, in the room. Read "The student who is not in the room" below before session one, and then put it away until Chapter 4.
background.heading: The pairing experiment
The staff room
background.body:
U.A.'s teaching staff are, individually, some of the most capable quirk users in the country, and collectively a slightly chaotic group of adults who have to share a kettle.

The principal, Sugitsu Jarvichi, can locate and read up to a hundred people across five miles and permanently store the details of ten. This is the safest school in Japan and every member of staff knows it and says so, frequently, right up until the point where it stops being true.

The homeroom teacher for 1-A is Nobara Forge, who eats ten pounds of food a day as a professional requirement and is completely unembarrassed about it.

One of them is a panda. He teaches maths. He is very good at it.

First-years hold no licence. Quirk use outside sanctioned training or a declared emergency is an offence, and the school is liable for it, which is why every teacher in this campaign spends real time on the question of what the class is permitted to do.

By Chapter 4 that question stops being administrative. The class will know things the Commission does not, will be told to stay on campus, and will have to decide what that instruction is worth.

The campaign's position is that staying on campus is often correct, and that the adults giving the order are neither cowards nor fools. Sugitsu in particular is right far more often than the class wants him to be.
background.heading: Provisional status and what the students can actually do

background.body:
There is no syndicate, no faction war, no ideological movement, and no city-wide conspiracy. Nobody is trying to overthrow hero society and nobody makes a speech about the system.

The whole plot is one man's appetite and four people's willingness to service it, and the reason it works on Class 1-A specifically is that Class 1-A spent two chapters becoming worth eating.

Run it as a school story that a horror film walks into halfway through.
background.heading: What this campaign is not
The student who is not in the room
background.body:
Read this once and then put it away until Chapter 4. Nothing in it appears anywhere the players can reach.

THE CLASS HAS A STUDENT CALLED HIRO. His quirk is registered as Doll: a body that was made rather than grown, jointed, dense and insensate. He does not bleed, tire, eat or feel pain, Nobara Forge maintains him, and he is in the support lab most Thursdays. All of that is true, all of it is on his sheet, and the class has known it since April.

THERE IS NO HIRO. There is a frame, and there is a girl called OTOWA SUZUME, and she has never been in the building.

Her quirk is Proxy. She pilots the frame from up to a mile away with full sight, hearing and speech and no sense of touch or pain, and her own body has been in a ground-floor room in Heights Alliance since term started — because Proxy came in at three years old, and a child who could be somewhere else was somewhere else more or less constantly, and that has a bill. She is entirely matter-of-fact about it. So is the school. So is her file.

The frame is a machine built to a design, not a portrait of anybody, and she has never given the class a reason to think about that either way. The voice is hers. They have been listening to it since April.

WHAT THE CLASS KNOWS — that Hiro is a doll. What they have never thought to ask is whether anybody is in it, because why would you. Her name is on the school register and not one member of Class 1-A has ever read it.

WHY SHE IS IN THIS CAMPAIGN — because a man is watching eleven hours of broadcast footage and building files on children, and there is one first-year in the year whose footage is of an empty machine. She is the campaign's thesis with a face on: the archive is a catalogue of bodies, and hers is not in it.

WHAT SHE COSTS THE PLAYERS — nothing, until Chapter 5, when the frame stops at the campus gate and she is the only member of Class 1-A who has to sit in a room and listen to the finale happen a mile away.

HOW TO PLAY HIM BEFORE CHAPTER 4 — as a quiet classmate who is always there and never eating, and whose constructed body is old news to everybody. Every clue in Chapters 2 and 3 is literally true, none of them is a trick, and all of them re-read cleanly afterwards. They are listed in "Hiro — the clues, in order" in the appendix. Plant three or four, do not press, and let the table find it or not.

THE REVEAL is in "Lockdown," in Chapter 4, and it comes from the principal as an administrative fact about slot allocation, in front of him, and Hiro is entirely unbothered by it.

campaigns.tone: A horror-edged U.A. campaign built around a single cruel piece of logic: the Sports Festival is the largest public catalogue of individually demonstrated quirks in Japan, and someone has been reading it. Chapters 2 and 3 are bright, competitive and genuinely fun — a class tournament, a national broadcast, forty first-years trying to be famous. Chapters 4 and 5 are the bill for that. The class's own ambition is what puts them on the list, and no amount of winning gets them off it. Comedy stays in the building the whole way through — this is a school with a maths teacher who is a panda — which is exactly what makes the quiet chapters land.
campaigns.tagline: Win the Sports Festival and the whole country learns your name. So does he.
